prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Rarity precedes extinction

info.statement: Species generally become rare before they become extinct, as seen in recent Tertiary formations and in animals exterminated by humans.
info.quote: We see in many cases in the more recent tertiary formations, that rarity precedes extinction; and we know that this has been the progress of events with those animals which have been exterminated, either locally or wholly, through man’s agency.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: In later geological periods new species have roughly balanced extinctions

info.statement: The number of species has not increased indefinitely, at least in the later geological periods, so the production of new forms has caused the extinction of about the same number of old forms.
info.quote: so that looking to later times we may believe that the production of new forms has caused the extinction of about the same number of old forms.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: New descendants mainly exterminate their parent species and closest relatives

info.statement: Because competition is most severe between the most similar forms, the improved descendants of a species generally cause the extinction of the parent species and of its nearest allies in the same genus.
info.quote: Hence the improved and modified descendants of a species will generally cause the extermination of the parent-species; and if many new forms have been developed from any one species, the nearest allies of that species, _i.e._ the species of the same genus, will be the most liable to extermination.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world

info.statement: The forms of marine life change almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense, throughout the world, so that formations in distant regions under different climates can be correlated by their fossils.
info.quote: Scarcely any palæontological discovery is more striking than the fact, that the forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms

info.statement: As a general rule, the older a fossil form is, the more it differs from living forms.
info.quote: The more ancient any form is, the more, as a general rule, it differs from living forms.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Extinct forms fill gaps between existing genera, families and orders

info.statement: All fossils can be classed in existing groups or between them, and extinct forms fill up the wide intervals between existing genera, families and orders, forming with living forms one natural system.
info.quote: That the extinct forms of life help to fill up the wide intervals between existing genera, families, and orders, cannot be disputed.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Older members of distinct groups differ less from each other than living members

info.statement: Groups that have changed much over known geological periods should, in older formations, approach each other slightly, so that their older members differ from each other in fewer characters than their living members do.
info.quote: All that we have a right to expect, is that those groups, which have within known geological periods undergone much modification, should in the older formations make some slight approach to each other; so that the older members should differ less from each other in some of their characters than do the existing members of the same groups
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones

info.statement: Fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other than fossils from two formations widely separated in time, and the fauna of each period is broadly intermediate between those before and after it.
info.quote: fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other, than are the fossils from two remote formations.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Later faunas would outcompete earlier faunas under similar conditions

info.statement: Because each new species arose by having some advantage over preceding forms, a more recent fauna or flora would beat and exterminate an older one if they were placed in competition under a similar climate, and in this sense recent forms are higher.
info.quote: If under a nearly similar climate, the eocene inhabitants of one quarter of the world were put into competition with the existing inhabitants of the same or some other quarter, the eocene fauna or flora would certainly be beaten and exterminated
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region

info.statement: Within the same continent or area, the extinct forms of the later Tertiary are closely allied to the living inhabitants (e.g. fossil and living marsupials in Australia, edentates in South America), because each area's inhabitants leave modified descendants there.
info.quote: the great law of the long enduring, but not immutable, succession of the same types within the same areas, is at once explained; for the inhabitants of each quarter of the world will obviously tend to leave in that quarter, during the next succeeding period of time, closely allied though in some degree modified descendants.
info.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas

info.statement: Neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of different regions can be explained by their climate and other physical conditions; regions with closely parallel conditions (e.g. Australia, South Africa and western South America at 25°–35° S) have utterly different faunas and floras.
info.quote: the first great fact which strikes us is, that neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of various regions can be accounted for by their climatal and other physical conditions.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Barriers to migration correspond closely to differences between regional biotas

info.statement: Barriers of any kind that obstruct free migration (oceans, isthmuses, mountain ranges, deserts, large rivers) are closely related to the differences between the inhabitants of different regions, and the more impassable and long-standing the barrier, the greater the difference.
info.quote: A second great fact which strikes us in our general review is, that barriers of any kind, or obstacles to free migration, are related in a close and important manner to the differences between the productions of various regions.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Species of the same continent or sea are related despite differing stations

info.statement: The inhabitants of the same continent or sea show a pervasive affinity to one another, so that distinct but related species replace one another from place to place and across different habitats, rather than being replaced by forms from other continents living under similar conditions.
info.quote: A third great fact, partly included in the foregoing statements, is the affinity of the productions of the same continent or sea, though the species themselves are distinct at different points and stations.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The bond linking inhabitants of the same area through space and time is inheritance

info.statement: The deep affinity uniting the living and extinct inhabitants of the same area, independent of physical conditions, is due to inheritance from common ancestors, while the differences among regions arise mainly from modification through natural selection and only subordinately from the direct influence of physical conditions.
info.quote: This bond, on my theory, is simply inheritance, that cause which alone, as far as we positively know, produces organisms quite like, or, as we see in the case of varieties nearly like each other.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Migration or isolation alone does not cause modification

info.statement: Migration and isolation do not by themselves cause modification; a group of competing species that migrates together into a new, isolated country will be little modified, because modification is driven by organisms being brought into new relations with one another.
info.quote: If, for instance, a number of species, which stand in direct competition with each other, migrate in a body into a new and afterwards isolated country, they will be little liable to modification; for neither migration nor isolation in themselves can do anything.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local

info.statement: Some families, many sub-families, very many genera and still more sections of genera are confined to a single region, and the most natural genera (those whose species are most closely related) are generally confined to one area.
info.quote: Some few families, many sub-families, very many genera, and a still greater number of sections of genera are confined to a single region; and it has been observed by several naturalists, that the most natural genera, or those genera in which the species are most closely related to each other, are generally local, or confined to one area.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there

info.statement: Each species was first produced in one area only and subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence allowed under past and present conditions, rather than arising independently at several points.
info.quote: Hence it seems to me, as it has to many other naturalists, that the view of each species having been produced in one area alone, and having subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence under past and present conditions permitted, is the most probable.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Continents and oceanic islands were not united by land in the recent period

info.statement: Although continents have undergone great oscillations of level, separate continents have not been continuously joined to each other and to the existing oceanic islands within the period of existing species, contrary to the land-bridge hypotheses of Forbes and others.
info.quote: But I do not believe that it will ever be proved that within the recent period continents which are now quite separate, have been continuously, or almost continuously, united with each other, and with the many existing oceanic islands.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: About a tenth of a flora's seeds could survive sea-drift across 900 miles

info.statement: Based on flotation and germination experiments, the seeds of roughly 10 per cent of the plants of a flora, after drying, could be floated by sea currents across about 900 miles of sea and still germinate.
info.quote: Therefore it would perhaps be safer to assume that the seeds of about 10/100 plants of a flora, after having been dried, could be floated across a space of sea 900 miles in width, and would then germinate.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents

info.statement: Occasional means of transport (sea currents, birds, drift timber, icebergs) suffice to carry organisms across a few hundred miles of sea, between islands or from a continent to a nearby island, but not between distant continents, so the floras of distant continents remain distinct.
info.quote: These means, however, would suffice for occasional transport across tracts of sea some hundred miles in breadth, or from island to island, or from a continent to a neighbouring island, but not from one distant continent to another.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period

info.statement: The same arctic and alpine species on widely separated mountain summits and in arctic regions are relicts of populations that spread across the intervening lowlands during the Glacial period and were stranded on mountains and in the far north as the climate warmed.
info.quote: Hence, when the warmth had fully returned, the same arctic species, which had lately lived in a body together on the lowlands of the Old and New Worlds, would be left isolated on distant mountain-summits (having been exterminated on all lesser heights) and in the arctic regions of both hemispheres.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land

info.statement: The relationship, with very little identity, between the temperate inhabitants of North America and Europe arises because a common biota inhabited the nearly continuous circumpolar land in warmer Pliocene times and then migrated southward, becoming separated and modified on each continent.
info.quote: On this view we can understand the relationship, with very little identity, between the productions of North America and Europe,—a relationship which is most remarkable, considering the distance of the two areas, and their separation by the Atlantic Ocean.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world

info.statement: The Glacial period, which lasted a very long time at each place, was at least in part simultaneous across the whole world, or at least along broad longitudinal belts from pole to pole, so that global temperature was lower at the same time.
info.quote: If this be admitted, it is difficult to avoid believing that the temperature of the whole world was at this period simultaneously cooler.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Plants of high mountains and temperate lowlands worldwide are identical or closely related

info.statement: Throughout the world, plants growing on high mountains (including tropical ones) and on the temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres are sometimes identical species but much more often distinct yet closely related species.
info.quote: Hence we see that throughout the world, the plants growing on the more lofty mountains, and on the temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres, are sometimes identically the same; but they are much oftener specifically distinct, though related to each other in a most remarkable manner.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Glacial interchange ran mainly north to south because northern forms were more dominant

info.statement: Many more identical and allied plant forms migrated from north to south during the Glacial period than in the reverse direction, because the greater land area of the north and the larger populations there had made northern forms more advanced and dominant through natural selection and competition.
info.quote: I suspect that this preponderant migration from north to south is due to the greater extent of land in the north, and to the northern forms having existed in their own homes in greater numbers, and having consequently been advanced through natural selection and competition to a higher stage of perfection or dominating power, than the southern forms.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse

info.statement: At the present day many European species have become naturalised and partly displaced the natives in La Plata and to a lesser degree in Australia, whereas extremely few southern-hemisphere species have become naturalised anywhere in Europe.
info.quote: Just in the same manner as we see at the present day, that very many European productions cover the ground in La Plata, and in a lesser degree in Australia, and have to a certain extent beaten the natives; whereas extremely few southern forms have become naturalised in any part of Europe,
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period

info.statement: Distinct species of genera confined to the southern hemisphere spread in radiating lines from the antarctic lands, which supported a peculiar flora during a warmer period before the Glacial period, reaching southern America, Australia and New Zealand by occasional transport and former islands.
info.quote: I am inclined to look in the southern, as in the northern hemisphere, to a former and warmer period, before the commencement of the Glacial period, when the antarctic lands, now covered with ice, supported a highly peculiar and isolated flora.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide

info.statement: Despite being separated by land and sea barriers, many fresh-water species of quite different classes have enormous ranges, and allied fresh-water species prevail throughout the world.
info.quote: Not only have many fresh-water species, belonging to quite different classes, an enormous range, but allied species prevail in a remarkable manner throughout the world.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents

info.statement: The same species of fresh-water fish never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents, although within a continent fish species often range widely and irregularly, different river systems sharing some species but not others.
info.quote: In regard to fish, I believe that the same species never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents. But on the same continent the species often range widely and almost capriciously; for two river-systems will have some fish in common and some different.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Water birds disperse seeds and eggs, explaining wide ranges of fresh-water life

info.statement: The wide distribution of fresh-water plants and lower fresh-water animals depends mainly on the transport of their seeds and eggs by animals, especially wide-flying fresh-water birds that move between often distant bodies of water.
info.quote: But the wide distribution of fresh-water plants and of the lower animals, whether retaining the same identical form or in some degree modified, I believe mainly depends on the wide dispersal of their seeds and eggs by animals, more especially by fresh-water birds, which have large powers of flight, and naturally travel from one to another and often distant piece of water.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Oceanic islands have fewer species than equal continental areas

info.statement: Oceanic islands are inhabited by far fewer species of all kinds than continental areas of equal size, a difference not explained by physical conditions.
info.quote: The species of all kinds which inhabit oceanic islands are few in number compared with those on equal continental areas
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species

info.statement: Although oceanic islands have few species, the proportion of their species that are endemic (found nowhere else) is often extremely large relative to their area, as expected if occasional colonists arriving in a new isolated district are especially liable to modification.
info.quote: Although in oceanic islands the number of kinds of inhabitants is scanty, the proportion of endemic species (_i.e._ those found nowhere else in the world) is often extremely large.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Island endemism is low in groups that arrive easily and in numbers

info.statement: Within one island, some groups are almost wholly endemic while others are not, because groups that immigrate readily and in a body (e.g. marine birds, sea-shells, regularly visiting land-birds) keep their mutual relations undisturbed and so are little modified.
info.quote: But it by no means follows, that, because in an island nearly all the species of one class are peculiar, those of another class, or of another section of the same class, are peculiar; and this difference seems to depend on the species which do not become modified having immigrated with facility and in a body, so that their mutual relations have not been much disturbed.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees

info.statement: Because trees rarely reach distant oceanic islands, herbaceous plants that colonise them gain an advantage by growing taller, so natural selection often converts insular herbaceous plants first into bushes and then into trees, explaining why islands have trees in orders that are elsewhere herbaceous.
info.quote: If so, natural selection would often tend to add to the stature of herbaceous plants when growing on an island, to whatever order they belonged, and thus convert them first into bushes and ultimately into trees.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands

info.statement: Batrachians (frogs, toads and newts) are naturally absent from oceanic islands, not because conditions there are unsuitable (introduced frogs thrive) but because they and their spawn are killed by sea-water and so cannot cross the sea.
info.quote: Bory St. Vincent long ago remarked that Batrachians (frogs, toads, newts) have never been found on any of the many islands with which the great oceans are studded. I have taken pains to verify this assertion, and I have found it strictly true.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: No native terrestrial mammals on islands more than 300 miles from a continent

info.statement: No native terrestrial mammal inhabits any island more than about 300 miles from a continent or large continental island, even though small mammals thrive when introduced there, because terrestrial mammals cannot cross wide stretches of sea.
info.quote: as yet I have not found a single instance, free from doubt, of a terrestrial mammal (excluding domesticated animals kept by the natives) inhabiting an island situated above 300 miles from a continent or great continental island;
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species

info.statement: Although terrestrial mammals are absent from oceanic islands, bats occur on almost every island, and remote islands often have their own endemic bat species, because bats can fly across wide spaces of sea and are then modified in their new homes.
info.quote: Though terrestrial mammals do not occur on oceanic islands, ærial mammals do occur on almost every island.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity

info.statement: Somewhat independently of distance, the depth of sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland is related to whether they share the same or allied mammal species: islands separated by shallow channels have the same or very similar mammals, those across deep water have distinct species and genera.
info.quote: there is also a relation, to a certain extent independent of distance, between the depth of the sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland, and the presence in both of the same mammiferous species or of allied species in a more or less modified condition.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent

info.statement: It is an almost universal rule that the endemic species of islands are related to those of the nearest continent or other nearby islands, even when the islands' physical conditions resemble those of a different, more distant region (e.g. Galapagos to America, Cape Verde to Africa).
info.quote: indeed it is an almost universal rule that the endemic productions of islands are related to those of the nearest continent, or of other near islands.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Species on islands of one archipelago are closest relatives of each other

info.statement: The distinct species inhabiting the separate islands of an archipelago are far more closely related to one another than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world, because the islands received immigrants from the same source or from each other.
info.quote: so that the inhabitants of each separate island, though mostly distinct, are related in an incomparably closer degree to each other than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Naturalised species are usually not closely allied to the natives they join

info.statement: Species that become naturalised in new countries are generally not closely allied to the native inhabitants but are very distinct, often belonging to genera absent from the region, whereas closely allied species equally well fitted to their places tend to keep separate.
info.quote: the forms which become naturalised in new countries are not generally closely allied to the aboriginal inhabitants, but are very distinct species, belonging in a large proportion of cases, as shown by Alph. de Candolle, to distinct genera.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Inhabitants of any area are modified colonists from the most accessible source

info.statement: The inhabitants of any area (oceanic islands, mountains, lakes, marshes, caves), where not identical, are plainly related to those of the region from which colonists could most readily have come, the colonists having since been modified and better fitted to their new homes.
info.quote: The principle which determines the general character of the fauna and flora of oceanic islands, namely, that the inhabitants, when not identically the same, yet are plainly related to the inhabitants of that region whence colonists could most readily have been derived,—the colonists having been subsequently modified and better fitted to their new homes,—is of the widest application throughout nature.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species

info.statement: Wherever two regions, however distant, contain many closely allied or representative species, they will also contain some identical species and many doubtful forms ranked variously as species or varieties, showing past migration between them.
info.quote: And it will, I believe, be universally found to be true, that wherever in two regions, let them be ever so distant, many closely allied or representative species occur, there will likewise be found some identical species
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The lower a group of organisms, the more widely it tends to range

info.statement: Organisms lower in the scale of nature tend to range more widely than higher ones, because they change more slowly and their seeds and eggs are minute and suited to distant transport.
info.quote: namely, that the lower any group of organisms is, the more widely it is apt to range.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Closer relatives tend to be closer together in time and space

info.statement: Because forms within each class are connected by ordinary generation, the more closely two forms are related by descent, the nearer they will generally be to each other in time and in geographic space.
info.quote: and the more nearly any two forms are related in blood, the nearer they will generally stand to each other in time and space;
info.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups

info.statement: The nested arrangement of organisms into groups within groups (species within genera, genera within families, and so on) results from the modified descendants of a single progenitor diverging in character while less divergent forms are exterminated.
info.quote: he will see that the inevitable result is that the modified descendants proceeding from one progenitor become broken up into groups subordinate to groups.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The Natural System expresses propinquity of descent

info.statement: The 'something more' than mere resemblance that naturalists seek in the Natural System is closeness of descent, which is the only known cause of similarity among organisms and is partially revealed by classifications.
info.quote: propinquity of descent,—the only known cause of the similarity of organic beings,—is the bond, hidden as it is by various degrees of modification, which is partially revealed to us by our classifications.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Characters least modified by adaptation are most constant and useful in classification

info.statement: The value of a character for classification depends on its constancy across large groups of species, and characters are constant when they have been little changed in adapting species to their conditions of life; hence parts least concerned with special habits are generally the most useful for classification.
info.quote: But their importance for classification, I believe, depends on their greater constancy throughout large groups of species; and this constancy depends on such organs having generally been subjected to less change in the adaptation of the species to their conditions of life.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary

info.statement: The relative value of groups such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families and genera is, at least at present, almost arbitrary, as shown by groups being raised in rank merely because more allied species were discovered.
info.quote: Finally, with respect to the comparative value of the various groups of species, such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families, and genera, they seem to be, at least at present, almost arbitrary.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Branches equally related by descent can differ greatly in amount of modification

info.statement: A natural arrangement of groups must be strictly genealogical, but branches that are equally closely related to a common progenitor may differ greatly in how much they have been modified, and these differing amounts of difference are what is expressed by ranking them as different genera, families or orders.
info.quote: I believe that the _arrangement_ of the groups within each class, in due subordination and relation to the other groups, must be strictly genealogical in order to be natural; but that the _amount_ of difference in the several branches or groups, though allied in the same degree in blood to their common progenitor, may differ greatly, being due to the different degrees of modification which they have undergone
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

nodes.label: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do

info.statement: Domestic and natural varieties fall into groups subordinate to groups (sub-varieties under varieties under species) for the same reason species do, namely closeness of descent combined with various degrees of modification.
info.quote: The origin of the existence of groups subordinate to groups, is the same with varieties as with species, namely, closeness of descent with various degrees of modification.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance

info.statement: However trifling a character, if it occurs throughout many species with very different habits of life it can be explained only by inheritance from a common parent, and so has high value for classification; for the same reason rudimentary structures can be as useful as other parts.
info.quote: if it prevail throughout many and different species, especially those having very different habits of life, it assumes high value; for we can account for its presence in so many forms with such different habits, only by its inheritance from a common parent.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form

info.statement: Animals from very distinct lines of descent can become adapted to similar conditions and so acquire a close external resemblance; such analogical or adaptive resemblances conceal rather than reveal blood-relationship, so they are almost worthless for classification between groups, although the same characters can indicate true affinity within a group.
info.quote: For animals, belonging to two most distinct lines of descent, may readily become adapted to similar conditions, and thus assume a close external resemblance; but such resemblances will not reveal—will rather tend to conceal their blood-relationship to their proper lines of descent.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes

info.statement: Larger and more dominant groups tend to keep increasing in size and to supplant smaller, feebler groups, which is why all organisms, recent and extinct, fall into a few great orders, still fewer classes, and a single natural system.
info.quote: The larger and more dominant groups thus tend to go on increasing in size; and they consequently supplant many smaller and feebler groups. Thus we can account for the fact that all organisms, recent and extinct, are included under a few great orders, under still fewer classes, and all in one great natural system.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction

info.statement: Aberrant or osculant groups are the surviving remnants of failing groups that suffered heavy extinction; consequently they are generally represented by very few species, and those species are usually very distinct from each other.
info.quote: And we have some evidence of aberrant forms having suffered severely from extinction, for they are generally represented by extremely few species; and such species as do occur are generally very distinct from each other, which again implies extinction.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Affinities of one group to another are usually general, not to any single species

info.statement: When a member of one group shows a real affinity to a quite distinct group, the affinity is usually general rather than to any particular species, because it retains characters of an ancient common progenitor of both groups.
info.quote: when a member belonging to one group of animals exhibits an affinity to a quite distinct group, this affinity in most cases is general and not special
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Gaps between groups, even whole classes, are due to extinction of connecting forms

info.statement: Extinction has defined and widened the intervals between groups; even the distinctness of whole classes, such as birds from other vertebrates, results from the loss of many ancient forms that once connected their early progenitors.
info.quote: We may thus account even for the distinctness of whole classes from each other—for instance, of birds from all other vertebrate animals—by the belief that many ancient forms of life have been utterly lost, through which the early progenitors of birds were formerly connected with the early progenitors of the other vertebrate classes.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions

info.statement: Within a class, homologous parts may change to almost any extent in form and size but always remain connected in the same order; for example, the bones of the arm and forearm are never transposed.
info.quote: the parts may change to almost any extent in form and size, and yet they always remain connected together in the same order.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Unity of type reflects a common progenitor's pattern modified by slight steps

info.statement: The shared pattern of homologous organs within a class is explained by descent from an ancient progenitor (an archetype) that already had that pattern, which natural selection then modified by slight successive steps for different uses without transposing parts.
info.quote: If we suppose that the ancient progenitor, the archetype as it may be called, of all mammals, had its limbs constructed on the existing general pattern, for whatever purpose they served, we can at once perceive the plain signification of the homologous construction of the limbs throughout the whole class.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Serially homologous parts derive from many repeated similar elements in progenitors

info.statement: Serial homologies within one individual (skull and vertebrae, jaws and legs of crustaceans, floral parts and leaves) arise because the progenitors of vertebrates, articulates and flowering plants had many repeated similar parts, which natural selection adapted to diverse purposes while inheritance retained a fundamental resemblance.
info.quote: An indefinite repetition of the same part or organ is the common characteristic (as Owen has observed) of all low or little-modified forms; therefore we may readily believe that the unknown progenitor of the vertebrata possessed many vertebræ; the unknown progenitor of the articulata, many segments; and the unknown progenitor of flowering plants, many spiral whorls of leaves.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Embryos of different animals in the same class are strikingly similar

info.statement: Embryos of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar, more so than the adults, and the points of resemblance often have no direct relation to their conditions of existence.
info.quote: The embryos, also, of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Active larvae are adapted to their own conditions as fully as adults

info.statement: Whenever an embryo or larva becomes active and must provide for itself, it is as perfectly adapted to its conditions of life as the adult, and such adaptations can make the larvae of allied species differ as much as or more than their adults, though most larvae still follow the law of embryonic resemblance.
info.quote: The period of activity may come on earlier or later in life; but whenever it comes on, the adaptation of the larva to its conditions of life is just as perfect and as beautiful as in the adult animal.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults

info.statement: The characteristic differences between domestic breeds produced by man's selection (in dogs, horses and pigeons) generally do not appear early in life and are inherited at a corresponding later age, so that the young of different breeds differ far less in proportions than the adults, with occasional exceptions such as the short-faced tumbler pigeon.
info.quote: the characteristic differences which give value to each breed, and which have been accumulated by man’s selection, have not generally first appeared at an early period of life, and have been inherited by the offspring at a corresponding not early period.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent

info.statement: Because the embryo is the animal in a less modified state that partly reveals the structure of its progenitor, two groups that pass through the same or similar embryonic stages are descended from the same or similar parents, however different their adults; this is why embryonic characters are the most valuable for classification.
info.quote: Thus, community in embryonic structure reveals community of descent.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Ancient extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants

info.statement: Since embryos partly show the structure of less modified ancient progenitors, ancient and extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants, though this may be obscured by early-appearing variations and may be undemonstrable because the geological record does not reach back far enough.
info.quote: we can clearly see why ancient and extinct forms of life should resemble the embryos of their descendants,—our existing species.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Embryological facts follow from late-appearing variations inherited at corresponding ages

info.quote: the leading facts in embryology, which are second in importance to none in natural history, are explained on the principle of slight modifications not appearing, in the many descendants from some one ancient progenitor, at a very early period in the life of each, though perhaps caused at the earliest, and being inherited at a corresponding not early period.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

nodes.label: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature

info.quote: Organs or parts in this strange condition, bearing the stamp of inutility, are extremely common throughout nature.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Rudimentary organs are highly variable

info.quote: Rudimentary organs in the individuals of the same species are very liable to vary in degree of development and in other respects.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Rudimentary organs are relatively larger in the embryo than in the adult

info.quote: It is also, I believe, a universal rule, that a rudimentary part or organ is of greater size relatively to the adjoining parts in the embryo, than in the adult
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Disuse is the main cause of rudimentary organs

info.statement: Disuse over successive generations has been the main agency reducing organs to rudiments (as with eyes of cave animals and wings of island birds), aided by natural selection where an organ becomes injurious; because reduction occurs at maturity and is inherited at a corresponding age, rudiments remain relatively larger in the embryo.
info.quote: I believe that disuse has been the main agency; that it has led in successive generations to the gradual reduction of various organs, until they have become rudimentary
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

info.quote: Therefore I cannot doubt that the theory of descent with modification embraces all the members of the same class.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

info.quote: I believe that animals have descended from at most only four or five progenitors, and plants from an equal or lesser number.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

info.quote: Nevertheless all living things have much in common, in their chemical composition, their germinal vesicles, their cellular structure, and their laws of growth and reproduction.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

nodes.label: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form

info.statement: By analogy, probably all organisms that have ever lived on earth have descended from a single primordial form.
info.quote: Therefore I should infer from analogy that probably all the organic beings which have ever lived on this earth have descended from some one primordial form, into which life was first breathed.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

info.quote: Hereafter we shall be compelled to acknowledge that the only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is, that the latter are known, or believed, to be connected at the present day by intermediate gradations, whereas species were formerly thus connected.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

info.quote: the most important of all causes of organic change is one which is almost independent of altered and perhaps suddenly altered physical conditions, namely, the mutual relation of organism to organism,—the improvement of one being entailing the improvement or the extermination of others
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

info.quote: it follows, that the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations probably serves as a fair measure of the lapse of actual time.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

info.quote: During early periods of the earth’s history, when the forms of life were probably fewer and simpler, the rate of change was probably slower; and at the first dawn of life, when very few forms of the simplest structure existed, the rate of change may have been slow in an extreme degree.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Known geological history is a fragment of the time since the first organism

info.quote: The whole history of the world, as at present known, although of a length quite incomprehensible by us, will hereafter be recognised as a mere fragment of time, compared with the ages which have elapsed since the first creature, the progenitor of innumerable extinct and living descendants, was created.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

info.quote: We can so far take a prophetic glance into futurity as to foretel that it will be the common and widely-spread species, belonging to the larger and dominant groups, which will ultimately prevail and procreate new and dominant species.

info.quote: As all the living forms of life are the lineal descendants of those which lived long before the Silurian epoch, we may feel certain that the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken, and that no cataclysm has desolated the whole world.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

nodes.label: Natural selection makes endowments tend towards perfection

info.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion

info.quote: These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms.
