nodes.label: Larger fish can sprint faster but cover similar distances and tire more slowly

info.statement: Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster and have less staying power.
info.quote: the singular result ought to follow that, in swimming for instance, the larger fish ought to be able to put on a spurt of speed far in excess of the smaller one; but the distance travelled by the year’s end should be very much alike for both of them.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3

info.statement: A bird of fixed proportions must fly at a minimum speed proportional to the square root of its linear size, so the work needed for flight varies as the 3½ power of linear size while the work its muscles can supply varies only as the cube; flight thus becomes harder as birds get larger (about 1.4 times harder per doubling of length).
info.quote: The work requiring to be done, then, varies as the power 3½ of the bird’s linear dimensions, while the work of which the bird is capable depends on the mass of its muscles, and therefore varies as the cube of its linear dimensions.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Ostrich and moa have passed the size at which muscular flight is possible

info.statement: The ostrich probably, and the moa certainly, reached a size at which flight by muscular action with ordinary bird anatomy became physiologically impossible, and a bird as large as a man could not fly.
info.quote: It is not improbable that the ostrich has already reached a magnitude, and we may take it for certain that the moa did so, at which flight by muscular action, according to the normal anatomy of a bird, has become physiologically impossible.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere

info.statement: The giant wingspans of Carboniferous dragonflies and the small bodies and huge wings of pterodactyls, which seem beyond present mechanical limits, can be explained if the Carboniferous and Jurassic atmosphere was notably denser, for example through more carbonic acid.
info.quote: we have only to suppose that in carboniferous and jurassic days the terrestrial atmosphere was notably denser than it is at present, by reason, for instance, of its containing a much larger proportion of carbonic acid, and we have at once a means of reconciling the apparent mechanical discrepancy.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size

info.statement: Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.
info.quote: in other words, that all animals, provided always that they are similarly fashioned, with their various levers etc., in like proportion, ought to jump, not to the same relative, but to the same actual height.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking

info.statement: Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.
info.quote: the general result, attained under very different conditions and arrived at by very different modes of reasoning, is in every case that the velocity tends to vary as the square root of the linear dimensions of the organism.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Doubling gravity would make terrestrial animals short-legged or serpent-like

info.statement: The form and actions of terrestrial animals are conditioned by the strength of gravity: if it were doubled, bipedal form would fail and most land animals would resemble short-legged saurians or serpents; if halved, animals would be lighter, more active and need less heart, lungs and blood.
info.quote: Were the force of gravity to be doubled, our bipedal form would be a failure, and the majority of terrestrial animals would resemble short-legged saurians, or else serpents.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass

info.statement: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.
info.quote: Throughout the whole field of morphology we may find examples of a tendency (referable doubtless in each case to some definite physical cause) for surface to keep pace with volume, through some alteration of its form.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres

info.statement: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.
info.quote: In like manner we shall find that the form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity, and largely if not mainly due to the force of surface-tension
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones

info.statement: Large and small organisms differ in kind in how form arises: in large organisms form is the direct result of unequal growth rates in different directions, but in minute organisms and individual cells intermolecular forces outweigh gravity and form is not simply correlated with growth.
info.quote: But it is by no means true that form and growth are in this direct and simple fashion correlative or complementary in the case of minute portions of living matter.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass

info.statement: Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.
info.quote: In short, however it may be brought about, the phenomenon of division of the cell will be precisely what is required to keep approximately constant the ratio between surface and mass, and to restore the balance between the surface-energy and the other energies of the system.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Cells of each kind vary little about a mean size, whatever the body size

info.statement: Cells of each kind vary little about a characteristic mean size and have absolute size limits, so dwarf and giant individuals of a species (e.g. Crepidula, sea-urchin larvae) differ in cell number rather than cell size.
info.quote: An immediate and remarkable result of the principles just described is a tendency on the part of all cells, according to their kind, to vary but little about a certain mean size, and to have, in fact, certain absolute limitations of magnitude.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells

info.statement: Across animals large and small, ganglion (nerve) cells vary in size only within narrow limits, and smaller species have simpler ganglia containing fewer cells than larger species.
info.quote: we may (with Enriques) lay it down as a general law that among animals, whether large or small, the ganglion-cells vary in size within narrow limits; and that, amidst all the great variety of structural type of ganglion observed in different classes of animals, it is always found that the smaller species have simpler ganglia than the larger, that is to say ganglia containing a smaller number of cellular elements.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller

info.statement: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.
info.quote: it will still be clear that the smallest known bodies which are described as organisms draw nigh towards molecular magnitudes, and we must recognise that the subdivision of the organism cannot proceed to an indefinite extent, and in all probability cannot go very much further than it appears to have done in these already discovered forms.
info.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions

info.statement: Except for certain very minute organisms whose form is set directly by molecular forces, the external form of an organism is accounted for by the ratio between its rates of growth in different directions.
info.quote: It is the ratio between the rates of growth in various directions by which we must account for the external forms of all, save certain very minute, organisms.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Constant growth-rate ratios preserve form; changing ratios produce development

info.statement: When the ratio between growth rates in different directions stays constant, an organism grows in bulk with little or no change of form; such constancy seldom lasts more than a season, and when the ratio alters the organism undergoes development, a steady and persistent change of form.
info.quote: It may sometimes be a very _constant_ one, in which case the organism, while growing in bulk, suffers little or no perceptible change in form; but such equilibrium seldom endures for more than a season, and when the _ratio_ tends to alter, then we have the phenomenon of morphological “development,” or steady and persistent change of form.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet

info.statement: The foldings of the blastoderm that produce the neural and amniotic folds result from unequal rates of growth, local accelerations and retardations, in what is at first an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue, in the way that a sheet buckles when parts of it expand or contract.
info.quote: the various foldings of the blastoderm, by which the neural and amniotic folds were brought into being, were essentially and obviously the resultant of unequal rates of growth,—of local accelerations or retardations of growth,—in what to begin with was an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Differences between related forms emerge gradually and are small in the young

info.statement: Because form differences are attained by growth at specific velocities over long periods, differences between any two related individuals or species must appear gradually and be little apparent in the young, and animals of very different adult size differ less and less in size and form when traced back through foetal stages.
info.quote: it is accordingly obvious that in any two related individuals (whether specifically identical or not) the differences between them must manifest themselves gradually, and be but little apparent in the young. It is for the same simple reason that animals which are of very different sizes when adult, differ less and less in size (as well as in form) as we trace them backwards through the foetal stages.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens

info.statement: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.
info.quote: The curve of growth for length or stature in man indicates a rapid increase at the outset, that is to say during the quick growth of babyhood; a long period of slower, but still rapid and almost steady growth in early boyhood; as a rule a marked quickening soon after the boy is in his teens, when he comes to “the growing age”
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Adult human stature declines well before fifty and markedly by old age

info.statement: Full adult stature in man lasts only for a time: it begins to decrease well before fifty, is notably lessened by sixty, and is much reduced in extreme old age, so that growth takes a negative value.
info.quote: We should see that a man’s full stature endures but for a spell; long before fifty it has begun to abate, by sixty it is notably lessened, in extreme old age the old man’s frame is shrunken and it is but a memory that “he once was tall.”
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth

info.statement: Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.
info.quote: whatever be the law of increment in a linear dimension, the law of increase in volume, and therefore in weight, will be that these latter magnitudes tend to vary as the cubes of the linear dimensions.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase

info.statement: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.
info.quote: In short, throughout all this period, it is a very _similar_ curve in the two sexes; but it has its notable differences, in amplitude and especially in _phase_.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown

info.statement: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.
info.quote: Whether the animal be long-lived, as man or the elephant, or short-lived, like horse or dog, it passes through the same phases of growth. In all cases growth begins slowly; it attains a maximum velocity early in its course, and afterwards slows down (subject to temporary accelerations) towards a point where growth ceases altogether.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically

info.statement: In cold-blooded animals such as fishes the slowing of growth is greatly protracted, so that size seems never to reach a maximum but only to approach a limit asymptotically.
info.quote: But especially in the cold-blooded animals, such as fishes, the slowing-down period is very greatly protracted, and the size of the creature would seem never actually to reach, but only to approach asymptotically, to a maximal limit.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth

info.statement: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).
info.quote: The size ultimately attained is a resultant of the rate, and of the duration, of growth. It is in the main true, as Minot has said, that the rabbit is bigger than the guinea-pig because he grows the faster; but that man is bigger than the rabbit because he goes on growing for a longer time.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth

info.statement: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.
info.quote: It will at once be seen that there is a “point of inflection” somewhere about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: up to that date growth proceeds with a continually increasing velocity; but after that date, though growth is still rapid, its velocity tends to fall away.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth

info.statement: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.
info.quote: We see, in short, that the amount of _variability_ in stature or in weight is a function of the _rate of growth_ in these magnitudes, though we are not yet in a position to equate the terms precisely, one with another.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Growth rate is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, metamorphosis

info.statement: Curves of growth show well-marked interruptions or changes of rate at physiological epochs such as birth and puberty, in man and in other animals, and most strikingly in animals that undergo a regular metamorphosis.
info.quote: Just as the human curve of growth has its slight but well-marked interruptions, or variations in rate, coinciding with such epochs as birth and puberty, so is it with other animals, and this phenomenon is particularly striking in the case of animals which undergo a regular metamorphosis.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Metamorphosis is often, perhaps always, accompanied by loss of bulk and weight

info.statement: Negative growth, an actual loss of bulk and weight, often and perhaps always accompanies metamorphosis, as in the eel, the silkworm before pupation and the frog tadpole.
info.quote: The negative growth, or actual loss of bulk and weight which often, and perhaps always, accompanies metamorphosis, is well shewn in the case of the eel.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain

info.statement: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.
info.quote: It is plain, then, that there is no simple and direct relation, holding good _throughout life_, between the size of the body as a whole and that of the organs we have just discussed; and the changing ratio of magnitude is especially marked in the case of the brain
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity

info.statement: In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.
info.quote: we see that _k_ is by no means constant, but steadily increases to a maximum, and afterwards slowly declines with the increasing size of the fish
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning

info.statement: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.
info.quote: With unchanging length, the weight and therefore the bulk of the fish falls off from about November to March or April, and again between May or June and November the bulk and weight are gradually restored. The explanation is simple, and depends wholly on the process of spawning, and on the subsequent building up again of the tissues and the reproductive organs.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends

info.statement: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.
info.quote: a very large part of the specific morphology of the organism depends upon the fact that there is not only an average, or aggregate, rate of growth common to the whole, but also a variation of rate in different parts of the organism, tending towards a specific rate characteristic of each different part or organ.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C

info.statement: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.
info.quote: this optimum temperature is very much the same for all the common plants of our own climate which have as yet been studied; in them it is somewhere about 26° C. (or say 77° F.), or about the temperature of a warm summer’s day
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction

info.statement: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).
info.quote: Van’t Hoff’s law, which has become a fundamental principle of chemical mechanics, is likewise applicable (with certain qualifications) to the phenomena of vital chemistry; and it follows that, on very much the same lines, we may speak of the “temperature coefficient” of growth.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage

info.statement: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.
info.quote: It would seem to be this double effect of temperature in the case of the organism which gives us our “optimum” curves, which are the expression, accordingly, not of a primary phenomenon, but of a more or less complex resultant.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve

info.statement: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.
info.quote: in short, our phenomenon is simply expressed by what is known as a “damped sine-curve.” Exactly the same thing occurs in man, though neither in his case nor in that of the fish have we sufficient data for its complete illustration.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity

info.statement: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.
info.quote: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism

info.quote: A large part of the phenomenon of growth, both in animals and still more conspicuously in plants, is associated with “turgor,” that is to say, is dependent on osmotic conditions; in other words, the velocity of growth depends in great measure (as we have already seen, p. 113) on the amount of water taken up into the living cells
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water

info.statement: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.
info.quote: _Pari passu_ with these changes, there is a marked change in the relative lengths of the fore and hind portions of the body, that is to say, of the “cephalothorax” and abdomen: the latter growing relatively longer, the salter the water.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis

info.statement: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can yet be asserted.
info.quote: it is sufficiently clear that the normal “curve of growth” of an organism, in all its general features, very closely resembles the velocity-curve of chemical autocatalysis.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions

info.statement: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
info.quote: We may take it, then, as an established fact, whose full extent and bearings are still awaiting investigation, that there exist substances both within and without the organism which have a marvellous power of accelerating growth, and of doing so in such a way as to affect not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Natural selection removes forms rather than originating them

info.statement: Since forms, including exaggerated ones such as the great Secondary reptiles and Tertiary mammals, can arise from changes in growth, natural selection is needed to explain their disappearance rather than their appearance; in general its function is not to originate but to remove.
info.quote: And we then, I think, draw near to the conclusion that what is true of these is universally true, and that the great function of natural selection is not to originate, but to remove
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

info.quote: And in this particular case, the equation _V_ _T_^2 = constant, holds very nearly true; that is to say the velocity varies, or tends to vary, inversely as the square of the time.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

info.statement: Regeneration is a particular case of growth obeying the same laws; the regeneration curve (short latent period, rapid rise to a maximum velocity, then slow decline) only appears different because ordinary growth curves start at birth, and a complete growth curve from zero has the same essential features.
info.quote: A complete curve of growth, starting from zero, has the same essential characteristics as the regeneration curve.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Claw reversal after amputation depends on regeneration versus growth rates

info.quote: It depends upon the respective rates of growth, upon a ratio between the rate of regeneration and the rate of growth of the uninjured limb
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

info.quote: If we add to this natural tendency towards fission of a cylindrical or tubular worm, the ordinary phenomenon of regeneration, we have all that is essentially implied in “reproduction by fission.”
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Growth velocity peaks and falls because surface resistance suddenly increases

info.statement: The abrupt change from increasing to decreasing growth velocity is more likely due to a sudden increase of resistance, such as the formation of a comparatively firm skin during histological differentiation, than to a decline of internal growth forces; the later slowing reflects waning growth forces against rising superficial resistance.
info.quote: I take it that the sudden arrest of velocity is much more likely to be due to a sudden increase of resistance than to a sudden diminution of internal energies: in other words, I suspect that it is coincident with some notable event of histological differentiation, such as the rapid formation of a comparatively firm skin
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

info.statement: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of recapitulation.
info.quote: From one form, or ratio of magnitude, to another there is but one straight and direct road of transformation, be the journey taken fast or slow; and if the transformation take place at all, it will in all likelihood proceed in the self-same way, whether it occur within the life-time of an individual or during the long ancestral history of a race.
info.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

info.quote: In short it would seem evident that, except in relation to a dynamical investigation, the mere study of cell structure has but little value of its own.
info.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

info.quote: So long as the fluid substance of the nucleus is qualitatively different from, and incapable of mixing with, the fluid or semi-fluid protoplasm which surrounds it, we shall expect it to be, as it almost always is, of spherical form.

info.quote: The so-called “secretion” of this cell-wall is nothing more than a sort of exudation, or striving towards the surface, of certain constituent molecules or particles within the cell; and the Gibbs-Thomson law formulates, in part at least, the conditions under which they do so.

info.statement: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.
info.quote: for the actual _precipitation_ takes place, as a rule, not in actively living, but in dead or at least inactive tissue: that is to say in the “formed material” or matrix which (as for instance in cartilage) accumulates round the living cells

nodes.label: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms

info.statement: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.
info.quote: the eggs of sea-urchins reared in lime-free water develop in apparent health, into larvae entirely destitute of the usual skeleton of calcareous rods, and in which, accordingly, the long arms of the Pluteus larva, which the rods support and distend, are entirely suppressed.

nodes.label: Biological molecular asymmetry may originate from circularly polarised sunlight

info.statement: The one-handed molecular asymmetry of organic products need not be a prerogative of life; it may have started from a non-vital asymmetric force, such as sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea, which acts unequally on right- and left-handed molecules.
info.quote: an example limited but yet crucial (_if confirmed_), of an asymmetric force, non-vital in its origin, which might conceivably be the starting-point of that asymmetry which is characteristic of so many organic products.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Pearls and bony-fish otoliths share the structure of artificial calcospherites

info.statement: The concentrically zoned, radiate structure of pearls and of the otoliths of molluscs and bony fishes is essentially the same as that of the calcospherites formed artificially when calcium carbonate is precipitated in albumin, implying the same physico-chemical mode of formation.
info.quote: The typical structure of a calcospherite is no other than that of a pearl, nor does it differ essentially from that of the otolith of a mollusc or of a bony fish.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons

info.statement: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.
info.quote: it is at least obvious, with the Liesegang phenomenon in view, that we have no right to _assume_ that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily bound up with, and indubitably brought about by, a periodic recurrence of particular _external_ conditions.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down

info.statement: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.
info.quote: The probability is, therefore, that the actual precipitation of the calcium salts is not due to the direct action of carbonic acid, etc. on a more soluble salt (as was at one time believed); but to catabolic changes in the proteids of the organism, which tend to throw down the salts already formed, which had remained hitherto in albuminous solution.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics

info.statement: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.
info.quote: The effect of _scale_, then, of which we had so much to say in our introductory chapter on Magnitude, is bound to be apparent in the study of skeletal fabrics, and to lead to essential differences between the big and the little, the massive and the minute, in regard to their controlling forces and their resultant forms.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic

info.statement: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.
info.quote: let us suppose that it is confined either within a cell-wall or in adhesion thereto; it at once follows that its line of growth will be simply a geodetic to the surface of the cell.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Like spicules in silica and calcite show form is set by external forces, not chemistry

info.statement: Holothurian spicules of calcium carbonate reproduce, often indistinguishably, the forms of siliceous sponge spicules, which shows that such spicule forms are determined by the external forces acting during growth (cell confinement), not by the chemical nature or molecular structure of the material.
info.quote: the Holothurian spicules are composed of calcium carbonate while those which we have just described in the case of sponges are usually, if not always, siliceous: this being just another proof of the fact that in such cases the form of the spicule is not due to its chemical nature or molecular structure, but to the external forces
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°

info.statement: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.
info.quote: It is plain, accordingly, that in any flattened or stratified assemblage of such cells, a solidified skeletal deposit which originates or accumulates either between the cells or within the thickness of their mutual partitions, will tend to take the form of triradiate bodies, whose rays (in a typical case) will be set at equal angles of 120°
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Six-rayed hexactinellid spicules reflect cubic, not closest, packing of vesicles

info.statement: The six-rayed spicules of hexactinellid sponges form because the vesicles that mould them are arranged in linear series (cubic packing) rather than closest packing, so the spicules follow the angles and edges of a system of cubes instead of hexagons or dodecahedra.
info.quote: the cells or vesicles by which they are conformed are not arranged in what is known as “closest packing,” but in linear series; so that in their arrangement, and by their mutual compression, we tend to get a pattern, not of hexagons, but of squares: or, looking to the solid, not of dodecahedra but of cubes or parallelopipeda.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally

info.statement: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.
info.quote: the distribution of species in space is curious and vague; many species are found all over the world, or at least every here and there, with no evidence of specific limitations of geographical habitat
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Agglutinated protist shells form by surface energy, not choice or skill

info.statement: The building of agglutinated shells from sand-grains, spicules or diatom frustules by rhizopods such as Difflugia is a purely physical consequence of foreign particles being trapped in the surface film by surface energy, with selectivity explained by specific surface-energies rather than volition.
info.quote: The formation of an “agglutinated” shell is thus seen to be a purely physical phenomenon, and indeed a special case of a more general physical phenomenon which has many other important consequences in biology.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles

info.statement: When the outer surface of a radiolarian is covered by a layer of nearly equal froth-like vesicles, silica secreted or adsorbed at the surface collects in the grooves between them, producing a spherical shell of rods in a regular hexagonal network; less regular vesicles give less regular meshes, and repeated layers give concentric shells.
info.quote: it will at once follow that they will show a tendency to aggregate in the grooves which separate the vesicles, and the result will be the development of a most delicate sphere composed of tiny rods arranged in a regular hexagonal network
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles

info.statement: Spherical hexagonal lattice shells are equally regular whether made of silica (oceanic Radiolaria), strontium sulphate (Acantharia) or an organic chitin-like substance (Clathrulina), showing that their form comes from moulding on an underlying vesicular structure, not from the material.
info.quote: This is only another proof (if proof be needed) that the peculiar conformation of these little skeletons is not due to the material of which they are composed, but to the moulding of that material upon an underlying vesicular structure.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Callimitra's skeleton is formed on the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of four cells

info.statement: The skeleton of the nassellarian Callimitra reproduces the interfacial film system of four soap-bubbles in tetrahedral contact (six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120°, edges meeting near 109°), so it must have been formed at the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of cells.
info.quote: It is obvious at a glance that this is such a skeleton as may have been formed (I think we may go so far as to say _must_ have been formed) at the interfaces of a little tetrahedral group of cells
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Regular dodecahedral radiolarian shells cannot arise by crystal-like space partitioning

info.statement: Radiolaria show all five regular polyhedra, including the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron which cannot occur in crystals; therefore the regular radiolarian dodecahedron is not produced by the space-partitioning principles that govern crystallisation.
info.quote: If we may safely judge from Haeckel’s figures, the pentagonal dodecahedron of the Radiolarian is perfectly regular, and we must presume, accordingly, that it is not brought about by principles of space-partitioning similar to those which manifest themselves in the phenomenon of crystallisation.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement

info.statement: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.
info.quote: The true symmetry of this figure, then, is hexagonal, with a polar axis, produced into two polar spicules; with six equatorial spicules, or rays; and with two sets of six spicular rays, interposed between the polar axis and the equatorial rays, and alternating in position with the latter.
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics

info.statement: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.
info.quote: But there are no obvious mechanical forces by which we can so explain this peculiar polarity. This at least is evident, that it arises in the central mass of protoplasm, which is the essential living portion of the organism
info.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

nodes.label: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics

info.quote: These three systems are all of frequent occurrence, and are all illustrated in the local thickenings of the wall of the cylindrical cells or vessels of plants.
info.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

nodes.label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex

info.statement: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.
info.quote: In a right cone, the spiral geodetic falls into closer and closer coils as the diameter of the cone narrows; and a very beautiful geodetic of this kind is exemplified in the sutural line of a spiral shell, such as Turritella
info.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

nodes.label: Two crossing systems of geodetic spirals are a common source of reticulated patterns

info.statement: In organic structures two opposite systems of geodetic spirals often coexist and interfere, forming a criss-cross arrangement, and this is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
info.quote: and it is also common to find the two systems interfering with one another, and forming a criss-cross, or reticulated arrangement. This is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
info.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

nodes.label: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves

info.statement: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).
info.quote: Thus the muscular fibres, as they wind over the curved surface of an organ, arrange themselves automatically in geodesic curves: in precisely the same manner as we also automatically construct complex systems of geodesics whenever we wind a ball of wool or a spindle of tow
info.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

nodes.label: Heart and stomach fibres stay geodetic after the twisting of the primitive tube

info.statement: The heart and stomach develop from simple tubes by dilatation and twisting; their originally circular and longitudinal fibres remain geodetic on the distorted surface, new geodetic systems (such as the oblique stomach fibres) appear on new pouches, and the heart contracts effectively only because its fibres run the shortest course.
info.quote: these systems of muscular fibres, geodetic to begin with, remain geodetic (in the sense in which we are using the word) after all the twisting to which the primitive cylindrical tube or tubes have been subjected.
info.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path

info.statement: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.
info.quote: And this axial rotation, just as in the case of a rifle-bullet, causes their natural swerve, which is always in the same direction as regards their own bodies, to be in a continually changing direction as regards space: in short, to make a spiral course around, and more or less approximate to, a straight axial line.
info.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

nodes.label: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral

info.statement: The permanent spiral forms found in organisms, such as the horns of ruminants, molluscan and foraminiferal shells and the arrangement of florets in the sunflower, are all logarithmic spirals; the outline of a cordate leaf is the one spiral-like organic outline that is not.
info.quote: Of the spiral forms which we have now mentioned, every one (with the single exception of the outline of the cordate leaf) is an example of the remarkable curve known as the Logarithmic Spiral.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one

info.statement: A deflecting force of constant direction acting from outside, such as wind or gravity, can only bend a growing structure towards a limiting direction and never into a spiral; a spiral arises only when the deflecting force is intrinsic to the growing body and turns with the direction of growth, as the columellar muscle does in the snail-shell.
info.quote: the growing curve will tend to wind round and round its point of origin. In the typical case of the snail-shell, such an intrinsic force is manifestly present in the action of the columellar muscle.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: A constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse growth rates yields a logarithmic spiral

info.statement: In a tubular structure whose growth is unequal on its two sides, a constant ratio between the rates of growth in the longitudinal and transverse directions generally produces a logarithmic spiral, the value of the ratio fixing the spiral's constant angle, with the circle and the straight line as limiting cases.
info.quote: In other words, in such a structure as we have presupposed, the existence or maintenance of a constant ratio between the rates of extension or growth in the vertical and transverse directions will lead, in general, to the development of a logarithmic spiral; the magnitude of that ratio will determine the character (that is to say, the constant angle) of the spiral;
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The scorpioid cyme traces a true logarithmic spiral

info.statement: In a scorpioid cyme, where each shoot arises from the last on the same side at an equal angle and successive shoots diminish in length in a constant ratio, the shoots are tangents to a true logarithmic spiral; in the helicoid cyme the same spiral is present but hidden by a superimposed twist.
info.quote: The result is that the successive shoots, or successive increments of growth, are tangents to a curve, and this curve is a true logarithmic spiral.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The shell grows in size without changing its shape

info.statement: A spiral shell, like the animal within it, increases in size without changing its shape, even though it grows at one end only; this constant similarity of form under terminal growth is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral and of no other curve.
info.quote: The shell, like the creature within it, grows in size _but does not change its shape_; and the existence of this constant relativity of growth, or constant similarity of form, is of the essence, and may be made the basis of a definition, of the logarithmic spiral.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it

info.statement: In horns, shells and all other organic forms showing a logarithmic spiral, the existing structure is partly old and partly new, and each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the whole pre-existing structure, that is, an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before.
info.quote: (2) it is characteristic of the growth of the horn, of the shell, and of all other organic forms in which a logarithmic spiral can be recognised, that _each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the entire pre-existing structure_.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts

info.statement: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.
info.quote: For it follows as a simple corollary to this theorem of gnomons that we must not expect to find the logarithmic spiral manifested in a structure whose parts are simultaneously produced, as for instance in the margin of a leaf, or among the many curves that make the contour of a fish.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression

info.statement: Careful measurement shows that the breadths of successive whorls along a radius of the Nautilus shell, and of spiral ammonitoid and gastropod shells generally, are in geometric progression, so that these shells are logarithmic spirals (for Nautilus each whorl is about three times as broad as the one before).
info.quote: It was by observing, with the help of very careful measurement, this continued proportionality, that Moseley was enabled to verify his first assumption, based on the general appearance of the shell, that the shell of Nautilus was actually a logarithmic spiral, and this demonstration he was immediately afterwards in a position to generalise by extending it to all the spiral Ammonitoid and Gastropod mollusca
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios

info.statement: The form of any turbinate shell is fixed by a small set of factors (shape of the generating curve, its rate of growth, its rate of rotation about the pole, its rate of translation along the axis, and its inclination), and all differences of form between one shell and another are differences of degree in the relative magnitudes of these factors.
info.quote: In short it is obvious that _all_ the differences of form which we observe between one shell and another are referable to matters of _degree_, depending, one and all, upon the relative magnitudes of the various factors in the complex equation to the curve.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°

info.statement: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.
info.quote: the constant angle is in the neighbourhood of 80°; and hence also that, in all the ordinary Ammonitoid shells, and in all the typically spiral shells of the Gastropods, the constant angle is also a large one, being very seldom less than 80°, and usually between 80° and 85°.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: Separation or overlap of whorls reflects the growth-rate ratio of outer to inner border

info.statement: Whether the whorls of a spiral shell stand apart, just touch, or overlap (up to complete involution, as in Nautilus pompilius versus N. umbilicatus) depends only on the ratio of the rate of growth of the outer border of the tube to that of its inner border.
info.quote: For the purposes of the morphologist, then, the main result of this last general investigation is to shew that all the various types of “open” and “closed” spirals, all the various degrees of separation or overlap of the successive whorls, are simply the outward expression of a varying ratio in the _rate of growth_ of the outer as compared with the inner border of the tubular shell.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry

info.statement: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the mathematical study of shell form.
info.quote: _To such phylogenetic hypotheses the mathematical or dynamical study of the forms of shells lends no valid support._ If we have two shells in which the constant angle of the spire be respectively 80° and 60°, that fact in itself does not at all justify an assertion that the one is more primitive, more ancient, or more “ancestral” than the other.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence

info.statement: Progressive change of growth ratios along a series of allied forms (orthogenesis) is real in some lineages, and the mathematical study of form can detect such series where they are not obvious, while also showing that strong resemblances of form may arise independently as numerical coincidences.
info.quote: And to my mind, the mathematical (as distinguished from the purely physical) study of morphology bids fair to help us to recognise this phenomenon of orthogenesis in many cases where it is not at once patent to the eye; and also, on the other hand, to warn us, in many other cases, that even strong and apparently complex resemblances in form may be capable of arising independently,
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: Ontogenetic change in spiral angle explains narrowing-whorled and uncoiling ammonites

info.quote: But let us suppose that the spiral angle increases somewhat rapidly; we shall then get a spiral with gradually narrowing whorls, and this condition is characteristic of Oekotraustes, a subgenus of Ammonites. If on the other hand, the angle α gradually diminishes, and even falls away to zero, we shall have the spiral curve opening out, as it does in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites,
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

info.quote: We see from this that shells so different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little indeed in the magnitude of the spiral angle α, that is to say in the relative velocities of radial and tangential growth. It is upon the angle θ that the difference in their form mainly depends:
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate

info.statement: The lines of growth on bivalve shells are not concentric but coaxial curves through the umbo, and they arise because the rate of growth varies as a simple function of direction; in the simplest case the lines are coaxial circles (as in Anomia), and with more complex functions they are coaxial ellipses or other figures (as in Lima or Solen).
info.quote: All that we are immediately concerned with is the simple fact that where a velocity, such as our rate of growth, varies with its direction,—varies that is to say as a function of the angular divergence from a certain axis,—then, in a certain simple case, we get lines of growth laid down as a system of coaxial circles,
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Incomplete moulting gives Estheria a mollusc-like spiral shell with growth lines

info.statement: The bivalved carapace of the crustacean Estheria resembles a lamellibranch shell, with lines of growth and a logarithmic spiral of small angle, because its moult is incomplete: each old carapace is retained and the new one grows beneath it and projects beyond its edge.
info.quote: But in Estheria (and one or two other small crustacea) the moult is incomplete: the old carapace is retained, and the new, growing up underneath it, adheres to it like a lining, and projects beyond its edge: so that in course of time the margins of successive old carapaces appear as “lines of growth” upon the surface of the shell.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint

info.statement: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with strongly flattened shells.
info.quote: It is obvious that the incipient curvature of the arms, and consequently the form and direction of the spirals, will be influenced by the surrounding pressures, and these in turn by the general shape of the shell. We shall expect, accordingly, to find the long outwardly directed spirals associated with shells which are transversely elongated, as Spirifer is; while the more rounded Atrypas will tend to the opposite condition.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone

info.statement: The shell and the aptychus of ammonites are probably the ventral and dorsal portions of a once united conical shell split by unequal growth, as in pteropods; other cephalopods retain only one of the two, the ventral one as the shell of Nautilus and the dorsal one as the shell of Sepia or Spirula.
info.quote: In short, I think there is reason to believe, or at least to suspect, that we have in the shell and Aptychus of the Ammonites, two portions of a once united structure; of which other Cephalopods retain not both parts but only one or other, one as the ventrally situated shell of Nautilus, the other as the dorsally placed shell for example of Sepia or of Spirula.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films

info.statement: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is sinuous.
info.quote: In all cases, provided only that the membrane be isotropic, the form assumed will be precisely that of a soap-bubble under similar conditions of attachment: that is to say, it will be (with the usual limitations or conditions) a surface of minimal area.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon

info.statement: The minutely branched, arborescent outline superposed on the lobes and saddles of some ammonite sutures, with branches ending in rounded arcs, is a surface-tension phenomenon of the same kind as the patterns made by milk on a greasy plate or oil on an alkaline solution.
info.quote: Superposed upon the usual sinuous outline, with its “lobes” and “saddles,” we have here a minutely ramified, or arborescent outline, in which all the branches terminate in wavy, more or less circular arcs,—looking just like the ‘landscape marble’ from the Bristol Rhaetic. We have no difficulty in recognising in this a surface-tension phenomenon.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The same spiral shell forms recur across unrelated groups, all ages and all seas

info.statement: Spiral shell forms appear with little relation to the kind of animal producing them, recurring in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and mathematically identical forms recur in every geological period and are found mixed together regardless of climate or local conditions.
info.quote: Again, we find the same forms, or forms which (save for external ornament) are mathematically identical, repeating themselves in all periods of the world’s geological history; and, irrespective of climate or local conditions, we see them mixed up, one with another, in the depths and on the shores of every sea.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Natural Selection plays no necessary part in producing spiral shell forms

info.statement: Natural Selection, in any strictly biological sense, has no necessary share in producing the varied forms of spiral shells, which arise from differences in growth rates and ratios.
info.quote: It is hard indeed (to my mind) to see where Natural Selection necessarily enters in, or to admit that it has had any share whatsoever in the production of these varied conformations.
info.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

nodes.label: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension

info.statement: The form of a single-chambered foraminiferal shell is explained by the laws of surface tension: the protoplasm behaves as a fluid drop whose equilibrium shape is fixed when it acquires its solid covering.
info.quote: wherever the shell is but a single unit or single chamber, its form may be explained in general by the laws of surface tension: the assumption being that the little mass of protoplasm which makes the simple shell behaves as a _fluid drop_, the form of which is perpetuated when the protoplasm acquires its solid covering.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Foraminifera are spiral because they grow by permanent increments added outside

info.statement: Foraminiferal shells tend towards a spiral form because they grow by successive increments added to the exterior, each of which becomes a permanent, rigid part of the structure.
info.quote: That the shell in the Foraminifera should tend towards a spiral form need not surprise us; for we have learned that one of the fundamental conditions of the production of a concrete spiral is just precisely what we have here, namely the gradual development of a structure by means of successive increments superadded to its exterior, which then form part, successively, of a permanent and rigid structure.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side

info.statement: Foraminiferal septa are convex outwards and those of Nautilus concave outwards because the pressure each membrane resisted when it set lay on opposite sides; in both cases the septum tends to a surface of minimal area.
info.quote: The one septum is, speaking generally, the reverse of the other; the organism, so to speak, is outside the one and inside the other; and in both cases alike, the septum tends to assume the form of a surface of minimal area, as permitted, or as defined, by all the circumstances of the case.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones

info.statement: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, recognisable by continued similarity: the large many-chambered shell has the same shape as the smaller, younger shell.
info.quote: The logarithmic spiral is easily recognisable in typical cases (and especially where the spire makes more than one visible revolution about the pole), by its fundamental property of continued similarity: that is to say, by reason of the fact that the big many-chambered shell is of just the same shape as the smaller and younger shell
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°

info.statement: In Fusulina the breadths of successive whorls stand in the nearly constant ratio 1 : 1.5, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral with a constant angle of about 86°, like that of ammonites.
info.quote: And this ratio of 1·5 between the breadths of successive whorls corresponds (as we see by our table on p. 534) to a constant angle of about 86°, or just such a spiral as we commonly meet with in the Ammonites
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
