nodes.label: Constant chamber-size ratio follows from growth proportional to existing mass

info.statement: Each foraminiferal chamber bears a constant ratio of size to the next because the rate of increase at each instant is proportional to the whole existing mass of the homogeneous organism.
info.quote: The law of increase by which each chamber bears a constant ratio of magnitude to the next may be looked upon as a simple consequence of the structural uniformity or homogeneity of the organism; we have merely to suppose (as this uniformity would naturally lead us to do) that the rate of increase is at each instant proportional to the whole existing mass.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Minimum potential energy plus proportional growth yields the logarithmic spiral

info.statement: Each new protoplasmic drop settles in a position of minimum potential energy (including minimal area), which makes each chamber similar to the last; proportional growth of size then gives the series the form of a logarithmic spiral. Rhumbler's specific 'law of the constant angle' of contact is too narrow an explanation.
info.quote: The physical law of minimum potential (including also the law of minimal area) is all that we need in order to explain, _in general terms_, the continued similarity of one chamber to another; and the physiological law of growth, by which a continued proportionality of size tends to run through the series of successive chambers, impresses upon this series of similar increments the form of a logarithmic spiral.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side

info.statement: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.
info.quote: The majority of spiral forms, on the other hand, are plane or discoid spirals, and we may take it that in these cases some force has exercised a controlling influence, so as to keep all the chambers in a plane. This is especially the case in forms like Rotalia or Discorbina (Fig. 316), where the organism lives attached to a rock or a frond of sea-weed
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability

info.statement: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.
info.quote: but for all we know of the life-history of the Foraminifera, it may well be that a great number of the other forms which we distinguish as separate species and even genera are no more than temporary manifestations of the same variability
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Foraminiferal forms follow such simple laws that none is fitter than another to survive

info.statement: Foraminiferal shells grow by laws so simple and so in harmony with their material and the forces acting on them that no form is better, fitter or less fit to survive than another, which accounts for the great diversity of types and their persistence since the Cretaceous.
info.quote: It leads one to imagine that these shells have grown according to laws so simple, so much in harmony with their material, with their environment, and with all the forces internal and external to which they are exposed, that none is better than another and none fitter or less fit to survive.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again

info.statement: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.
info.quote: It invites one also to contemplate the possibility of the lines of possible variation being here so narrow and determinate that identical forms may have come independently into being again and again.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution

info.statement: Against Rhumbler, niceties of shell form have little effect on survival: delicate foraminiferal shells survive unbroken in vast numbers, so breakage is not a constant danger and increased strength is not a selective advantage guiding their evolution.
info.quote: And so I am not inclined to believe that niceties of form affect the case very much: nor in general that foraminiferal life involves a struggle for existence wherein breakage is a constant danger to be averted, and increased strength an advantage to be ensured.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Foraminifera are absent from coarse gravels because of hydraulic sorting by currents

info.statement: Foraminiferal shells are absent from coarse sands and gravels not because they avoid concussion but because light shells are sorted by currents like any other graded sediment, settling where water is still.
info.quote: The coarseness or fineness of the sediment on the sea-bottom is a measure of the current: where the current is strong the larger stones are washed clean, where there is perfect stillness the finest mud settles down; and the light, fragile shells of the Foraminifera find their appropriate place, like every other graded sediment, in this spontaneous order of lixiviation.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity

info.statement: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.
info.quote: But in so far as forms can be shewn to depend on the play of physical forces, and the variations of form to be directly due to simple quantitative variations in these, just so far are we thrown back on our guard before the biological conception of consanguinity, and compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny.
info.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

nodes.label: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio

info.statement: The rhinoceros horn grows faster anteriorly than posteriorly in a constant ratio, so it curves as a logarithmic spiral; lying in the median plane, it has no lateral twist and forms a plane spiral.
info.quote: Its longitudinal growth proceeds with a maximum velocity anteriorly, and a minimum posteriorly; and the ratio of these velocities being constant, the horn curves into the form of a logarithmic spiral in the manner that we have already studied.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

info.statement: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.
info.quote: But the two horns are in symmetry one with another; they form “conjugate” spirals, one being the “mirror-image” of the other.

info.quote: But in the great majority of horns, we have no difficulty in recognising a continuous logarithmic spiral, nor in referring it, as before, to an unequal rate of growth (parallel to the axis) on two opposite sides of the horn, the inequality maintaining a constant ratio as long as growth proceeds.

nodes.label: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component

info.quote: In all of these the constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is very much the same, but the shearing component differs greatly.
info.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

nodes.label: A horn is a plane spiral only if fastest and slowest growth lie diametrically opposite

info.statement: If the maximal and minimal growth rates around the basal growth zone of a horn lie diametrically opposite, the horn is a plane spiral; otherwise it is a spiral in space with a helical component, which is the usual case because the horn's field of force has no such plane of symmetry.
info.quote: If the maximal and minimal velocities of growth be precisely at opposite sides of the zone of growth, the resultant spiral will be a plane spiral; but if they be not precisely or diametrically opposite, then the spiral will be a spiral in space, with a winding or helical component

info.quote: had its elongation more retarded on one side than the other (prior to its complete solidification) by varying degrees of adhesion or membranous attachment to the bone core within, then the net result would be a spiral curve precisely such as would have arisen from initial inequalities in the rate of growth itself. It seems highly probable that this is a very important factor

info.quote: I think it may be said that, on the whole, the thicker the horn, the greater is its spiral curvature.

info.quote: But there is yet another and a very remarkable phenomenon which we may discern in the growth of a horn, when it takes the form of a curve of double curvature, namely, an effect of torsional strain; and this it is which gives rise to the sinuous “lines of growth,” or sinuous boundaries of the separate horny rings, of which we have already spoken.

info.statement: Following Tait, if a single genetic spiral exists and one pair of parastichy numbers from the series 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is present, all the lower pairs of the series are necessarily present in the same system.
info.quote: These are the very series which we have found to be common, or normal; and so far as our investigation has yet gone, it has proved to us that, if one of these exists, it entails, _ipso facto_, the presence of the rest.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

nodes.label: Most phyllotaxis has between two and three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral

info.statement: The prevalence of Fibonacci parastichy numbers arises because in the great majority of fir-cones and other phyllotactic systems there are more than two but fewer than three leaves in one turn of the genetic spiral (t = 2); other observed series correspond to t = 3, 4, 5.
info.quote: And, determined in this manner, it is found in the great majority of cases, in fir-cones and a host of other examples of phyllotaxis, that _t_ = 2.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

nodes.label: Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence

info.statement: Which of the implicit spiral families is conspicuous does not depend on the angle of divergence but on the proportions of the leaves or scales, strictly on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area.
info.quote: the conspicuousness of one set or another does not depend upon angular divergence. It depends on the relative proportions in length and breadth of the leaves themselves; or, more strictly speaking, on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboidal figure by which each leaf-area is circumscribed.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

nodes.label: Convergence of phyllotactic ratios to the golden mean has no biological significance

info.statement: That the phyllotactic fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/5… converge to 0.618…, the golden mean, is a mathematical coincidence without biological significance; the precise divergence angle and orthostichies are likewise unimportant.
info.quote: And lastly, the fact that the successional numbers, expressed as fractions, 1/2, 2/3, 3/5, represent a convergent series, whose final term is equal to 0·61803..., the _sectio aurea_ or “golden mean” of unity, is seen to be a mathematical coincidence, devoid of biological significance
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

nodes.label: Close approximations to the golden mean are rare; poor ones like 2/3 are common

info.statement: Against the 'ideal angle' theory, phyllotactic arrangements that closely approximate the golden mean (8/13, 13/21, 34/55 and higher) are comparatively rare, while poorer approximations such as 3/5, 2/3 and 1/2 are extremely common.
info.quote: the arrangements by which a better approximation is got, such as 8/13, 13/21, and the very close approximations such as 34/55, 55/89, 89/144, etc., are comparatively rare, while the much less close approximations of 3/5 or 2/3, or even 1/2, are extremely common.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

nodes.label: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle

info.statement: If leaves benefit from being spread apart for exposure to air, lengthening the axis to separate them vertically has a far greater effect than any adjustment of the divergence angle, so the azimuthal 'ideal angle' cannot be the plant's means of optimising exposure.
info.quote: then it is surely manifest that the simple way to do so is to elongate the axis, and to set the leaves further apart, lengthways on the stem. This has at once a far more potent effect than any nice manipulation of the “angle of divergence.”
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

nodes.label: The Fibonacci series has no adaptive role introduced by natural selection

info.statement: The Fibonacci series in phyllotaxis, its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis that natural selection introduced it into plant structure have no place in the study of botanical phenomena.
info.quote: We come then, without more ado, to the conclusion that the “Fibonacci series,” and its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis of its introduction into plant-structure through natural selection, are all matters which deserve no place in the plain study of botanical phenomena.
info.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

nodes.label: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate

info.statement: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.
info.quote: It is an obvious but by no means negligible fact that the egg, while often pointed, is never flattened or discoidal; it is a prolate, but never an oblate, spheroid.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

nodes.label: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird

info.statement: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.
info.quote: It can be shown, at least as a very common rule, that those eggs which are most unsymmetrical, or most tapered off posteriorly, are also eggs of a large size relatively to the parent bird.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

nodes.label: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones

info.statement: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.
info.quote: In the case of the common fowl we can trace a direct relation between the size and shape of the egg, for the first eggs laid by a young pullet are usually smaller, and at the same time are much more nearly spherical than the later ones
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Peristaltic pressure behind the egg's middle makes the front blunt and rear pointed

info.statement: Peristaltic contraction of the oviduct applies greatest pressure behind the middle of the forming egg, making the anterior end broader and the posterior narrower; the resulting tapered form also favours movement down the oviduct blunt end first.
info.quote: from the nature and direction of motion of the peristaltic wave the pressure will be greatest somewhere behind the middle of the egg; in other words, the tube is converted for the time being into a more conical form, and the simple result follows that the anterior end of the egg becomes the broader and the posterior end the narrower.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Egg shape is caused by radial pressure of the oviduct before the shell hardens

info.statement: The essential cause of the form and variation of form of an egg is the regularly varying, largely radial pressure applied by successive rings of the oviduct before the shell solidifies, not adaptation to nesting circumstances.
info.quote: this factor, the unknown but regularly varying, largely radial, pressure applied by successive annuli of the oviduct, is the essential cause of the form, and variations of form, of the egg.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Egg form obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P, the equation of all eggs

info.statement: The shape of an egg, as an extensible membrane filled with incompressible fluid under external pressure, obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P (external normal pressure plus membrane tension times total curvature equals internal pressure), which Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.
info.quote: In fact, in so far as the postulates correspond near enough to actualities, the above equation is the equation of _all eggs_ in the universe.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Membrane tension peaks at the small end, where abnormal eggs are irregular

info.statement: In conical eggs with spherical ends, the tension of the envelope is greatest at and near the small end, so that is where eggs are most likely to be distorted or to burst and where abnormal eggs most often show irregularities.
info.quote: further, that the tension _T_ is greatest at and near the small end of the egg. It is here, in short, that the egg is most likely to be irregularly distorted or even to burst, and it is here that we most commonly find irregularities of shape in abnormal eggs.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Lateral spine of Schistosoma eggs is moulded in the ootype, not a species mark

info.statement: Following Looss, the lateral spine of some Schistosoma eggs is moulded mechanically in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus, so lateral- and terminal-spined eggs are mechanical variants of one thing and do not show the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni.
info.quote: It ascribes to a mechanical cause a curious peculiarity of form; it shews, by reference to this mechanical principle, that two conditions which were very different to the systematic naturalist’s eye, were really only two simple mechanical modifications of the same thing; and it destroys the chief evidence for the existence of a supposed new species of worm
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity

info.statement: The vertical outlines of regular sea-urchin shells are the forms of liquid drops depressed by gravity (with the pull of the tube-feet), their degree of flattening varying with the tension or strength of the shell: strong shells (Palaeechinus) stay nearly spherical, soft flexible ones (Phormosoma) are most flattened.
info.quote: but we have no difficulty in seeing that the various forms represented in a series of sea-urchin shells are no other than those which we may easily and perfectly imitate in drops.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Vessel wall thickness tracks radius in large arteries but falls off in small ones

info.statement: Under constant pressure the wall thickness of a blood-vessel should vary as its radius (P = T/R); because pressure falls with friction from large to small arteries, wall thickness is proportional to vessel size in larger vessels but becomes disproportionately thin in small arteries and capillaries.
info.quote: and accordingly we find that while, for a time, the cross-sections of the larger and smaller vessels are symmetrical figures, with the wall-thickness proportional to the size of the tube, this proportion is gradually lost, and the walls of the small arteries, and still more of the capillaries, become exceedingly thin, and more so than in strict proportion to the narrowing of the tube.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber

info.statement: Within each cavity of the heart, where pressure is uniform, wall thickness t varies inversely as the mean curvature, t(1/r + 1/r′) = C, so the highly curved apex of the left ventricle is thinnest.
info.quote: that is to say, that the thickness (_t_) of the wall varies inversely as the mean curvature.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Left ventricle wall is 6–7 times right's, matching the pressure ratio

info.statement: The left ventricle requires six to seven times the dilating pressure of the right, and its wall thickness is greater in the same proportion.
info.quote: we find (1) that we have had to use a pressure in the left ventricle from six to seven times as great as in the right ventricle, and (2) that the thickness of the walls is just in the same proportion.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Blood-vessels are arranged for minimum effort and minimum wall-surface

info.statement: The form and arrangement of blood-vessels are such that circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort and a minimum of wall-surface (and hence of friction).
info.quote: The general principle is that the form and arrangement of the blood-vessels is such that the circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort, and with a minimum of wall-surface, the latter condition leading to a minimum of friction and being therefore included in the first.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Small arterial branches leave at large angles, large branches at small angles

info.statement: Small arterial branches come off the main stem at large angles (about 70°–90° for the smallest) and large branches at small angles, with equal branches diverging at equal angles, as Roux's rules state.
info.quote: In other words, it would seem that for small branches a large angle of bifurcation, and for large branches a small one, is always the better.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch

info.statement: The most favourable angle at which an arterial branch leaves its trunk is that whose cosine equals the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel to that in the branch (cos x = L/L′).
info.quote: That is to say, the most favourable angle of branching will be such that the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of the loss of energy which the blood undergoes, per unit of length, in the main vessel, as compared with that which it undergoes in the branch.
info.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Mechanical adaptations of form are demonstrable, unlike colour adaptations

info.statement: Unlike explanations of colouration as cryptic, warning or mimetic, which cannot be demonstrated, the fitness of organic form for mechanical functions such as swimming or flight can be analysed and established in detail by statics and dynamics.
info.quote: But of a very different order from all such “adaptations” as these, are those very perfect adaptations of form which, for instance, fit a fish for swimming or a bird for flight. Here we are far above the region of mere hypothesis, for we have to deal with questions of mechanical efficiency where statical and dynamical considerations can be applied and established in detail.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression

info.statement: Fresh bone resists tearing almost as well as it resists crushing (tensile strength about 9–12 and crushing strength about 13–16 kg per sq. mm), which makes it an economical structural material that can serve equally as tie or strut.
info.quote: At first sight, bone seems weak indeed; but it has the great and unusual advantage that it is very nearly as good for a tie as for a strut, nearly as strong to withstand rupture, or tearing asunder, as to resist crushing.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Structures that must resist bending are built as hollow tubes

info.statement: Where stiffness against bending in all directions is required, organisms use a hollow cylindrical construction with little or no material in the core, as in the thin-walled, almost empty wing bones of long-winged birds such as the albatross, quills, and hollow stems of reeds and straw.
info.quote: it is appropriate in every case where _stiffness_ is required, where bending has to be resisted. The long bone of a bird’s wing has little or no weight to carry, but it has to withstand powerful bending moments; and in the arm-bone of a long-winged bird, such as an albatross, we see the tubular construction manifested in its perfection
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft

info.statement: Because bending strain is greatest at mid-length of a bent column, the walls of a long bone such as the femur are thickest in the middle of the shaft and thin gradually towards the ends, so that wall thickness forms a graph of the bending moments along the bone.
info.quote: Hence, if our cylindrical column be exposed to strong bending stresses, it will be prudent and economical to make its walls thickest in the middle and thinning off gradually towards the ends; and if we look at a longitudinal section of a thigh-bone, we shall see that this is just what nature has done.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress

info.statement: The trabeculae of cancellous bone, as in the head of the femur, are arranged along the principal lines of compressive and tensile stress of the loaded bone, crossing one another at right angles, exactly as in the engineer's stress diagram of a comparable structure such as a crane-head.
info.quote: and we have no difficulty in seeing that the anatomical arrangement of the trabeculae follows precisely the mechanical distribution of compressive and tensile stress or, in other words, accords perfectly with the theoretical stress-diagram of the crane.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Shear removes obliquely laid trabeculae, leaving those aligned with stress lines

info.statement: Trabecular alignment arises because a trabecula laid down along a pressure or tension line is undisturbed, since there is no shear along those lines, whereas one lying obliquely is acted on by shearing force and displaced until it comes into line with the stress.
info.quote: If it lie in the direction of one of the pressure-lines, for instance, it will be in a position of comparative equilibrium, or minimal disturbance; but if it be inclined obliquely to the pressure-lines, the shearing force will at once tend to act upon it and move it away.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Trabecular architecture remodels to new force patterns after malunited fracture

info.statement: Trabecular arrangement is produced by the forces acting on the bone, not by heredity: when a fracture heals with the parts displaced so that the stress lines are redistributed, the trabecular system is entirely remodelled within weeks to align with the new forces, even at a distance from the injury.
info.quote: If a bone be broken and so repaired that its parts lie somewhat out of their former place, so that the pressure-and tension-lines have now a new distribution, before many weeks are over the trabecular system will be found to have been entirely remodelled, so as to fall into line with the new system of forces.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Mechanical strain directly stimulates growth

info.statement: A state of strain produced by stress is a direct stimulus to growth, so that tissues under increased load grow stronger or thicker, as when the fibula of a puppy whose tibia was excised grew as thick as or thicker than the normal tibia.
info.quote: a condition of _strain_, the result of a _stress_, is a direct stimulus to growth itself. This indeed is no less than one of the cardinal facts of theoretical biology.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: The quadruped backbone is a double-armed cantilever girder, not an arch

info.statement: Because the jointed legs cannot resist the horizontal thrust of an arch and there is no tie between its ends, the backbone of a standing quadruped is not an arch, tied arch or bowstring girder but is mechanically comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
info.quote: The structure is not an arch, nor a tied arch, nor a bowstring girder: but it is strictly and beautifully comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Height of vertebral spines is proportional to the local bending moment

info.statement: In the vertebral girder, ligaments form the upper tension member, vertebral bodies the lower compression member and the spines the web, and the height of the vertebral spines at each point along the back is proportional to the bending moment at that point.
info.quote: secondly we observe that the depth of the web, or distance apart of the principal members,—that is to say the height of the vertebral spines,—must be proportional to the bending-moment at each point along the length of the girder.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs

info.statement: In large quadrupeds the fore-legs carry considerably more of the body weight than the hind-legs (about 55–58% in horses and elephants and about two-thirds in camels and llamas).
info.quote: It will be observed that in all these animals the load upon the fore-feet preponderates considerably over that upon the hind, the preponderance being rather greater in the elephant than in the horse, and markedly greater in the camel and the llama than in the other two.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines

info.statement: Animals whose head and neck form a large fraction of body weight have large bending moments over the fore-legs and correspondingly tall spines over the withers, whereas animals with light heads and heavy tails (anteaters, Diplodocus) or that are bipedal (kangaroo, Iguanodon) have their tallest spines over the loins and haunches.
info.quote: Wherever we have a heavily loaded anterior cantilever arm, that is to say whenever the head and neck represent a considerable fraction of the whole weight of the body, we tend to have large bending-moments over the fore-legs, and correspondingly high spines over the vertebrae of the withers.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Aquatic mammals lack the tall withers and haunch spines of land quadrupeds

info.statement: Because buoyancy neutralises gravity so that there are no piers or cantilevers, all aquatic mammals (whales, seals, sea-cows) have lost the high arched vertebral spines over the withers and haunches, and aquatic birds have a weak, straight pelvis compared with terrestrial birds.
info.quote: For here the effect of gravity is neutralised; we have neither piers nor cantilevers; and we find accordingly in all aquatic mammals of whatsoever group—whales, seals or sea-cows—that the high arched vertebral spines over the withers, or corresponding structures over the hind-limbs, have both entirely disappeared.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Fish vertebral processes are set at about 120° to one another for uniform stiffness

info.statement: In ordinary fishes such as cod and haddock (and partly in whales), the backbone is stiffened by three series of ligament-connected processes, dorsal and two transverse, arranged at nearly equal angles of 120°, which gives the greatest and most uniform strength possible for such a system.
info.quote: And here we see (as we see partly also among the whales), that these three series of processes, or struts, tend to be arranged well-nigh at equal angles, of 120°, with one another, giving the greatest and most uniform strength of which such a system is capable.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Backbone girders are shallower than engineers would build because flexibility is needed

info.statement: The vertebral girder of large animals such as Diplodocus or Stegosaurus is shallower than an engineer's cantilever of comparable load, because a deeper girder would increase rigidity, and an animal's backbone must combine strength with flexibility.
info.quote: If we adopt a much greater depth (or ratio of depth to length) as in the modern cantilever, we shall greatly increase the _strength_ of the structure; but at the same time we should greatly increase its _rigidity_, and this is precisely what, in the circumstances of the case, it would seem that nature is bound to avoid.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Skeletal form is largely a diagram of mechanical stress

info.statement: Skeletal form, as produced by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical stress: material is laid down along the lines of stress so as to avoid shear, from the trabeculae within each bone to the arrangement of the bones in the whole skeleton.
info.quote: Let us not press either argument or hypothesis too far: but be content to see that skeletal form, as brought about by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical considerations, and tends to manifest itself as a diagram, or reflected image, of mechanical stress.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Mechanically shaped single bones are unreliable guides to phylogenetic affinity

info.statement: Because the form of bones such as the scapula or vertebrae reflects the mechanical stresses of an animal's mode of life, resemblance or difference in a single such bone is no reliable evidence for or against blood-relationship, as in comparing Zeuglodon with whales.
info.quote: That the Zeuglodon has a scapula like that of a whale is to my mind no necessary argument that he is akin by blood-relationship to a whale: that his dorsal vertebrae are very different from a whale’s is no conclusive argument that such blood-relationship is lacking.
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: New mechanical forces modify many correlated parts together, not isolated bones

info.statement: When altered environment and habits introduce new forces, the resulting modifications of form appear not as isolated changes in single parts but as slow, general, graded modifications spread over many correlated parts or the whole body.
info.quote: And if this be really so, it will further imply that modifications of form will tend to manifest themselves, not so much in small and _isolated_ phenomena, in this part of the fabric or in that, in a scapula for instance or a humerus: but rather in some slow, _general_, and more or less uniform or graded modification, spread over a number of correlated parts
info.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Organic forms depart from mathematical ideals only as inanimate forms do

info.statement: There is no essential difference between organic and inorganic form: living forms depart from ideal mathematical figures only because secondary forces act alongside the main one, just as no chain hangs as a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere.
info.quote: There is no such essential difference between these phenomena of organic form and those which are manifested in portions of inanimate matter. No chain hangs in a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere: and this for the simple reason that forces and resistances other than the main one are inevitably at work.
info.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Specific differences in form are mainly differences of relative magnitude

info.statement: The essential differences in form between species of the same group are differences of proportion or relative magnitude (Aristotle's 'excess and defect'), and these are the main cause of specific differences.
info.quote: It is precisely this difference of relative magnitudes, this Aristotelian “excess and defect” in the case of form, which our co-ordinate method is especially adapted to analyse, and to reveal and demonstrate as the main cause of what (again in the Aristotelian sense) we term “specific” differences.
info.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

nodes.label: Evolution varies the whole body in correlation, not character by character

info.statement: Because dissimilar related fishes can be referred as wholes to the same figure in different coordinate systems, variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines under a comprehensive law of growth affecting the whole structure, rather than by independent variation of separate parts as the usual conception of natural selection assumes.
info.quote: But if, on the other hand, diverse and dissimilar fishes can be referred as a whole to identical functions of very different co-ordinate systems, this fact will of itself constitute a proof that variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines, that a comprehensive “law of growth” has pervaded the whole structure in its integrity
info.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

prov.file: claim graph (dashboard/public/data.json, built from the TriG claim records)

info.statement: The forms of related organisms can, as a general rule, be mapped onto one another by a simple and symmetrical deformation of a Cartesian coordinate grid, such as would result from a slight and simple change in the system of forces acting on the growing organism.
info.quote: We are dealing in this chapter with the forms of related organisms, in order to shew that the differences between them are as a general rule simple and symmetrical, and just such as might have been brought about by a slight and simple change in the system of forces to which the living and growing organism was exposed.

info.quote: the contained fossils are apt to be so curiously and yet so symmetrically deformed (usually by a simple shear) that they may easily be interpreted as so many distinct and separate “species.”
info.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

info.quote: In other words, the main (and perhaps the only) difference between the two bones is simply that that of the sheep is elongated, along the vertical axis, as compared with that of the ox in the relation of 3/2.

info.quote: If we now alter the ratio between the radial and tangential velocities of growth—in other words, if we increase the angles between corresponding radii—we pass successively through the various configurations which the botanist describes as the lanceolate, the ovate, and finally the cordate leaf.

info.quote: the so-called unsymmetrical leaf of a begonia, in which one side of the leaf may be merely ovate while the other has a cordate outline, is seen to be really a case of _unequal_, and not truly asymmetrical, growth on either side of the midrib.

info.statement: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time dilation follow.
info.quote: And the crucial point is that whenever the underlying system is causal invariant the exact same underlying rules will account for what one sees in slices at different angles. And what this means is that in effect the same rules will apply regardless of how fast one is going.
info.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

info.quote: An immediate possibility that I suspect is actually not too far from the mark is that such particles are analogs of the localized structures that we saw earlier in this book in systems like the class 4 cellular automata shown below.

info.quote: But despite such results, it is still conceivable that there could in the end be simple relations between truly fundamental particle masses—since it turns out that the masses that have actually been observed in effect also include varying amounts of interaction energy.

info.quote: But in fact the leading correction to the number of nodes reached is always quite simple: it is just proportional to what is called the Ricci scalar curvature, multiplied by r^(d + 1).

info.quote: But I suspect that if one has replacement rules that are causal invariant and that in effect successfully maintain a fixed number of dimensions they will almost inevitably lead to behavior that follows something close to the Einstein equations.

info.quote: For if one looks at axiom systems that are widely used in mathematics they almost all tend to be complete enough to prove at least a fair fraction of statements either true or false.
info.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

nodes.label: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms

info.statement: Enumerating simple axiom systems for a binary operator shows that the vast majority allow operators of many different forms (many models), so they are not about any one particular operator and are far from complete; only a few, such as those for logic, force essentially a single form.
info.quote: But what the pictures on the next two pages [804, 805] show is that the vast majority of axiom systems actually allow operators with all sorts of different forms.
info.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

nodes.label: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems

info.quote: So what this means is that if one were just to go through a list of the simplest few thousand axiom systems one would already be quite likely to find one that represents logic.
info.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

info.hypothesis: If Darwin's denudation argument holds, the time elapsed since the latter part of the Secondary (Mesozoic) period, i.e. since the youngest Chalk, is roughly 300 million years or more on the modern radiometrically calibrated timescale.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) chronostratigraphic boundary ages as served by the Macrostrat API (defs/intervals, timescale 'international ages'), which carries the ICS chart's numeric ages in Ma. Quantities: age of the top of the Maastrichtian (= Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, the end of Chalk deposition) and age of the base of the Campanian (start of the youngest Chalk stages). SUPPORTS if the top-of-Maastrichtian age is >= 225 Ma (within 25% of 300 Myr, or older). Reported alongside: the base-of-Campanian age and the ratio of Darwin's 306.7 Myr to the measured age.

measured.unit: Ma, age of the top of the Maastrichtian (end of the Chalk); Darwin's figure was 306.7 million years

caveats: Darwin's 300 million years is 4.6 times the radiometric age of the end of the Chalk; Darwin withdrew the calculation in the third edition after Phillips's criticism, so this refutes the claim as stated in the first edition, which is how the claim graph records it.
The test uses the ICS ages through Macrostrat's API rather than the chart PDF; the two agree for these stages and the version is recorded.
This is a one-number test with no sampling uncertainty; it does not evaluate Darwin's erosion rate, only the duration he inferred.

Readings check: under the three numeric readings of Darwin's figure (lower bound since the end of the Chalk; duration of the Weald denudation; time since the start of the Late Cretaceous) the measured age is 3.1 to 4.6 times smaller than 300 Myr, so the verdict is unchanged; only the purely qualitative reading ('geological time is immense') would be supported, and the claim graph's statement is the numeric one.

prov.file: claim-tests/darwin-origin/darwin1859-ch09-03/result.json

info.hypothesis: If the Glacial period lasted a very long time at each place and was at least in part simultaneous across the whole world, then (a) a globally mixed marine proxy of ice volume and deep-water temperature (benthic d18O) shows prolonged cold, ice-rich states lasting well over 10 thousand years and recurring through the Pleistocene, with the last glacial maximum in such a state, and (b) a southern-hemisphere high-latitude temperature record (Antarctic ice core) is cold at the same times as the global proxy is ice-rich, within age-model uncertainty.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: (1) LR04 benthic d18O stack of Lisiecki and Raymo (2005), the LR04stack.txt file served by the author (columns: age in ka, benthic d18O in per mil, error), and (2) EPICA Dome C deuterium-derived temperature anomaly on the EDC3 age scale (Jouzel et al. 2007), the NOAA paleoclimatology file edc3deuttemp2007.txt. Criterion A (long-lasting cold states): with d18O linearly interpolated to a 1-kyr grid over 0-2600 ka, d18O >= 4.0 per mil during at least 20% of the interval AND at least 5 separate contiguous intervals with d18O >= 4.0 per mil each lasting >= 10 kyr. Criterion B (last glacial maximum): mean d18O over 18-26 ka >= 4.5 per mil. Criterion C (simultaneity, north-dominated ice volume vs southern temperature): both series interpolated to a 1-kyr grid over 0-800 ka; the maximum Pearson correlation between EDC temperature anomaly and negative d18O across lags of -6 to +6 kyr (to allow for independent age models) is >= 0.6. SUPPORTS if A, B and C all hold.

measured.unit: fraction of the last 2.6 Myr with benthic d18O >= 4.0 per mil (pre-registered threshold 0.20)

caveats: Darwin pictured one long Glacial period; the record shows dozens of glacial cycles. The test asks only whether long (>= 10 kyr), globally registered cold states recur and whether the southern high latitudes are cold at the same times, which they are (correlation 0.88 at a 2 kyr lag).

Benthic d18O mixes ice volume (mostly northern hemisphere ice sheets) with deep-water temperature; the Antarctic record is a single site. Simultaneity is shown at orbital (10-100 kyr) resolution and does not speak to millennial-scale bipolar anti-phasing.
The 4.0 and 4.5 per mil thresholds are absolute values of a stack whose mean level drifts over 2.6 Myr; early Pleistocene glacials are shallower, which the 20% criterion absorbs.
Darwin's 'whole world' includes the tropics and the ocean, which these two records do not resolve.

prov.file: claim-tests/darwin-origin/darwin1859-ch11-13/result.json

supports — fisher-infinitesimal

info.hypothesis: If adult height is governed by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect, then (a) a child's height given the parents' heights is approximately Gaussian with a residual variance (segregation plus environment) that does not depend on the parental mean, and (b) full siblings are correlated at least as strongly as parent and offspring, because dominance and shared environment add to the sibling covariance but not to the parent-offspring covariance.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Galton's 1886 family height records as distributed in the R HistData package (GaltonFamilies: 934 adult children in 205 families with father, mother and child heights in inches and child sex). Female child heights are multiplied by 1.08, as Galton did, to put both sexes on a common scale; mid-parent height is (father + 1.08*mother)/2. Residuals r are taken from the ordinary-least-squares regression of adjusted child height on mid-parent height. Criterion A (homoscedasticity): Levene's test (median-centred, Brown-Forsythe) of residual variance across the three mid-parent terciles gives p > 0.05 AND the ratio of the largest to the smallest tercile residual variance is < 1.5. Criterion B (normality): residual sample skewness |g1| < 0.5 and excess kurtosis |g2| < 1.0. Criterion C (sibling vs parent-offspring): the full-sibling intraclass correlation of adjusted height (one-way random-effects ANOVA estimator over families with >= 2 children) is >= r_po - 0.05, where r_po is the single-parent-offspring correlation implied by the child-on-mid-parent correlation r_mp as r_po = r_mp / sqrt(2) (which assumes uncorrelated parents). SUPPORTS if A, B and C all hold.

measured.unit: ratio of largest to smallest residual variance across mid-parent terciles (model predicts 1)
measured.n: 934 children in 205 families (172 families with 2+ children)

caveats: In-sample classic data: Fisher (1918) built the model to explain exactly these biometric regularities, so the test shows the model's distributional predictions hold on Galton's families, not that they hold out of sample.

The sibling correlation (0.39) exceeds the implied parent-offspring correlation (0.35) as predicted, but shared family environment, not only dominance, can produce that excess; the two are not separable here.
Heteroscedasticity could be masked by the modest sample (about 311 children per tercile) and by Galton's rounding of heights; the variance ratio of 1.08 is nonetheless close to 1.
Galton's 1.08 female adjustment and the assumption of uncorrelated parents (observed father-mother r = 0.10) are approximations.

nodes.label: mixed — fisher-sex-ratio

info.hypothesis: If parents are selected to invest equally in sons and daughters and a son costs the same as a daughter, then the primary (birth) sex ratio of human populations should be close to one male per female and should not vary widely between populations.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: United Nations World Population Prospects 2024, Demographic Indicators, medium variant CSV (WPP2024_Demographic_Indicators_Medium.csv.gz), variable SRB (sex ratio at birth, males per 100 female births), rows with LocTypeName == 'Country/Area', years 1950 to 1979 inclusive (before prenatal sex determination was widely available, so the ratio reflects biology rather than sex-selective abortion), country-years with total mid-year population >= 1 million. Criterion A (equality): the median SRB across qualifying country-years lies in [95, 105] (within 5% of equal numbers). Criterion B (uniform near-equality): at least 95% of qualifying country-years lie in [90, 110]. SUPPORTS if A and B both hold.

measured.unit: median sex ratio at birth, males per 100 females, country-years 1950-1979 (equal numbers = 100)

caveats: Verdict is 'mixed' by the pre-registered rule: every one of 4222 country-years lies within 10% of equality (criterion B, the strong-constraint prediction, holds with no exceptions), but the median is 105.2, just outside the 5% band of criterion A, and the excess of male births is systematic (minimum country mean 101.0).

The standard Fisherian reading of the 5% male excess is that boys die more often before the end of parental investment, so investment is nearer equality than births are; this test did not measure sex-specific child mortality and so cannot confirm that reconciliation.
WPP values are UN estimates reconstructed from censuses and registration systems, smoothed and not independent across years within a country; the effective sample size is far below 4222.
Only humans were tested, and only the 'equal cost' case; Fisher's principle predicts equal investment, which the birth ratio measures only approximately.

mixed — hamilton-senescence

info.hypothesis: If the force of selection on survival declines with age after reproduction begins so that senescence is inevitable, then in age-structured matrix population models of unmanipulated wild animal populations, age-specific mortality should rise across the adult (reproductive) age classes in the great majority of species.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: COMADRE Animal Matrix Database v4.26.4.0 (RData file served at compadre-db.org/Data/ComadreDownload; data user agreement and citation guidelines accepted). Matrix selection: MatrixCriteriaAge == 'Yes' (age-classified), MatrixSplit == 'Divided' (U and F submatrices available), MatrixComposite in {'Individual', 'Mean'}, MatrixTreatment == 'Unmanipulated', MatrixCaptivity == 'W' (wild), matrix dimension >= 5, no missing entries in U or F. For each qualifying matrix, survival of age class a is the column sum of U for class a; the last class is dropped from the trend if U has a non-zero diagonal entry there (an open-ended plus group whose survival mixes ages). Mature classes are those whose F column sum is > 0. For each species, qualifying matrices of the same dimension are averaged element-wise (so each species contributes once); species with fewer than 4 mature age classes after dropping the plus group are excluded. Rising adult mortality = Spearman rho between age-class index and mortality (1 - survival) over the mature classes is > 0. SUPPORTS if at least 80% of qualifying species show rising adult mortality AND the mean rho across species is > 0.3. AMENDMENT (2026-10-31, before any data were downloaded, at the request of the holdout thread): species of class Aves are excluded from the primary analysis and from all criteria above; bird species are held out and only reported separately, unfitted, as a holdout check. Class is taken from COMADRE's 'Class' metadata column.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying non-bird species with Spearman rho(age, adult mortality) > 0

caveats: Verdict 'mixed' by the pre-registered rule (57% rising, between the 50% refute and 80% support thresholds): adult mortality rises with age in a majority of species but far from the 'great majority' that 'inevitable senescence' implies, and 13 of 35 species show falling adult mortality. This is the same direction as Jones et al. (2013) but weaker evidence, because matrix models have few age classes and noisy late-age estimates.
Sample is small (35 non-bird species, 20 of them mammals) and dominated by well-studied ungulates, carnivores and fishes; it is not a random sample of animal life histories.

Published age-classified matrices usually truncate age with a plus group, so the oldest ages, where senescence is strongest, are often missing; this biases the test against the claim. Conversely, class index is calendar age for most studies but not all.

The proved part of the claim (the formula for the age-specific force of selection) is not tested; only the biological corollary that mortality must rise with adult age. Class Aves (8 species) is held out and scorable later with 'analysis.py --exam'; the first run of the script, before the gate was added, printed the birds' fraction rising once and it was not used.

info.hypothesis: If a neutral allele's probability of eventual fixation equals its initial frequency, then in Buri's (1956) 107 replicate Drosophila populations, each started with the bw75 allele at frequency 0.5 in 16 flies, the lines that have reached fixation or loss by the last recorded generation should be split evenly between fixation of bw75 and loss of bw75.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the 'fly' matrix in the CRAN package popgenr 0.2 (CC0; Laruson and Reed 2021), a 19 x 107 matrix of the number of bw75 allele copies (out of 32) in each replicate at each generation, transcribed from Buri (1956). At the last recorded generation, a line is 'fixed' if the count is 32 and 'lost' if the count is 0; m = fixed + lost, k = fixed. SUPPORTS if m >= 20 AND the two-sided exact binomial test of k against Binomial(m, 0.5) gives p > 0.05 AND |k/m - 0.5| < 0.15. Reported but not decisive: the mean bw75 frequency across all 107 lines at the last generation (predicted 0.5 under neutrality, since the expected frequency is constant under drift) and the number of fixed-or-lost lines.

measured.unit: fraction of fixed-or-lost populations fixed for bw75 at the last recorded generation (neutral prediction 0.5)
measured.n: 58 fixed-or-lost populations of 107 (28 fixed, 30 lost) after 19 generations

caveats: Only the neutral limit u(p) = p at p = 0.5 is tested; the selection-dependent formula is untested because s for bw75 is not independently known. The mean bw75 frequency drifted from 0.500 to 0.472 over 19 generations, a slight deficit that Buri attributed to weak selection; it is within what drift alone produces in 107 lines and does not change the fixed/lost balance.
The popgenr object is a transcription of Buri's published table; transcription accuracy was not checked against the 1956 paper (not open access).

Censoring: 49 of 107 lines were still segregating at the last generation; the test uses only lines that had resolved. Effective size from heterozygosity decay is about 8 (census 16), consistent with Buri's own estimate, so most fixations occurred before 4Ne generations had elapsed.

refutes — kimura-heterozygosity

info.hypothesis: If neutral equilibrium heterozygosity H = theta/(1+theta) with theta = 4*Ne*mu holds and effective size scales with census size across species, then genome-wide nucleotide diversity (pi, the per-site heterozygosity) across metazoan species rises with census population size N: for pi << 1, H is approximately 4*Ne*mu, so log10(pi) should increase with log10(N) with a slope near 1 when mu and Ne/N are comparable across species, and the rank correlation between pi and N should be strongly positive.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Buffalo (2021) combined_data.tsv from github.com/vsbuffalo/paradox_variation (commit b8f91d5, 2021-09-27), metazoan species (kingdom == Animalia) with a non-missing diversity value (pairwise nucleotide diversity, column 'diversity') and a non-missing census-size estimate (column 'log10_popsize', the posterior mean of log10 census size from the author's range x density model; if the file carries another census-size point estimate instead, the column actually used is recorded in 'method'). One row per species. SUPPORTS if Spearman rho(log10 pi, log10 N) > 0.5 with p < 0.001 AND the ordinary-least-squares slope of log10 pi on log10 N has a point estimate >= 0.3 with a 95% confidence interval that includes some value >= 0.5 (diversity rises at least about a third as fast as census size on a log scale, i.e. within a factor of about 3 of the law's slope of 1). AMENDMENT (2026-10-31, before any data were downloaded, at the request of the holdout thread): species of class Aves are excluded from the primary analysis and from all criteria above; bird rows are held out and only reported separately, unfitted, as a holdout check. The taxonomic class is taken from the file's own taxonomy columns.

measured.unit: OLS slope of log10(pi) on log10(census N); the law with Ne proportional to N predicts about 1
measured.n: 160 non-bird metazoan species (diversity sources: {'Leffler et al.': 90, 'Romiguier et al.': 58, 'Corbett-Detig et al.': 12})

caveats: Census size stands in for effective size and per-site mutation rate is not included, so the refutation is of the law as operationalized (diversity should track census size), which is exactly Lewontin's paradox: diversity does rise with N (rho about 0.5, p < 1e-10) but roughly ten times too slowly on a log scale, across 12 orders of magnitude of N.

Census sizes are model-based estimates (species range times a body-size-predicted density) with large uncertainty; measurement error in N attenuates the slope, but not by the factor of ten needed to rescue the law (Buffalo 2021 reaches the same conclusion with error-in-variables models).
Diversity estimates mix synonymous, non-coding and genome-wide measures from three collations, and are averaged where several entries exist for a species.

Class Aves (13 species) was excluded before fitting at the holdout thread's request and can be scored later with 'analysis.py --exam'. The first run of the script, before the gate was added, printed the birds' mean residual once; it was not used to change anything.

info.hypothesis: If a favourable mutation's sweep removes variation at linked neutral sites, and more so where recombination is weaker relative to selection, then across windows of a human chromosome nucleotide diversity should be positively correlated with the local recombination rate.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 chromosome 22 genotype VCF (release 20130502, all 2504 samples) and the HapMap Phase II GRCh37 genetic map for chromosome 22. SNP filter: records with VT=SNP in INFO, biallelic (no MULTI_ALLELIC flag, single ALT), FILTER PASS. Windows: non-overlapping 200 kb windows starting at 16,000,000 bp (GRCh37) up to the last SNP. Diversity per window: pi = sum over SNPs of 2p(1-p) * 2n/(2n-1), with p the INFO AF value and 2n = 5008 chromosomes, divided by the window length (200,000 bp). Windows with fewer than 200 qualifying SNPs are excluded as unassessable (centromere-proximal or low-accessibility regions). Recombination rate per window: (map cM at window end minus map cM at window start) / 0.2 Mb, with cM linearly interpolated from the genetic map. SUPPORTS if Spearman rho(pi, recombination rate) across windows is >= 0.2 with two-sided p < 0.01.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between per-window nucleotide diversity and recombination rate (cM/Mb), chr22, 200 kb windows

caveats: A positive diversity-recombination correlation is also produced by background selection (purifying selection removing linked neutral variation), so the result supports the pattern hitchhiking predicts but does not isolate sweeps as the cause; separating the two needs site-frequency or sweep-scan evidence.

Diversity is computed from allele frequencies pooled over all 26 populations; population structure inflates pi uniformly and does not create the correlation, but the absolute pi values are not a single-population estimate.

All SNPs are used, not only neutral sites; gene density and GC content covary with recombination in humans and could contribute to the correlation through mutation-rate variation. Windows with < 200 SNPs (none on chr22 above 16 Mb) would have been excluded.
One chromosome (22, about 35 Mb of assessable sequence) was tested, as pre-registered, to keep the download small; the pattern is well known genome-wide (Hellmann et al. 2003).

supports — thompson1917-ch03-07

info.hypothesis: If weight varies as the cube of a linear dimension during growth, then across childhood and adolescence the population mean body weight scales with the population mean stature with a log-log exponent near 3, so the weight-for-age curve is approximately the cube of the stature-for-age curve.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: US NHANES examination data, cycles 2013-2014, 2015-2016 and 2017-2018 (Body Measures BMX_H/I/J and Demographics DEMO_H/I/J XPT files), examined participants aged 2 to 19 years with measured standing height (BMXHT, cm) and weight (BMXWT, kg). For each sex, compute MEC-exam-weighted (WTMEC2YR) mean height and mean weight in 1-year age bins (18 bins), regress log(mean weight) on log(mean height) by ordinary least squares, and also fit the constrained model weight = k * height^3 with k estimated by least squares on the log scale. SUPPORTS if, for both sexes, the free exponent b lies in [2.5, 3.5] AND the cubic model reproduces the age-bin mean weights with R^2 >= 0.90 on the original scale.

measured.unit: log-log exponent of mean weight on mean height across ages 2-19, males (pre-registered band 2.5-3.5); females given in extra
measured.n: 4905 males and 4810 females in 18 age bins each

caveats: The free exponent is below 3 in both sexes (2.74 and 2.86) and the male CI excludes 3, so weight grows a little slower than the cube of stature across childhood; Thompson's 'mainly (though not wholly)' is borne out literally: the cube reproduces the weight curve with R^2 of 0.98-0.99 but is not exact.
Cross-sectional population means from 2013-2018 US children, who are heavier at given height than Thompson's early-20th-century tables; the exponent, not the constant k, is what the claim concerns.
Binned means over 18 ages leave 16 degrees of freedom; the CI reflects bin-to-bin scatter, not individual variation.

Post-hoc discriminating-power check (perturbation.py, added 2026-10-31 after the result; simulation, not observation): with the observed mean heights and bin scatter, the pre-registered rule passes in 100% (males) and 99.95% (females) of 2000 simulations under the cube law, in 0% under an exponent of 2 or 4, and in about 47 to 49% at the band edges 2.5 and 3.5; so the rule rejects surface-law and fourth-power alternatives and is indifferent only at its own pre-registered boundaries.

mixed — thompson1917-ch03-10

info.hypothesis: If fishes approach a maximal size only asymptotically, then mean length at age in well-sampled wild fish populations keeps increasing, by ever smaller but still positive increments, through the oldest well-sampled ages, and an asymptotic growth model fits the length-at-age means better than a model in which length reaches a fixed maximum at a finite age and then stays there.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: ICES DATRAS North Sea IBTS (NS-IBTS) age records (CA record type), quarters 1 and 3, survey years 2000-2024, all species; length class converted to cm; records with a plus-group flag or missing age excluded. A species qualifies if it has at least 7 consecutive age classes starting at age 1, each with at least 50 aged fish (sum of CANoAtLngt); the included age range ends at the oldest class with at least 50 fish. For each species, mean length at age is computed (weighted by CANoAtLngt) and two 3-parameter models are fitted by weighted least squares (weights = number of fish): (i) asymptotic von Bertalanffy L = Linf (1 - exp(-K (a - t0))) with K > 0, and (ii) determinate quadratic-plateau L = Lmax - c (tc - a)^2 for a < tc, L = Lmax for a >= tc, with tc constrained to at most (oldest included age - 1) so that the model asserts a maximum actually reached inside the data. dAIC = AIC_det - AIC_VB (positive favours the asymptotic model). Late-age increments are the three increments of mean length between the last four included age classes. SUPPORTS if the asymptotic model is favoured (dAIC > 2) in at least two thirds of qualifying species AND at least 75% of all late-age increments pooled across species are positive. Requires at least 5 qualifying species; otherwise inconclusive (underpowered).

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying species in which the asymptotic model is favoured by dAIC > 2 (pre-registered threshold 2/3); fraction of late-age increments positive = 0.758 (threshold 0.75)
measured.n: 11 species, 33 late-age increments, 1111408 aged fish from 986385 CA rows

caveats: The pre-registered supports condition was narrowly missed: 7/11 = 0.636 species favour the asymptotic model against the required 2/3, while the late-increment condition (0.758 >= 0.75) was met. The result is therefore 'mixed' by rule, although most of the evidence points toward protracted growth.

In the two species where the reached-maximum model wins (whiting, lemon sole) mean length at age actually declines over the oldest ages, which neither model predicts for individual growth; the most likely cause is size-selective (fishing) mortality removing the faster growers (Lee's phenomenon) and ageing error, not cessation of growth. This biases the test against the claim.

Cross-sectional survey means pool cohorts and years (2000-2024, Q1 and Q3) and so mix cohort effects with age effects; the oldest age classes are sparsely sampled (>= 50 fish required) and trawl gear under-samples the largest fish.

The determinate alternative had to be given a specific functional form (quadratic rise to a plateau); a different plateau model could change individual dAIC values. Model selection used AIC on 7-18 age-class means, not individual-level likelihoods.

info.hypothesis: If chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen, with few below six and fewer still above sixteen, then across plant species the haploid (gametic) number n has most of its mass in 6 <= n <= 16, a small lower tail (n < 6) and a still smaller upper tail (n > 16).
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB, Rice et al. 2015), 'statistics' API output (one row per resolved species name with the median gametophytic/sporophytic counts) retrieved per major group (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes) in CSV. One n per species: the median resolved gametophytic count; where only a sporophytic (2n) count is given, n = 2n/2; species with no usable count excluded. SUPPORTS if all three hold: (a) at least 70% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; (b) fewer than 15% have n < 6; (c) the share with n > 16 is smaller than the share with n < 6.

measured.unit: share of plant species with haploid number n > 16 (claim: 'fewer still' than the share with n < 6, which is given in extra)

caveats: Thompson's central range is roughly right (64% of species have 6 <= n <= 16, mode n = 9), but the upper tail is 20 times larger than the lower tail (34% above 16 versus 1.7% below 6), the opposite of 'fewer still have more than sixteen': polyploidy, unknown in 1917, puts a third of angiosperms and 96% of ferns above 16.
Plants only; the animal half of the claim is untested here (animal karyotype compilations were not pursued in this batch).
The CCDB is a compilation of published counts with uneven taxonomic coverage; the median per species name hides within-species cytotype variation, which is the intended treatment of polyploid races.
Species with only a sporophytic count: the CCDB statistics service reports counts at the gametophytic level (confirmed on reference species), so no halving was applied.

info.hypothesis: If the sutural line of a turreted shell such as Turritella is a geodesic of the shell's enveloping right cone, then the number of whorls the suture makes cannot exceed the number of turns a conical geodesic can make: a geodesic on a right cone of apical angle alpha develops into a straight line on a sector of angle 2*pi*sin(alpha/2), sweeps at most pi of that sector, and therefore turns at most N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) times in total (and only half of that while approaching the apex). Measured whorl counts of Turritella shells must therefore satisfy N_obs <= N_geo.
info.pass: Pre-registered. From published per-specimen measurements of Turritellidae giving both the apical angle alpha and the total whorl number N_obs (Pandita et al. 2013, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6, 50 specimens of 5 species), compute N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) and the ratio R = N_obs / N_geo for every specimen with both values. SUPPORTS if at least 90% of specimens have R <= 1 (whorl count within the geodesic bound).

measured.unit: median ratio of observed whorl number to the maximum number of turns a conical geodesic can make (R = N_obs / N_geo); R > 1 is impossible for a geodesic

caveats: The test refutes the identification of the suture with a geodesic of the enveloping right cone; it does not test Thompson's purely geometric statement that a conical geodesic coils more closely toward the apex (true) nor whether the suture is locally geodesic-like over a fraction of a whorl.

The bound assumes the shell envelope is a right circular cone, which is what Thompson states; real turritellid envelopes are slightly convex or concave, but the Clairaut relation on any such surface of revolution still forbids a geodesic from winding many times toward a narrowing apex unless the sides are almost parallel.

Specimens are Neogene fossils from West Java, not the type species Turritella terebra; fossil apices are often incomplete, so whorl counts are if anything underestimates, which makes the test conservative. Apical angles are the authors' gross measurements to 0.5 degree.
Whorl counts include early whorls where the cone approximation is roughest; subtracting two whorls from every count leaves all 34 specimens above the bound.
