refutes — thompson1917-ch11-06

info.hypothesis: If every increment of a spirally grown shell is a gnomon to the whole structure before it (the enlarged whole stays similar to itself), then a molluscan shell is geometrically self-similar through growth: dimensionless shape indices of the conch measured at successive diameters along one specimen's ontogeny (conch width index CWI = ww/dm, umbilical width index UWI = uw/dm, whorl expansion rate WER) stay constant, apart from measurement noise, from the end of the embryonic shell to maturity.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Walton & Korn (2018) ontogenetic conch-parameter series for 177 Devonian-Jurassic ammonoid species (Dryad 10.5061/dryad.c17p8), measured on median cross-sections at successive diameters dm. For each species keep the post-embryonic points (dm >= 2 mm) and require at least 4 points spanning at least a fourfold range of dm. For each retained index compute the log-range D = max ln(index) - min ln(index) over the series. A species is 'gnomonic' if D <= ln(1.25) (at most 25% change) for CWI, UWI and WER alike; 'allometric' if D >= ln(1.5) (at least 50% change) for at least one index; otherwise intermediate. SUPPORTS if at least two thirds of the qualifying species are gnomonic. As a secondary descriptor, the fraction of species whose indices show a monotonic trend with ln dm (|Spearman rho| >= 0.7, p < 0.05, for at least one index) is reported; it does not enter the verdict.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying ammonoid series in which at least one conch shape index changes by >= 50% over post-embryonic growth (pre-registered refutes threshold 2/3); fraction gnomonic = 0.006 (supports threshold 2/3)

caveats: The refutation is carried almost entirely by the umbilical width index: UWI changes by >= 50% in 92% of series (median change 204%), whereas the whorl expansion rate, which encodes the spiral angle, stays within 25% in 80% of series (median change 17%). The spiral itself is therefore close to logarithmic (gnomonic in Thompson's sense), while the whorl section and the degree of involution change through growth, so the enlarged conch is not similar to its earlier self. Dropping UWI, only 34% of series (27% at dm >= 5 mm) are allometric and the pre-registered rule would give 'mixed'.

Walton & Korn chose their 177 species to study pachyconic and globular ammonoids with phased ontogenies, so the sample is probably enriched in species with strong ontogenetic shape change relative to ammonoids at large.

UWI is the noisiest index at small diameters (small umbilical widths); the 2 mm cut-off and the requirement of a monotonic trend (met by 94% of series) limit but do not remove this effect; at dm >= 5 mm the allometric fraction is still 84%.

Scope: Palaeozoic-Jurassic ammonoid conchs only; Thompson's gnomon claim also covers gastropod and bivalve shells, opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns and tusks, which were not tested. The 25% and 50% thresholds are pre-registered conventions, not derived from Thompson.

info.hypothesis: If buoyancy has removed the tall arched neural spines over the withers and haunches, then secondarily aquatic mammals (pinnipeds, cetaceans) should show no anterior-thoracic ('withers') peak of relative neural-spine height along the thoracolumbar column, and their anterior-thoracic spines should be relatively shorter than those of terrestrial quadrupeds; the haunch (posterior lumbar) spines should likewise not be elevated.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Per vertebra, relative spine height h = (neural spine apex to centrum reference distance) / cranial centrum height. Per species: W = mean h over T1-T4 ('withers'); P = mean h over the posterior thoracics T10-T13 (terrestrial trough region); WI = W/P ('withers index'); HI = mean h over the last three lumbars / P ('haunch index'). Test A (Carnivora landmark data, Figueirido et al. 2021): SUPPORTS-component if every pinniped species has W below the 25th percentile of terrestrial carnivoran W and one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests give p < 0.05 for pinnipeds < terrestrial on both W and WI. Test B (cetacean linear data, Gillet et al. 2019, h = Lnp/Hc; W over the first three thoracics, P over the last three thoracics, WI = W/P): SUPPORTS-component if the median cetacean WI <= 1 and at least 80% of cetacean species have WI below the minimum WI of the terrestrial carnivorans from Test A. Overall verdict 'supports' only if both components support.

measured.unit: withers index WI (mean of the two pinniped species); terrestrial carnivoran WI min 1.238, median 1.910
measured.n: 45 carnivoran species (951 vertebrae) incl. 2 pinnipeds; 74 cetacean species (204 specimens, 8722 vertebrae)

caveats: Only two pinniped species (one phocid, one otariid) are in the carnivoran dataset; sirenians are absent from both datasets, and the bird-pelvis half of the claim was not tested at all. The verdict therefore covers pinnipeds and cetaceans only, not Thompson's 'all aquatic mammals'.

The 'haunch' part is not discriminating in Carnivora: terrestrial carnivorans themselves show no posterior-lumbar spine peak (median HI 0.80 < 1), and pinniped HI falls inside the terrestrial range (p = 0.77). Thompson's haunch spines refer mainly to ungulates, for which no comparable public data were used.

Pinniped anterior-thoracic spines are reduced (W 2.3-2.7 vs terrestrial 2.6-5.3) and the withers peak is absent (WI about 1.0), but the spines have not literally 'entirely disappeared'; Otaria byronia's W lies above the lowest terrestrial species (Martes foina).

Relative spine height from landmarks includes the neural arch and depends on where the authors placed the spinous-process landmarks; the cetacean values come from a different measurement protocol, so only the within-column ratio WI is compared across datasets.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right that domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species (he had in mind wolves and jackals), then some domestic dog maternal lineages should trace to a wild canid species other than the grey wolf: a non-trivial fraction of dog mitochondrial genomes should be closer to Canis aureus, C. lupaster, C. latrans, C. simensis, Cuon alpinus or Lycaon pictus than to any wild Canis lupus.
info.pass: Using complete mitochondrial genomes from GenBank (a systematic one-in-three sample of all 'Canis lupus familiaris' records, every wild 'Canis lupus' record, and every record of the other wild canid species), with CYTB and COX1 coding sequences extracted and compared by ungapped p-distance: at least 3 dog sequences AND at least 2 % of sampled dog sequences have their nearest non-dog sequence in a species other than Canis lupus. That outcome supports a multi-species origin.

measured.unit: sampled dog mitogenomes whose nearest non-dog sequence belongs to a species other than Canis lupus

caveats: Every one of 446 sampled dog mitogenomes is nearer to a wild grey wolf (mean 0.15 %, maximum 0.41 % p-distance) than to any other canid species (minimum 3.0 %, to Canis lupaster); no dog maternal lineage traces to a jackal, coyote, dhole, Ethiopian wolf or African wild dog. Darwin's 'several wild species' therefore fails for maternal ancestry.

Mitochondrial DNA is a single maternally inherited locus. Nuclear-genome studies (e.g. Freedman et al. 2014 PLoS Genetics; Frantz et al. 2016 Science; Bergstrom et al. 2020 Science) reach the same conclusion, that dogs derive from one wild species, the grey wolf, possibly from more than one wolf population; those are literature, not data used here. Low-level admixture from other canids into particular dog populations would not be excluded by this test.

GenBank 'Canis lupus' records include some African wolves labelled as the former subspecies C. lupus lupaster, which is why the minimum wolf-to-other-species distance is 0.11 %; this inflates the 'wild wolf' set with a few non-wolf sequences and could only have made a non-wolf dog origin easier, not harder, to detect.

None of the dog records carries a /breed qualifier, so breed coverage of the sample cannot be documented from metadata; the 1,357 records come from many independent studies (village dogs, ancient DNA, breed panels) and the systematic one-in-three sample was fixed before any sequence was examined.

info.hypothesis: If all domestic pigeon breeds descend from Columba livia (with its geographical sub-species) and not from several wild stocks, then every domestic-breed mitochondrial sequence should fall within the Columba livia cluster: nearer to C. livia sequences than to any other Columba species, and within intraspecific distance of C. livia.
info.pass: Using GenBank mitochondrial records of Columba livia and of all other Columba species, aligned by best ungapped offset to the COI and CYTB genes of the C. livia reference mitogenome NC_013978: every domestic-labelled sequence (organism 'Columba livia domestica', a /breed qualifier, or a breed name in the record) has its nearest non-domestic sequence in C. livia (or in a wild C. livia subspecies), and the maximum p-distance from any domestic sequence to the nearest C. livia sequence is < 2 %. Requires >= 10 domestic-labelled sequences from >= 5 named breeds or 'domestica' records; otherwise inconclusive (underpowered).

measured.unit: domestic-labelled Columba livia records whose nearest non-domestic mitochondrial sequence (COI or CYTB) belongs to another Columba species

caveats: 107 domestic records covering 22 named breeds (English and Indian Fantail, Kassel and other Tumblers, Jacobin, Hungarian Cropper (a pouter), Runt, King, Mondain, German Nun, German Magpie, German Beard, Vienna Highflier, Archangel, Ice pigeon, Lahore, Wroclaw Meat, Shiqi, three Egyptian breeds, 'Lucky') are all nearest to C. livia (mean 0.10 %, maximum 1.37 % p-distance) rather than to any of 20 other Columba species; none approaches C. oenas, C. palumbus, C. guinea or C. leuconota, the species Darwin's contemporaries proposed as alternative stocks. Carriers and Barbs, two breeds Darwin emphasised, are not among the named records.

Discriminating power against Columba rupestris is limited: the hill pigeon is only 1.2-2.6 % from domestic sequences in COI/CYTB, and C. livia and C. rupestris are sister species that hybridise. Every domestic record is nonetheless nearer to C. livia than to C. rupestris (0 of 115 record-gene comparisons the other way). Darwin's own wording ('with its geographical sub-species') would arguably absorb rupestris anyway.

Mitochondrial DNA tests maternal ancestry only; nuclear genomic work (Shapiro et al. 2013 Science; Stringham et al. 2012 Current Biology) also places all breeds within C. livia and is literature, not data used here.

Several GenBank 'Columba janthina' COI barcodes are identical to C. livia sequences and are almost certainly mislabelled; they never became the unique nearest neighbour because an equally close C. livia record always existed, so they did not affect the count.

info.hypothesis: Among flowering plants, species that are trees have separate sexes (dioecy or monoecy, i.e. unisexual flowers) more often than non-woody (herbaceous) species, and this excess recurs across orders rather than being confined to one or two clades.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using the GIFT database public API, join the sexual-system trait (3.4.1: dioecious / monoecious / bisexual) to the growth-form trait (1.2.1: tree / shrub / herb / other) for angiosperm species (Angiospermae in the GIFT taxonomy), keeping species whose growth-form value is a single category. 'Separate sexes' = dioecious or monoecious. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the odds ratio of separate sexes in trees versus herbs is >= 1.5 with two-sided Fisher exact p < 0.01, and (ii) among orders with at least 10 trees and at least 10 herbs in the joined data, the proportion of species with separate sexes is higher in trees than in herbs in at least two-thirds of orders.

measured.unit: odds ratio of separate sexes (dioecious or monoecious) in trees versus herbs, angiosperms in GIFT

caveats: GIFT sexual-system coverage is small (2,977 species, 1,865 usable angiosperms) and evidently enriched for dioecious species (55% of the trees and 7% of the herbs are dioecious, against roughly 6% of all angiosperms), so absolute proportions are not representative; the test relies on the contrast between growth forms, which would be biased only if the references coding sexual systems targeted dioecious trees more than dioecious herbs. Published syntheses with larger samples (e.g. Renner 2014; Vamosi et al. 2003) report the same association of dioecy with woody growth.

Only three orders (Apiales, Malpighiales, Rosales; derived/orders.csv) have >= 10 trees and >= 10 herbs with sexual-system data; trees exceed herbs in all three, but a sign test on three orders cannot be significant (p = 0.125), so the 'across all Orders' part of the claim is only weakly tested.
Shrubs are intermediate (60% separate-sexed), and trees still exceed shrubs (OR 2.1, p = 0.001), so the effect is not just woody vs herbaceous.
Species are treated as independent; no phylogenetic correction was applied, and the growth-form categories ignore within-species variation (species with mixed growth-form values were excluded).

info.hypothesis: For a regional flora, the number of genera added by naturalised (introduced) plants, as a proportion of the native genera, exceeds the number of naturalised species as a proportion of native species.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For every TDWG level-3 botanical country in the World Checklist of Vascular Plants with at least 100 native accepted species and at least 20 introduced accepted species, compute r_sp = (introduced species not native to the area) / (native species) and r_gen = (genera represented only by introduced species) / (genera with at least one native species). The claim is SUPPORTED if r_gen > r_sp in at least 80% of qualifying areas AND the median of r_gen / r_sp across areas is at least 1.25.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying level-3 areas with r_gen > r_sp

caveats: Both pre-registered thresholds are met only marginally (0.822 vs 0.80; median ratio 1.2535 vs 1.25), so the descriptive generalisation holds for most floras but the excess of genera is modest, not 'far more' as Darwin wrote; the 95% CI of the fraction of areas is [0.778, 0.859].

The secondary null model points the other way from Darwin's interpretation: in every area, drawing the same number of species at random from the non-native global pool would add more new genera than the real naturalised flora does (observed/expected new genera median 0.61). Naturalised plants are thus more concentrated in genera already native to the recipient flora than random species would be; the r_gen > r_sp pattern is largely an arithmetic consequence of genera being fewer than species, not evidence that naturalised plants are generically distinct from natives.

WCVP 'introduced' covers established aliens as recorded by Kew's editors and is incomplete for some regions (e.g. parts of tropical Asia and the Pacific, where the fraction of supporting areas is lowest); areas are TDWG level-3 units of very unequal size.
Darwin's examples (Gray's 1856 US flora, Britain) used 1850s genus concepts; current genera are narrower and more numerous.

info.hypothesis: In a phylogeny containing obligate cave (troglobitic/stygobitic) animals and surface animals from North America and Europe, each cave lineage is nested among, or sister to, taxa of its own continent; American and European cave taxa do not form clades with each other to the exclusion of surface taxa.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on the taxa listed in derived/taxa.csv (continent assignment verified with GBIF occurrences), for every cave taxon compute the node-count distance to the nearest same-continent taxon (cave or surface, d_same) and to the nearest other-continent cave taxon (d_othercave). The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) d_same <= d_othercave for at least 70% of cave taxa, and (ii) the induced tree contains no clade that includes at least one North American and at least one European cave taxon while containing no surface taxon ('exclusive transcontinental cave clade').

measured.unit: fraction of cave taxa with nearest same-continent taxon at least as close as nearest other-continent cave taxon

caveats: The synthetic tree has no branch lengths and several groups are poorly resolved (Asellidae genera, Niphargus/Crangonyctidae, Cholevinae), so node-count distances are coarse; both failing cases (Monolistra caeca, Ptomaphagus hirtus) arise where the induced tree places same-continent relatives in a deeper or unresolved position, and Ptomaphagus hirtus sits in a Staphylinoidea polytomy with the European Leptodirini.

The surface comparators are a pre-registered selection, not an exhaustive sample of each continent's fauna; adding taxa could only shorten d_same, so the design is lenient toward the claim in that respect, but the second criterion (no exclusive transcontinental cave clade) does not depend on how many surface taxa were sampled within the included families.

Proteus anguinus (Europe) is sister to Necturus (North America, surface) in the tree: a transatlantic family-level link that is not a cave-to-cave link; d_same for Proteus is the distance to European Salamandridae.
No European obligate cave fishes were available, so Amblyopsidae were not included; the cross-continent comparison therefore covers salamanders, amphipods, isopods, beetles and cave crickets only.

info.hypothesis: Electric organs (Darwin's stated example) occur in fish lineages that are separated on an independently estimated phylogeny by lineages lacking electric organs, so that the organ must have arisen more than once rather than being inherited from one common ancestor; the same holds for light-producing organs in insects (his second example).
info.pass: Pre-registered: on the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on a fixed list of electric-organ-bearing fish families and a fixed list of non-electric fish families, count (i) the Dollo minimum number of independent origins = number of maximal clades whose tips are all electric, and (ii) the Fitch parsimony minimum number of state changes. SUPPORTS if, for the electric-fish case, (i) >= 3 and (ii) >= 3 (no reconstruction with a single origin and fewer than three changes exists). The insect light-organ case is scored the same way and reported; it does not decide the verdict because the claim is existential ('has sometimes').

measured.unit: minimum independent origins (Dollo) of electric organs among fish families on the Open Tree synthetic tree

caveats: The six electric clades recovered (Torpediniformes, Rajidae, Mormyroidea, Gymnotiformes, Malapteruridae, Uranoscopidae) are separated by many non-electric families, so the result is insensitive to the exact background sample; it also matches the count in the modern literature, which was not used as input.
Only the pattern half of the claim (independent origins) is tested; whether natural selection on 'analogous variations' produced them is not addressed by a phylogeny.

Seven of 52 fish names (Narcinidae, Gymnotidae, Sternopygidae, Hypopomidae, Rhinobatidae, Serranidae, Lamnidae) could not be placed as tips because they are non-monophyletic in the synthetic tree or pruned from it; every dropped electric family belongs to a clade (Torpediniformes, Gymnotiformes) that is already represented, so the count is unchanged.

The luminous-insect case gives 2 independent origins (Lampyridae + Rhagophthalmidae; Keroplatidae) because Elateridae and Phengodidae could not be placed as tips; the literature count is higher. It was pre-registered as reported-only.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right that the migratory instinct varies within species in extent and may be lost, then partial migration (some individuals or populations of a species migrate while others of the same species stay resident) is a common condition among birds rather than a rare anomaly, and species classified as partial migrants show measurably more winter presence inside their breeding latitudes than obligate migrants do.
info.pass: Primary (AVONET, Tobias et al. 2022, BirdLife taxonomy sheet): P = share of bird species with a coded Migration score that are coded 2 (partially migratory) among all species, and Q = share coded 2 among non-sedentary species (score 2 or 3). Secondary (GBIF occurrence counts, Northern Hemisphere, years 2000 onward, non-fossil non-captive records, 5-degree latitude bands 0-80 N): for 12 pre-registered species, W = fraction of December-February records that fall in the latitude bands holding the central 80 % of June-July records (winter residency index). Partial-migrant set: Erithacus rubecula, Turdus merula, Sylvia atricapilla, Fringilla coelebs, Sturnus vulgaris, Turdus migratorius. Obligate-migrant set: Hirundo rustica, Apus apus, Phylloscopus trochilus, Setophaga striata, Tyrannus tyrannus, Cuculus canorus. Supports if P >= 0.20 and W is higher in the partial-migrant set than in the obligate set by a one-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05 with median W of the partial set >= 0.25.

measured.unit: share of bird species coded as partially migratory (AVONET Migration = 2) among all species with a migration score

caveats: P = 1196 / 10986 = 10.9 % of all bird species are coded as partial migrants, below the pre-registered 20 % 'common' threshold but far above the 5 % 'rare' threshold, so the primary criterion lands in the mixed zone. The threshold was set against all birds, most of which (80 %) are sedentary tropical species for which the migratory instinct does not arise; among the 2,182 species that migrate at all, 54.8 % (Q) are partial migrants, i.e. within-species variation in migratory extent is the majority condition among migrants. Had the pre-registration used Q the verdict would have been supports; it is reported as mixed because the rule is fixed in advance.

The secondary GBIF test passes clearly: median winter residency index W = 0.8561 for the six species pre-registered as partial migrants versus 0.2998 for the six obligate long-distance migrants (one-sided Mann-Whitney p = 0.0022). Winter records per summer record in the breeding core are 0.37-2.5 for the partial set versus 0.0007-0.11 for the obligate set, so the pattern Darwin described (some individuals of a species stay where others leave) is directly visible in occurrence data.

AVONET's codes for the six species I pre-registered as partial migrants are 3, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3 (Erithacus rubecula, Turdus merula and Sylvia atricapilla are coded fully migratory, Turdus merula sedentary), illustrating that a single species-level code compresses continuous within-species variation and will be assigned by predominant behaviour; this makes P a conservative estimate of how many species show some within-species variation in migration.

W for obligate migrants is inflated by a small number of winter records that are probably misidentifications, stragglers or data errors (e.g. Cuculus canorus W = 0.72 from 4,863 winter records against 579,201 summer records, a 0.8 % ratio); W is a ratio among winter records only and does not weight by how few they are. The winter/summer ratio reported above corrects for this.

info.hypothesis: If close interbreeding lessens fertility and an occasional cross with a distinct stock increases it, then (i) in a pedigreed wild mammal population, litter size should decline with the mother's inbreeding coefficient, and (ii) in experimentally inbred Drosophila populations, fecundity should be lower than in the outbred control and should rise again when individuals from different inbred populations are crossed (heterosis).
info.pass: Dataset 1 (Auclair et al. 2025, Pyrenean brown bear, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.w9ghx3g1s, file litter_size_dt.csv): the slope of litter size on maternal inbreeding coefficient (ordinary least squares, one row per litter; if the file supplies repeated mothers, a mother-level mean is also reported) is negative with one-sided p < 0.05, or, if the coefficient is categorical, mean litter size of the most inbred category is below that of the least inbred with p < 0.05. Dataset 2 (Pekkala et al. 2014, Drosophila littoralis, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.10154): (a) mean fecundity of inbred populations is below the outbred control in at least two of the three population-size treatments (N = 2, 10, 40), and (b) mean fecundity of inter-population crosses exceeds that of within-population matings (heterosis > 0) in a majority of population pairs or treatments for which both are reported. Verdict 'supports' if dataset 1 passes and both 2(a) and 2(b) pass; 'mixed' if dataset 1 passes but only one of 2(a)/2(b), or dataset 1 fails while both 2(a) and 2(b) pass; 'refutes' if litter size does not decline with inbreeding and inbred fecundity is not below control.

measured.unit: cubs per litter per unit maternal inbreeding coefficient (OLS slope)

caveats: The pre-registered bear test is marginal (one-sided p = 0.044, n = 66 litters); the litter's own inbreeding coefficient gives a clearer signal (p = 0.001). In the fly data the N = 40 treatment was not less fecund than the N = 500 control, so inbreeding depression in fecundity appears only at the two smallest population sizes, although fecundity declines significantly with the estimated inbreeding coefficient overall.
Two datasets only (one wild mammal population of a few dozen mothers; one laboratory Drosophila experiment); Darwin's claim is about plants and animals generally.

The pre-registered bear test uses the mother's inbreeding coefficient; the litter's own coefficient (closeness of the parents) is the more literal reading of 'close interbreeding' and is reported as an extra.

Bear litter sizes are counts (1-3) observed in the field; detection delay and maternal age are confounders that the simple regression does not model (the source paper fits mixed models with these covariates).

info.hypothesis: If first-generation hybrids are only slightly variable while later generations are extremely variable, then in an experimental cross the phenotypic variance of F2 hybrids should exceed that of F1 hybrids for most measured traits, and F1 variance should be no greater than that of the parental species.
info.pass: Dataset: Dryad doi:10.25338/B8QS5T (Cakile edentula x C. maritima artificial crosses with F1, F2 and backcross generations; CC0). For every continuous trait recorded for both F1 and F2 individuals from the artificial crosses (identified from the data files after download; traits with < 8 individuals in either generation are excluded), compute the variance of log-transformed values (equivalent to a squared coefficient of variation for positive traits; for traits with zero or negative values use the variance of the trait divided by its squared mean) in F1 and in F2. Primary statistic: the median across traits of the variance ratio F2/F1. Pass ('supports') if the median ratio is >= 1.5 AND the F2 variance exceeds the F1 variance in a majority of traits with an exact binomial sign-test p < 0.05. 'Mixed' if F2 exceeds F1 in a majority of traits with p < 0.05 but the median ratio is between 1.0 and 1.5 (more variable, but not 'extremely' so relative to F1), or if the median ratio is >= 1.5 but the sign test is not significant. The comparison of F1 variance with parental variance is reported as an extra and does not enter the verdict.

measured.unit: median across traits of the F2/F1 ratio of mean-scaled phenotypic variance

caveats: The outcome (median F2/F1 variance ratio between 1.0 and 1.5 with a bare, non-significant majority of traits more variable in F2) fell in a gap of the pre-registered decision rule; it is recorded as 'mixed'. By trait the pattern is strongly heterogeneous: floral and plant-size traits are 3-8 times more variable in F2, whereas seed mass, germination, phenology and fruit/seed counts are less variable in F2 than in F1.
A single interspecific plant cross with 36 F2 plants; Darwin's generalisation covers many plant and animal hybrids.
F1 plants come from many independent parental pairs (families), which adds between-family variance to F1 that a single-pair F1 would not have; this biases against the claim.
Mean-scaled variance compares dispersion across traits of different units but is sensitive to small means for count traits.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, more than 300 million years have elapsed since the latter part of the Chalk formation (the close of the Secondary, i.e. Mesozoic, era), so the radiometric age of the top of the Cretaceous / Mesozoic must exceed 300 Ma, and the denudation of the Weald (removal of the Chalk and underlying beds over the Wealden dome) could have occupied about 300 million years.
info.pass: The age of the Cretaceous-Paleogene (Mesozoic-Cenozoic) boundary in the current International Chronostratigraphic Chart, as served by Macrostrat and cross-checked against the Paleobiology Database timescale, is >= 300 Ma; equivalently the maximum possible duration of post-Chalk denudation (time since the youngest Chalk) is >= 300 Myr.

measured.unit: Ma (age of the top of the Cretaceous / Mesozoic = end of Chalk deposition)

caveats: The test accepts the ICS radiometric calibration of the geological time scale as correct; the result rests on that body of dating, not on an independent measurement made here.

Darwin hedged his own number ('some crude notion'), and in the 3rd edition (1861) he withdrew the passage; the claim as stated in the 1st edition is nevertheless a definite figure and is what is tested.

Which bed counts as 'the latter part of the Secondary period' moves the target by at most a few tens of Myr (Cenomanian base 100.5 Ma to Maastrichtian top 66 Ma); no reading comes within a factor of 2.9 of 300 Ma.

API responses can change when the servers adopt a newer ICS chart, so the SHA-256 values record the responses at retrieval time rather than a versioned archive file; the boundary age of 66.0 Ma has been stable across ICS chart versions since 2012.

info.hypothesis: Clause 1 (absolute): wholly soft-bodied organisms leave no fossils, so animal phyla without mineralised or sclerotised hard parts should have zero fossil occurrences. Clause 2 (bias): the fossil record is strongly biased toward organisms with hard parts, so fossil occurrences per living species should be far higher for biomineralising phyla than for wholly soft-bodied phyla.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Wholly soft-bodied phyla: Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Nemertea, Chaetognatha, Priapulida, Onychophora, Nematoda, Nematomorpha, Xenacoelomorpha, Gastrotricha, Placozoa, Rotifera, Tardigrada. Biomineralising phyla: Mollusca, Brachiopoda, Echinodermata, Bryozoa, Porifera, Cnidaria. For each phylum, count fossil occurrences in the Paleobiology Database (occs/list, rowcount) and accepted living species in the GBIF backbone taxonomy. Clause 1 is REFUTED if the soft-bodied phyla together have >= 10 fossil occurrences spread over >= 3 phyla, and SUPPORTED if they have 0. Clause 2 is SUPPORTED if the median of (fossil occurrences / living accepted species) over biomineralising phyla is >= 100 times the median over soft-bodied phyla, and REFUTED if it is < 10 times. Overall verdict: 'supports' if clause 1 supported and clause 2 supported; 'mixed' if clause 1 refuted and clause 2 supported; 'refutes' if clause 2 refuted (whatever clause 1 shows).

measured.unit: PBDB body-fossil occurrences in the 13 wholly soft-bodied phyla

caveats: Clause 1 (absolute) is refuted: 937 body-fossil occurrences are recorded for 12 of the 13 soft-bodied phyla, including unambiguous ones such as ctenophores (Chengjiang, Hunsrück), nematodes and nematomorphs in amber, nemerteans (Solnhofen) and rotifers (Dominican amber). Even excluding phyla whose fossils are mostly sclerites or spines (Priapulida incl. palaeoscolecids, Chaetognatha incl. protoconodonts, Onychophora incl. Microdictyon plates), 184 occurrences remain in 9 phyla.

Clause 2 (bias) is strongly supported: the median mineralised phylum has 4.6 fossil occurrences per living species, the median soft-bodied phylum 0.005 (ratio ~960; pooled ratio 6.1 vs 0.017). Brachiopoda alone (316 per living species) reflect their far greater past diversity, not only preservation.

GBIF Backbone extinct flags are incomplete, so 'living species' (total minus flagged extinct) overestimates living diversity for groups with many unflagged fossil species (Mollusca), which makes the mineralised ratios conservative.

Some PBDB identifications of soft-bodied fossils are contested (e.g. the single 'Placozoa' and two 'Xenacoelomorpha' records from the Triassic of Troistedt); the clause-1 refutation does not depend on them.

info.hypothesis: If oceans have occupied their present areas and continents theirs since the earliest Silurian, then at every time from ~440 Ma to the present the geographic locations now occupied by land were occupied by continental land, and the locations now occupied by ocean were ocean.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using the GPlates Web Service with the Merdith et al. (2021) plate model, the model's coastline polygons are reconstructed to 440, 400, 350, 300, 250, 200, 150, 100 and 50 Ma. On a 2x2 degree global grid (area-weighted by cos latitude), classify each present-day grid cell as land or ocean from the time-0 coastlines. L_all = area fraction of present land cells that fall inside reconstructed coastline polygons at every one of the nine times; O_all = area fraction of present ocean cells that fall outside them at every time. The claim is SUPPORTED if L_all >= 0.75 and O_all >= 0.75.

measured.unit: area fraction of present-day land that lies within reconstructed continental coastlines at all nine times 440-50 Ma (MERDITH2021)

caveats: At 440 Ma only 22% of present land area lay under reconstructed continental land at the same geographic location, less than the 29% expected if continents were placed at random, and 78% of present ocean area was ocean, close to the random expectation of 71%; essentially no present land (0.07%) was land continuously at all nine times, and only 34% of present ocean was ocean throughout (the Pacific). PALEOMAP gives the same picture (0.5% and 34%).

Plate models place continents in a palaeomagnetic or mantle reference frame; palaeolongitude is poorly constrained in the Palaeozoic, so the exact overlap at 440-300 Ma is uncertain, but no reference-frame choice can keep the Atlantic and Indian Ocean basins (which opened after 200 Ma) in place, so the refutation does not depend on the deep-time frame.

The coastline polygons are present-day coastlines carried rigidly with their plates, not palaeo-shorelines; they approximate continental crust rather than emergent land, which if anything favours Darwin's 'large tracts of land' reading.
The 2 degree grid and even-odd test treat polygon edges coarsely; this affects the fractions at the percent level only.

info.hypothesis: If different classes and genera change at different rates, then taxonomic turnover measured as the stratigraphic duration of extinct genera in the Paleobiology Database should differ substantially among major animal classes, and, within classes, among orders.
info.pass: Using PBDB genus-rank taxa with first- and last-appearance ages for 14 higher taxa (Trilobita, Brachiopoda, Bivalvia, Gastropoda, Cephalopoda, Anthozoa, Echinoidea, Crinoidea, Ostracoda, Bryozoa, Mammalia, Reptilia, Actinopterygii, Chondrichthyes), restricted to extinct genera with >= 5 occurrences, genus duration = midpoint of first-appearance range minus midpoint of last-appearance range. Clause A (between classes): a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across the higher taxa has p < 0.001 AND epsilon-squared effect size >= 0.02 AND the ratio of the largest to the smallest group median duration is >= 2. Clause B (between genera grouped by order, within classes): within each higher taxon having >= 3 orders with >= 20 qualifying genera each, a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across orders has p < 0.001 and epsilon-squared >= 0.02; clause B passes if this holds in a majority of eligible higher taxa. Verdict 'supports' if A and B pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if neither.

measured.unit: ratio of largest to smallest median genus duration among the 14 higher taxa (Myr/Myr)

caveats: Genus duration is a taxonomic proxy for rate of change; it conflates true evolutionary rate with preservation potential, sampling intensity and how finely each class is split by taxonomists.
Durations of genera with few occurrences are truncated; the >= 5 occurrence filter (and the >= 20 sensitivity run) reduces but does not remove range truncation, which differs among classes.
Groups are not all of class rank (Brachiopoda and Bryozoa are phyla) because PBDB class membership is unstable for them.

Only extinct genera are included (extant genera have open-ended durations), which excludes the long-lived 'living fossil' lineages Darwin also had in mind and so is conservative with respect to the spread of rates.

info.hypothesis: For extinct marine-invertebrate families, the number of genera recorded per geological stage rises from a low value at the family's first appearance to an interior maximum and then declines to a low value at its last appearance, rather than appearing or disappearing at or near maximal diversity or showing several separate peaks.
info.pass: Pre-registered: a family's trajectory is scored 'Darwinian' when, with R_i = range-through genus richness in stage bin i (from the family's first to last bin) and M = max R_i: (a) R_first <= 0.5 M, (b) R_last <= 0.5 M, and (c) the set of bins with R_i > 0.5 M is contiguous (a single peak). The claim is SUPPORTED if at least two thirds (>= 0.667) of qualifying families are Darwinian, where qualifying = extinct family within the sampled higher taxa with >= 10 genera having occurrences and a duration spanning >= 6 stage bins.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying extinct families with low start, low end and a single peak

caveats: The two 'gradual' components of the claim are strongly supported: 93% of families start and 95% end at <= half their maximum genus richness, and only 2.6% peak in their first and 1.0% in their last stage. What fails is the single-maximum component: 34% of families have two or more separate peaks above half-maximum, so the overall fraction (0.58) falls in the pre-registered MIXED band.

Range-through counting at stage resolution structurally favours low first and last bins (a family's first bin can only contain genera that originate in it), so the start/end components are partly a counting artefact; peak position (median 0.43 of the way through the family's duration) and the medians of 6 bins of rise and 8 bins of fall are more informative.

Raw PBDB counts were used without sampling standardisation; uneven rock record and research effort produce spurious secondary peaks and troughs, which bias against the single-peak condition. Stage bins vary in length (about 2-15 Myr).

Only extinct families were used, so the result says nothing about families still at or before their maximum. 'Group' was read as family and 'number of species' as number of genera; species-within-genus counts were not tested.

info.hypothesis: If Tertiary extinctions were gradual and place-by-place rather than catastrophic, the last occurrences of extinct genera should be spread across many Tertiary stages rather than concentrated in one or two, and genera recorded on several continents should usually disappear from those continents at demonstrably different times, more often than genera killed in the known K-Pg catastrophe.
info.pass: Two groups are analysed separately with Paleobiology Database genus-level occurrences from the Campanian through the Pliocene: Mollusca and Mammalia. Clause A (no catastrophic concentration): among PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence (midpoint of its age range) falls in the Tertiary (Danian to Piacenzian, 17 ICS stages), the single stage holding the most last occurrences holds < 1/3 of them, and at least 4 stages are needed to accumulate 50% of them when stages are ranked by count. Clause B (place by place): among those Tertiary-extinct genera that have >= 2 occurrences on each of >= 2 continents (PBDB continent codes), the fraction whose regional last occurrences are staggered (the earliest-vanishing continent's last-occurrence minimum age is older than the last-vanishing continent's last-occurrence maximum age, i.e. non-overlapping age ranges) is > 0.5 AND exceeds the same fraction computed for the K-Pg control set (PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence midpoint falls in the Maastrichtian, using Campanian-Maastrichtian occurrences). A clause passes only if it passes in both groups. Verdict 'supports' if both clauses pass, 'mixed' if exactly one passes, 'refutes' if neither passes.

measured.unit: mean over the two groups of the fraction of multi-continent Tertiary-extinct genera with staggered regional last occurrences

caveats: Regional staggering is only detectable at the resolution of the occurrence dating: when a genus's last occurrences on two continents are both dated only to the same stage (common for mammals, whose records are often dated to land-mammal ages spanning several stages, and for all Maastrichtian records in the control), the ranges overlap and the genus is scored 'not staggered'. The mammal result for clause B is therefore partly a dating-resolution result, and the K-Pg control's zero staggering reflects the same effect as much as the catastrophe itself.
The Mammalia K-Pg control set is empty (no extinct mammal genus with >= 2 Maastrichtian occurrences on each of two continents), so for mammals clause B rests only on the > 0.5 condition.

Genus last occurrences in PBDB are truncated by sampling (Signor-Lipps), so both the spread across stages and the regional staggering are biased toward looking gradual; the Maastrichtian control set calibrates this for clause B but not for clause A.
The Tertiary window ends at the Piacenzian; genera that actually died out in the Pleistocene but have no PBDB Pleistocene record are counted as Piacenzian extinctions, inflating the youngest stage.

info.hypothesis: Marine faunas on different continents change in step: the genus composition of a stage on one continent identifies the same (or an adjacent) stage on the other continents, and the magnitude of faunal change between consecutive stages is correlated across continents.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per ICS stage (stages >= 1 Myr) for each of six PBDB continents (North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia), (A) for every continent-stage with >= 100 genera, find the stage whose pooled genus list from the other five continents has the highest Jaccard similarity with it; and (B) for every continent, compute the series of proportional genus loss between consecutive stages (fraction of genera in stage i absent from stage i+1, both stages >= 100 genera) and the Spearman correlation of this series between every pair of continents. The claim is SUPPORTED if in (A) the best-matching stage is the same or an adjacent stage for >= 85% of continent-stages, AND in (B) the mean pairwise Spearman correlation is > 0 with permutation p < 0.01 (independent permutation of stage order within each continent, 2000 permutations).

measured.unit: fraction of continent-stages (>= 100 genera) whose fauna best matches the same or an adjacent stage on the other continents

caveats: Test (A) fell short of the pre-registered 85% bar: 78.4% (95% Wilson CI 73.9-82.4%) of continent-stages are best matched by the same or an adjacent stage elsewhere (53.8% exact, 87.4% within two stages, median offset 0). Test (B) passed clearly: mean pairwise Spearman rho of proportional genus loss = 0.31, permutation p = 0.0005; 12 of 13 continent pairs positive. The pre-registered rule therefore gives 'mixed'.

Matching success depends strongly on sampling: Europe 88%, Asia 86%, North America 85% (the three continents with median > 300 genera per stage) versus Africa 66%, Australia 55%, South America 54% (median 165-185 genera per stage). The failures are mostly a sampling-depth problem rather than faunal provinciality: for the 77 mismatched continent-stages the true stage's Jaccard is on average 79% of the best stage's, i.e. the correct stage is nearly tied.

Mismatches concentrate in the Neogene-Quaternary (e.g. Calabrian faunas of three continents best match the Aquitanian) where genus-level turnover is low and many genera persist for the whole period, and in thin Permian/Oligocene records. Low turnover is the opposite of what would falsify Darwin's claim (asynchronous change), so the 'mixed' verdict understates support for synchrony of change while correctly recording that genus lists alone cannot date stages to within one stage on poorly sampled continents.

PBDB stage assignments of collections rest partly on biostratigraphic correlation, so some cross-continent agreement in (A) is expected by construction; test (B) uses magnitudes of turnover, which are not used in dating, and is the more independent test. The PBDB is a live database; the retrieved responses are hashed and dated so the run can be audited but later runs may differ.

info.hypothesis: The taxonomic similarity of marine fossil faunas from two geological stages decreases with the time separating them, consecutive stages being far more similar than widely separated ones, and the fauna of each stage is intermediate between the faunas of the stages before and after it.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per international stage (ICS 2020 scale as served by PBDB; stages shorter than 1 Myr excluded; stages with fewer than 200 genera excluded), compute Jaccard similarity between all stage pairs. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the Spearman correlation between pairwise Jaccard similarity and the separation of stage midpoints (Myr) is <= -0.5 with Mantel permutation p < 0.001, (ii) the mean Jaccard similarity of consecutive stage pairs is at least 2 times the mean similarity of pairs separated by 5 or more intervening stages, and (iii) for at least 80% of stages i with both neighbours, J(i-1, i+1) <= min(J(i-1, i), J(i, i+1)) (intermediacy).

measured.unit: Spearman rho between pairwise Jaccard genus similarity of stages and their midpoint age separation (Myr)

caveats: PBDB collections are assigned to stages partly by biostratigraphy, so some of the within-stage homogeneity is built into the data; the graded decay over 2-20 stages (0.29, 0.22, 0.17, ... 0.02) is not explicable by that alone, and the ratio at exactly five stages' separation (0.29 / 0.12) still exceeds the pre-registered factor of 2.
The 'remote' mean (gap >= 5 stages, 0.023) is dominated by very distant pairs; the profile by separation is given in measured.extra so the reader can choose a different threshold.

Genus sharing is a proxy for Darwin's 'closely related'; shared genera undercount relatedness between remote stages that share families but no genera, so the measured decay is steeper than a phylogenetic distance would be.
Intermediacy failed for 12 of 92 stages, mostly short or poorly sampled stages where sampling noise makes the two neighbours marginally more similar to each other than to the middle stage.

info.hypothesis: If each area's later-Tertiary inhabitants left modified descendants in the same area, then the families of terrestrial mammals recorded as fossils on a continent in the Miocene-Pliocene should have living members on that same continent more often than they have living members on any other continent.
info.pass: Fossil side: PBDB Miocene-Pliocene (23.03-2.58 Ma) occurrences of Mammalia on each of five continents (Africa, Eurasia = PBDB EUR+ASI, North America, South America, Australia), excluding marine orders/families (Cetacea, Sirenia, Desmostylia, Phocidae, Otariidae, Odobenidae), giving for each continent the set of fossil families with >= 2 occurrences there. Living side: GBIF non-fossil, non-captive occurrence facets by family for Mammalia on each GBIF continent (Europe+Asia merged), a family counting as living on a continent if it has >= 20 such records there (same marine exclusions). For each continent X, S(X) = fraction of X's fossil families that are living on X, and O(X) = mean over the other four continents Y of the fraction of X's fossil families living on Y. Pass if S(X) > O(X) for all five continents AND the pooled ratio mean S / mean O >= 1.2 AND, in a permutation test that randomly reassigns the five living-family sets to continents (all 120 permutations, i.e. exact), the observed sum of S(X) is the maximum or tied maximum (p <= 1/120 + ties). The same statistics at genus level (fossil genera that are extant and living on the same continent) are reported as an extra and do not enter the verdict.

measured.unit: ratio of mean same-continent survival fraction to mean other-continent survival fraction, later-Tertiary mammal families

caveats: Family-level alliance is coarse; cosmopolitan families (Bovidae, Felidae, Canidae, Muridae) raise both same- and other-continent fractions and dilute the signal, while endemic families (marsupial and xenarthran families) carry it, as in Darwin's own examples.
GBIF 'living on a continent' includes introduced and feral species (e.g. Muridae and Leporidae in Australia), which biases toward sharing with other continents and so against the claim.
PBDB family assignments and GBIF backbone family names are mostly but not entirely harmonised; mismatched spellings or re-ranked families count as 'not living', equally on all continents.

The Great American Biotic Interchange (c. 3 Ma) means part of South America's Pliocene fauna is of North American origin, which Darwin could not know; it makes the North/South America comparison conservative.

info.hypothesis: Across regions of the world, the taxonomic similarity of their biotas is explained by which land mass they belong to (shared history and barriers) rather than by the similarity of their climates; in particular, climatically matched regions on different continents (e.g. the Mediterranean-climate belts of Australia, South Africa and Chile) share fewer taxa than climatically different regions on the same continent.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For the 23 regions in derived/regions.csv (5x5 degree boxes, pre-assigned to a continent and to one of six climate classes), genus lists of mammals, birds and vascular plants are taken from GBIF occurrences (genera with >= 3 georeferenced records in the box), and climate from the NASA POWER climatology (annual mean 2 m temperature, annual precipitation, seasonal temperature range at five points per box). For each taxon group, pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity between regions is regressed on standardised climate distance and a same-continent indicator (permutation test over region labels, 2000 permutations). The claim is SUPPORTED if, in at least 2 of the 3 taxon groups, (a) the same-continent effect is significant (p < 0.05) and its partial R-squared exceeds that of climate distance, and (b) the mean Jaccard similarity of climate-matched pairs on different continents is lower than the mean similarity of climate-mismatched pairs on the same continent.

measured.unit: taxon groups (of 3) in which same-continent membership outweighs climate distance and climate-matched cross-continental pairs are less similar than climate-mismatched same-continent pairs

caveats: For vascular plants the result is reversed: climate distance explains more of the genus-level dissimilarity (partial R2 0.36) than continent (0.08), although the same-continent effect is still significant and climate-matched cross-continental pairs are still (non-significantly) less similar than mismatched same-continent pairs. Genus-level plant composition is strongly shared across continents (cosmopolitan and Holarctic genera, plus introduced species in GBIF), so the claim holds for mammals and birds but not, at genus rank, for plants.

GBIF occurrences include introduced and vagrant taxa and uneven sampling; the >= 3 record filter removes only the rarest. Introduced species inflate cross-continental similarity and bias the test against the claim.

Climate is summarised by three variables from a 0.5 degree reanalysis-based climatology at five points per box; finer climatic structure (soils, topography) is not represented. The 'same continent' indicator also absorbs geographic distance, which Darwin treated as part of the same explanation (barriers and history).

Darwin's own triad (SW Australia, Western Cape, central Chile) shares a mean of 16% of mammal genera and 24% of bird genera, versus 30% and 57% for climatically different regions on the same continent.

info.hypothesis: Across pairs of regions of similar size, the species-level dissimilarity of their terrestrial faunas increases with the impassability and age of the barrier separating them (none < large river < shallow recently-dry strait < mountain range or desert < deep never-bridged strait < ocean basin), and this ordering persists after controlling for the geographic distance between the regions.
info.pass: Pre-registered: 26 fixed region pairs are assigned a barrier rank (0 none, 1 large river, 2 shallow strait dry at glacial low stands, 3 mountain range or desert, 4 deep strait never bridged, 5 ocean basin). For each pair and each of three groups (Rodentia, Squamata, Amphibia) the Sørensen dissimilarity (1 - 2|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|)) of species sets (GBIF occurrences, >= 3 records per species in the box) is computed and averaged over the three groups. SUPPORTS if Spearman's rho between mean dissimilarity and barrier rank is >= 0.5 with p < 0.01 (n = 26), AND the partial Spearman correlation controlling for log centroid distance is > 0 with p < 0.05, AND mean dissimilarity of the rank-0 (no barrier) pairs is lower than that of every barrier class with rank >= 2.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between barrier rank and mean species-level Sørensen dissimilarity (Rodentia, Squamata, Amphibia)

caveats: Rodentia reached the 10-species minimum in only 13 of 25 pairs (islands and arid regions are thinly recorded), so most pairs are averaged over Squamata and Amphibia; all three groups individually show positive rank correlations (0.51, 0.70, 0.70).

Distance is only partly controlled: the desert and ocean pairs are much farther apart (2000-8600 km) than the others, and climate differs across the Sahara, Nullarbor and Sierra Nevada pairs. The partial correlation (0.80) and the fact that the mountain and deep-strait pairs (240-910 km) are more dissimilar than the no-barrier pairs at 560-1120 km address but do not remove this.
Barrier ranks are a pre-registered judgement; replicate counts per class are small (river 1, desert 2, ocean 2, mountains 3).
Introduced species remain in the data except Rattus and Mus; they lower dissimilarity across the widest barriers and so bias against the claim.

info.hypothesis: Within one continent, the genus-level composition of the fauna/flora of two strongly contrasting habitats (hot desert vs. humid tropical forest) is more similar than the composition of the same habitat type on two different continents; i.e. geographic region, not habitat, is the primary predictor of taxonomic affinity.
info.pass: Pre-registered: for each of five taxonomic groups (Mammalia, Aves, Squamata, Amphibia, Magnoliopsida), compute the Sørensen similarity of genus sets (2|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|), GBIF occurrence-derived genus lists, genera with >= 5 records per region) for (i) the 5 within-continent / different-habitat region pairs and (ii) the 20 between-continent / same-habitat region pairs. The claim is SUPPORTED if the mean of (i) exceeds the mean of (ii) in at least 4 of the 5 groups AND a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test pooling all groups' pairs (i) vs (ii) gives p < 0.01.

measured.unit: groups (of 5) where within-continent/different-habitat mean genus Sørensen > between-continent/same-habitat mean

caveats: Magnoliopsida is the one group where the same habitat on another continent is as similar (0.307) as a different habitat on the same continent (0.295); introduced weeds and genuinely cosmopolitan plant genera both contribute, and GBIF cannot flag introductions reliably.

Amphibia is underpowered (as few as 4 genera in the Thar desert box) but the criterion was still met in 4 groups with >= 20 genera everywhere (Mammalia, Aves, Squamata, Magnoliopsida); Amphibia is reported but did not decide the verdict.
Genus sharing is a pre-phylogenetic proxy for 'affinity'; no phylogenetic beta-diversity was computed.
Introduced and vagrant species other than the 11 excluded commensal genera remain in the lists; they bias toward between-continent similarity, i.e. against the claim.

info.hypothesis: Across well-recorded classes of animals and plants, most genera (and a larger share of genera than of families) have essentially all of their modern occurrence records within a single continental region; and among mammal genera, those whose species are most closely related (youngest crown age in a dated phylogeny) occupy fewer regions and are more often confined to a single region than genera whose species are more distantly related.
info.pass: Clause 1 (regional confinement by rank): in each of the analysed classes (Mammalia, Aves, Amphibia, Reptilia, Magnoliopsida, Liliopsida, Pinopsida; GBIF backbone), the fraction of assessable genera that are confined to one region (>= 95% of their continent-assigned, non-fossil, non-captive occurrence records in one of six regions: Africa, Eurasia, North America, South America, Oceania, Antarctica) is > 0.50 in at least five of the seven classes, and in at least five of seven classes the confined fraction for genera exceeds the confined fraction for families. Clause 2 (natural genera are local, mammals): the Spearman partial correlation between genus crown age (MRCA age of the sampled congeneric species in the Upham et al. 2019 DNA-only MCC tree) and the number of regions holding >= 5% of the genus's records, controlling for log(number of sampled species in the genus), is positive with p < 0.05, AND the single-region fraction among genera in the youngest crown-age tercile exceeds that in the oldest tercile. The claim is 'supports' if both clauses pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if both fail.

measured.unit: mean across classes of the fraction of assessable genera with >= 95% of records in one region

caveats: GBIF 'Reptilia' (classKey 358) is a pro-parte synonym with no occurrences in the current backbone, so the pre-registered reptile class was run as Squamata (classKey 11592253), which holds most reptile genera.

GBIF continents are a coarse proxy for Darwin's biogeographic regions; merging Europe and Asia follows the Palaearctic but leaves Wallace's line and the Nearctic/Neotropical boundary at the continental edge.

Genus-level 'assessable' counts include extinct genera that have non-fossil basis-of-record entries and genera whose records are introductions or captives not flagged as LIVING_SPECIMEN; both bias against confinement, so clause 1 is conservative.

Recording effort is very uneven (Europe and North America dominate); the >= 20 record floor reduces but does not remove under-recording of tropical taxa, which could make some truly widespread genera look confined.

info.hypothesis: If now-separate continents and the existing oceanic islands were not continuously or almost continuously joined by land during the period of existing species, then even at the lowest Quaternary sea level (about -130 m) the sea floor between them should remain submerged: oceanic islands should not connect to any continent, and the Atlantic, Indian and Southern Ocean gaps between continents should not close.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using the NOAA ETOPO 2022 global relief model exported from the NCEI image service onto a 0.1-degree grid, cells with elevation >= -130 m are treated as potentially emergent and labelled into connected components (with longitude wrap). The 45 pre-registered oceanic islands in derived/sites.csv are checked for membership of a continental component (continent seeds in the same file). Five continental gaps are tested for connection at -130 m: (T1) Eurasia-North America via the Atlantic, with the Bering region (lat > 55 N, lon 160 E to 160 W) masked as deep; (T2) Africa/Eurasia-South America; (T3) Australia/New Guinea-Asia; (T4) Antarctica-South America; (T5) Antarctica-Australia. The claim is SUPPORTED if none of T1-T5 is connected at -130 m and at least 90% of the oceanic islands are unconnected. A set of 20 continental (shelf or fragment) islands is run as a positive control and is not part of the verdict.

measured.unit: fraction of pre-registered oceanic islands whose emergent component at -130 m contains no continent seed

caveats: Deviation from the pre-registration, disclosed: the plan named the NCEI ArcGIS ImageServer (DEM_all mosaic) exportImage as the access route; it was replaced by the NCEI THREDDS subset service of the ETOPO 2022 60 arc-second file itself because the ImageServer mosaic blends ETOPO with higher-resolution coastal DEMs and resamples bilinearly, whereas the THREDDS route delivers unmodified ETOPO 2022 samples. The dataset (ETOPO 2022, DOI 10.25921/fd45-gt74), grid resolution and all analysis rules are as pre-registered.

Result: 0 of 5 continental gaps are connected at -130 m (sill depths: Eurasia-North America via the North Atlantic -757 m, Africa-South America -3750 m, Australia-Asia -1321 m, Antarctica-South America and Antarctica-Australia -3422 m); 0 of 45 oceanic islands join a continent at -130 m, and 43 of 45 remain isolated even at -1000 m (the two exceptions, Iceland and the Faroes, join Europe only at -608 m across the Greenland-Scotland Ridge). The Bering connection, excluded from the verdict as explained in the pre-registration, has a sill of -45 m and joins Eurasia and North America at -130 m, as Darwin himself allowed.

Positive controls behave as expected: 14 of 20 continental islands connect at -130 m with shallow sills (Great Britain -30 m, Ireland -53 m, Borneo -35 m, Sumatra -20 m, Java -32 m, New Guinea -13 m, Tasmania -58 m, Newfoundland -63 m, Taiwan -56 m, Hainan -21 m, Trinidad -14 m, Sakhalin -3 m, Sri Lanka -8 m, Honshu -119 m), while the continental fragments (Madagascar, New Zealand, New Caledonia, Seychelles) are isolated to -1000 m, Cuba joins only at -728 m and the Falklands at -163 m. The method therefore discriminates shelf islands from isolated ones at the resolution used.

Nine small oceanic islands (Ascension, Diego Garcia, Cocos Keeling, Amsterdam, Juan Fernandez, Pitcairn, Norfolk, Lord Howe, Raoul) are not sampled as land on the 0.1-degree grid; six were located by their -130 m bank and three (Cocos Keeling, Amsterdam, Pitcairn) have no emergent cell within 0.5 degrees, so they are counted as unconnected because the surrounding sampled sea floor is far below -130 m. Excluding them changes nothing (36/36 resolved islands unconnected).

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right that the temperature of the whole world was simultaneously cooler during the Glacial period, then within one and the same dated interval of the last glaciation (the Last Glacial Maximum chronozone, 19-23 ka) surface temperature should have been below modern values everywhere: in both hemispheres, at all latitudes, and in every ocean basin, not only in the northern regions where glacial geology was first described.
info.pass: In the MARGO gridded compilation of LGM (19-23 ka) sea-surface temperature anomalies (modern minus LGM, annual mean, 5x5 degree cells), (i) >= 90 % of cells with data show cooling (anomaly > 0), (ii) in every 30-degree latitude band of each hemisphere with >= 5 cells, and in each of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific basins, >= 80 % of cells show cooling and the area-weighted mean anomaly is > 0 with a one-sample t-test p < 0.01, and (iii) the area-weighted global mean anomaly is >= 1 degree C.

measured.unit: fraction of 5x5 degree ocean grid cells with LGM (19-23 ka) annual SST below modern

caveats: Within the single LGM chronozone 84.4 % of 307 ocean cells were cooler than today (area-weighted mean cooling 2.06 C, p = 2e-39), both hemispheres (82 % and 88 %), every latitude band and every basin cooled on average with p < 1e-9, except the 60-90 N band (50 % of cells, p = 0.10). No subset shows majority warming, so the refutation condition is far from met; the 'supports' thresholds (>= 90 % globally, >= 80 % in every subset) are missed by the global figure, the Atlantic (79.5 %), the Pacific (79.3 %) and the Nordic Seas. Darwin's hedged version ('along broad longitudinal belts from pole to pole') is clearly supported; the literal 'whole world' is supported as a mean statement but not cell by cell.

Of the 48 cells warmer than modern, only 5 are warmer by more than MARGO's stated total error, and 142 of 307 cells rest on a single record; among cells with >= 2 records 88.5 % are cooler. The warm cells cluster in the Nordic Seas and the north-west Pacific, where foraminiferal transfer functions are known to give ambiguous LGM estimates (sea-ice and seasonality effects), i.e. where the proxy is least reliable rather than where the climate was demonstrably warmer.

Only sea-surface temperature is tested; terrestrial pollen- and glacier-based LGM reconstructions show cooling on all continents but were not used here because no comparable gridded text-format compilation with quantified errors was located.

Simultaneity is inherited from the MARGO chronozone (19-23 ka, independently dated at each site); the test shows that the same dated interval was cold almost everywhere, which is what Darwin asserted, but it does not test the longer onset/termination phasing between hemispheres.

info.hypothesis: The vascular-plant floras of high tropical mountains share a few identical species and many more genera with the temperate lowland floras of both hemispheres, and they share more genera with those temperate floras than the tropical lowlands at the foot of the same mountains do; the temperate lowland floras of the two hemispheres are likewise related at the genus level beyond what tropical lowlands share with them.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Regions: 4 tropical high-mountain regions M (GBIF records with elevation >= 3500 m in the N Andes and Trans-Mexican volcanic belt, >= 3000 m in the East African mountains and New Guinea highlands), their 4 tropical-lowland controls C (same bounding box, elevation <= 800 m), 3 northern (N) and 3 southern (S) temperate lowland regions L (elevation <= 600 m). Species/genus present if >= 3 records. For a pair (X, L): f_sp = |species(X) ∩ species(L)| / |species(X)|, f_gen = |genera(X) ∩ genera(L)| / |genera(X)|. SUPPORTS requires all of: (A) in >= 20 of the 24 (M, L) pairs, 0 < f_sp < 0.5 f_gen (identical species exist but are the minority of allied relationships); (B) in >= 20 of 24 (M, L) pairs f_gen(M, L) > f_gen(C_M, L) (one-sided binomial sign test vs 0.5, p < 0.01); (C) in >= 7 of the 9 (N, S) pairs f_gen(N, S) exceeds the mean over k of f_gen(C_k, S).

measured.unit: of 24 (tropical mountain, temperate lowland) pairs in which the mountain flora shares a larger fraction of its genera with the temperate flora than the adjacent tropical lowland flora does

caveats: Introduced species inflate species identity: e.g. 28% of the Central European lowland species set is also recorded in lowland New Zealand, mostly European weeds and crops. Criterion (A) (identical species exist but are a minority) is therefore satisfied partly for the wrong reason; the genus-level criteria (B) and (C) are less affected because the comparison is against tropical lowland controls that also receive introductions.

f_gen normalises by the source region's genus count, so the very genus-rich Andean lowland control (2206 genera) is penalised relative to the Andean alpine set (595); the Mexican and East African controls, which are similar in size to their mountain sets, show the same ordering, so the result does not depend on this.

Elevation comes from the GBIF 'elevation' field, which is missing on many records; regional sets are therefore samples of the flora, not checklists, and are unevenly sampled (e.g. 12.8k records in lowland Patagonia vs 1.0M in lowland New Zealand).
Genus sharing is a pre-phylogenetic proxy for 'related in a most remarkable manner'; no phylogenetic distances were computed.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, many more European species have become naturalised in La Plata (and, to a lesser degree, in Australia) than species from those southern regions have become naturalised anywhere in Europe: the Europe-to-south naturalisation count should exceed the south-to-Europe count several-fold for each region.
info.pass: Using World Checklist of Vascular Plants native and introduced distribution records by TDWG level-3 unit: A_LP = number of species native in Europe (TDWG level-1 region 1) and not native in La Plata that are recorded as introduced in La Plata (units AGE Argentina Northeast and URU Uruguay); B_LP = number of species native in La Plata and not native in Europe that are recorded as introduced in any European unit; likewise A_AU and B_AU for Australia (TDWG level-2 region 50: WAU, NTA, SOA, QLD, NSW, VIC, TAS). Supports if A_LP >= 5 * B_LP and A_AU >= 5 * B_AU.

measured.unit: ratio of European plant species naturalised in La Plata to La Plata species naturalised in Europe (WCVP)

caveats: Primary result: A_LP = 465 European species naturalised in La Plata versus B_LP = 341 La Plata species naturalised in Europe (ratio 1.36, below the refute threshold of 2); A_AU = 837 versus B_AU = 274 (ratio 3.06, between the thresholds). Darwin's direction of asymmetry holds for both regions, but its magnitude ('very many' versus 'extremely few') does not: hundreds of South American and Australian species are coded as introduced in Europe.

Per source species the pattern is reversed for La Plata: 58 of every 1000 La Plata natives are naturalised in Europe, versus 17 of every 1000 European natives naturalised in La Plata, because the European native pool (27,000 species) is far larger than that of AGE+URU (5,832).

WCVP's 'introduced' flag mixes long-established invaders with regionally established aliens whose European foothold may be small; many Australian species recorded as introduced in Europe (Atriplex, Austrostipa, Calotis, Acacia) were historically wool or garden aliens, and some may now be casual or extinct. WCVP intends to exclude casuals, but its coding leans on regional floras of varying strictness, so B counts may be inflated relative to Darwin's 'naturalised'.

Conversely, the South-American-to-Europe list includes pantropical or widespread weeds (Amaranthus, Alternanthera, Bidens pilosa) that are native in La Plata but may have reached Europe from elsewhere. The continent-confined sensitivity removes these and gives ratios of 0.09 (La Plata) and 0.43 (Australia), but that restriction is biased against Europe, whose natives are mostly shared with Asia or North Africa (only 15 Europe-confined species are naturalised in La Plata), so it is a lower bound on the asymmetry, not a preferred estimate.

info.hypothesis: Within each of three classes (insects, molluscs, flowering plants), species of fresh-water families occupy more continents than species of related terrestrial families, and fresh-water genera are more often spread over several continents than terrestrial genera.
info.pass: Pre-registered: for every family in the fixed fresh-water and terrestrial lists, GBIF occurrence facets give the set of species and genera recorded (>= 3 records) on each of the six inhabited continents. Per class, compute P_sp = proportion of species recorded on >= 3 continents and P_gen = proportion of genera recorded on >= 3 continents, separately for the fresh-water and the terrestrial family set. SUPPORTS if in all three classes P_sp(fresh-water) > P_sp(terrestrial) AND P_gen(fresh-water) > P_gen(terrestrial), and the pooled species-level continent counts differ in the fresh-water direction (one-sided Mann-Whitney, p < 0.001).

measured.unit: classes (of 3 usable) in which both the proportion of species and of genera on >= 3 continents is higher for fresh-water than for terrestrial families

caveats: The species-level effect in insects is small (P_sp 0.021 vs 0.018, mean continents 1.14 vs 1.12) although the genus-level effect is large (0.22 vs 0.12); the verdict for insects rests mainly on genera, which is the 'allied species prevail throughout the world' half of the claim.

Human-mediated introductions inflate multi-continent occurrence in both sets (e.g. Physa acuta, Pomacea, Sphaeriidae among fresh-water taxa; Helicidae, Achatinidae, Rosaceae and Solanaceae crops and weeds among terrestrial taxa) and cannot be separated in GBIF.
GBIF 'continent' is interpreted from coordinates; records of Oceania and islands are coarse, and species with >= 3 records on 3 continents is a crude proxy for 'enormous range'.

Family lists were fixed in advance but are a judgement sample, not the whole class; several fresh-water families (Hydrophilidae, Elmidae, Haloragaceae, Menyanthaceae) include terrestrial or amphibious members, which dilutes the contrast.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, no strictly fresh-water, non-diadromous fish species has a native range that includes two continents separated by ocean (e.g. Eurasia and North America, Africa and South America, Asia and Australia).
info.pass: Among FishBase species flagged as fresh-water only (Fresh = 1, Brack = 0, Saltwater = 0) and not anadromous, catadromous, amphidromous or oceanodromous, zero species have 'native' or 'endemic' country status (FishBase country table) in at least one country on each side of any ocean-separated continent pair. Ocean-separated pairs are all pairs among {Eurasia (Europe + Asia), Africa, North America (incl. Central America and the Caribbean), South America, Oceania (Australia + New Guinea + Pacific)} except Eurasia-Africa and North America-South America, which are joined by land.

measured.unit: strictly fresh-water, non-diadromous fish species native (>= 2 countries each side) on both sides of an ocean-separated continent pair

caveats: The pre-registered mechanical count is 6 robust species (>= 5, 'refutes'), but inspection shows that count is partly artefactual: Upeneus guttatus is a marine goatfish mis-flagged as fresh-water only, Cichlasoma bimaculatum's 'native' Eurasian records are status errors, and three Indo-Pacific gobies/pipefishes (Glossogobius clitellus, Redigobius oyensi, Lophocampus retzii) reach Oceania from the Philippines/Indonesia; such island gobioids have marine larval phases that FishBase does not always code as amphidromous. 72 of the 77 Eurasia|Oceania 'shared' species are Indonesian-Papua vs Papua New Guinea/Australia records on the single landmass of New Guinea/Sahul, an artefact of FishBase filing Indonesia under Asia.

The verdict nevertheless stands on the genuine Holarctic cases: under the strict filter Thymallus arcticus (robust), Prosopium coulterii and Dallia pectoralis are native in both Siberia and North America; admitting brackish-tolerant non-diadromous species (post hoc) adds Esox lucius, Lota lota, Catostomus catostomus, Cottus cognatus and Prosopium cylindraceum (10 species listed, of which Atractosteus spatula and Gasterosteus microcephalus look like status errors). Northern pike and burbot in both England and Canada falsify 'never' on Darwin's own terms.

Darwin's generalization is nonetheless very nearly true: 6 of 16,174 species (0.04 %) meet the robust rule and 83 (0.5 %) share any country pair across an ocean, almost all of them artefacts; genuine sharing is confined to the Bering Strait region, where a Pleistocene land connection joined river systems, which is the mechanism Darwin himself proposed for dispersal of fresh-water fish.

FishBase treats Alaska, Canada and USA as separate 'countries', which makes North American counts easier to satisfy than Russian ones (a single country for all of Siberia); this biases the robust rule against Eurasia|North America cases, not in favour of them.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, an oceanic island supports far fewer native species than a continental area of the same size, after allowing for the physical conditions he thought could not explain the difference; for vascular plants (de Candolle's case) native species richness of oceanic island units should fall well below the continental species-area relationship.
info.pass: Fit log10(native vascular plant species) = a + b*log10(area km2) + c*|centroid latitude| by ordinary least squares on continental (mainland-connected) TDWG level-3 botanical countries from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, then predict richness for each pre-registered oceanic island unit at its own area and latitude. Supports if (i) the median ratio of observed to predicted richness across oceanic units is <= 0.5, (ii) >= 80 % of oceanic units lie below the continental prediction, and (iii) a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the oceanic log-residuals against zero gives p < 0.01.

measured.unit: median ratio of observed native vascular plant species on oceanic island units to the richness predicted for a continental area of equal size and latitude

caveats: All 28 oceanic island units (Hawaii 0.52, Fiji 0.66, Galapagos 0.21, Vanuatu 0.58, Samoa 0.46, Iceland 0.58, South Georgia 0.03, Canary Is. 1.00, ...) lie at or below the continental prediction; median ratio 0.44 (IQR 0.19-0.61), Wilcoxon p = 3.7e-9. The area-only model gives the same answer (median 0.45). Shelf and continental-fragment islands (n = 66, median 0.80, 61 % below) show a much weaker deficit, which matches Darwin's distinction between oceanic and continental islands.

Two codes in the pre-registered oceanic list were transcription errors discovered when the first run printed unit names: 'TVL' is Northern Provinces (South Africa), not Tuvalu ('TUV'), and 'TRT' is Trinidad-Tobago, a shelf island, not Trindade (which has no level-3 unit). They were corrected before the reported run; in the first run the only units at or above prediction were those two mis-coded units and the Canary Islands (ratio 1.00), so the verdict does not depend on the correction.

32 oceanic units smaller than the smallest continental unit (196 km2) are excluded by the pre-registered range rule; all of them have far fewer species than any continental unit, so the exclusion is conservative. TDWG polygons for some small remote islands are coarse (Kerguelen is drawn at 40 km2 against a true 7,200 km2), another reason to keep the small-island exclusion.

Only vascular plants are tested; Darwin's 'species of all kinds' extends to animals, for which no native-status-coded global checklist at consistent regional units is public. de Candolle's plant case is, however, the one Darwin cites.
