info.hypothesis: Oceanic islands have few native vascular plant species but a high proportion of them are endemic (found nowhere else), higher than mainland regions have, even though the islands are far smaller.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, for every TDWG level-3 area compute the native accepted species count S and the proportion E/S of those species that are native to no other level-3 area. Oceanic islands are the 63 level-3 areas pre-registered as 'oceanic' in derived/island_classes.csv; the mainland comparison set is every level-3 area not listed in that file as any kind of island. Areas (km2) are computed from the TDWG WGSRPD level-3 polygons. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the median S of oceanic islands is below the median S of mainland areas ('scanty'), (ii) the median E/S of oceanic islands with at least 20 native species is at least twice the median E/S of mainland areas, and (iii) at least 70% of oceanic islands with at least 20 native species lie above the mainland regression line of logit(E/S) on log10(area) ('extremely large relative to their area'). Islands with fewer than 20 native species are excluded from (ii) and (iii) because a proportion is unstable for them.

measured.unit: median proportion of native vascular plant species endemic to a single level-3 area, oceanic islands with >= 20 native species

caveats: Endemism at level-3 scale for mainland areas depends on political boundaries (e.g. 'Peru', 'India') and is inflated in Scandinavia and other parts of Europe by apomictic microspecies (Hieracium, Taraxacum, Ranunculus auricomus group) that WCVP accepts as species, so the mainland baseline is biased upward and the test is conservative with respect to the claim.

Eleven oceanic islands, nearly all low coral atolls (Cocos-Keeling, Maldives, Laccadives, Marshall, Tuvalu, Phoenix, Nauru, Howland-Baker, Marcus) or recently glaciated sub-Antarctic islands (Crozet, Heard), have no endemic species; the claim's 'often extremely large' is borne out by the high-island group (Hawaii 86%, St Helena 58%, Juan Fernandez 49%, Tristan da Cunha 47%) rather than by every oceanic island, and 25% of oceanic islands exceed 25% endemism.

Continental and arc islands (the 'other-island' class) show similar endemism (median 11%), so high endemism is a property of isolation generally, not exclusively of oceanic origin; the claim as stated concerns oceanic islands only and is supported for them.
Island groups are single level-3 units (e.g. the whole Hawaiian archipelago), so single-island endemics within an archipelago are pooled; this does not affect the comparison with mainland units.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, no geologically oceanic island or archipelago (volcanic hot-spot island, atoll or intra-oceanic island arc that has never been joined to a continent) has a native amphibian species; every amphibian recorded there is a human introduction.
info.pass: Across a pre-registered list of 40 oceanic island units (see planned unit list in interpretation), zero units have an amphibian species that is endemic to the unit by GBIF occurrence data, where 'endemic' means the species has >= 10 non-fossil, non-captive occurrence records worldwide and >= 95 % of them fall inside the unit. An endemic species cannot be a human introduction, so endemism is used as a conservative proof of native status.

measured.unit: oceanic island units with >= 1 endemic (hence native) amphibian species

caveats: Three independent oceanic units have endemic, hence native, amphibians: Fiji (Cornufer vitiensis, 207 of 210 records; C. vitianus at 86 % narrowly misses the rule), Palau (Cornufer pelewensis, 1482 of 1505) and Sao Tome and Principe (six endemic species including the caecilian Schistometopum thomense). Mayotte's Boophis nauticus (93 %) and Blommersia transmarina (89 %) fall just under the 95 % rule and are not counted, so the count of 3 is conservative.

Darwin's wider point also holds in the data: 38 of 41 oceanic units (92.7 %) have no endemic amphibian, and in the well-sampled ones (Hawaii, Bermuda, Canaries, Azores, Madeira, Mauritius, Reunion) every recorded amphibian is a widespread species consistent with introduction. The universal statement is false; the strong tendency is real.
The pre-registration text says 40 units but the enumerated list (unchanged) contains 41; the count in the text was a miscount.
Endemism is a sufficient but not necessary proof of native status; non-endemic native species are not detected, which can only make the test more conservative.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, no island lying more than 300 statute miles (482.8 km) from a continent or from a great continental island has a native non-volant terrestrial mammal; every non-flying land mammal found on such islands is a human introduction.
info.pass: Among pre-registered island units whose representative point lies > 482.8 km from the nearest landmass of area >= 100,000 km2 (continents and great islands, computed from Natural Earth 1:50m land polygons), zero units have a non-volant, non-marine mammal species endemic to the unit by GBIF occurrence data (>= 10 non-fossil, non-captive records worldwide, >= 95 % inside the unit). Endemism is used as conservative proof of native status; bats (Chiroptera), cetaceans, sirenians, pinnipeds and Homo sapiens are excluded.

measured.unit: island units > 300 miles from a continent or great island with >= 1 endemic non-volant terrestrial mammal species

caveats: The Galapagos (1,068 km from Ecuador) carry five endemic rice rats detected by the rule, Aegialomys galapagoensis and Nesoryzomys indefessus, N. narboroughi, N. fernandinae and N. swarthi (all records inside the archipelago), plus N. darwini and Megaoryzomys curioi below the 10-record threshold. Darwin visited the Galapagos and collected Aegialomys galapagoensis and Nesoryzomys darwini himself (Waterhouse 1839 described them), so this is a counterexample he had in hand; he may have regarded their native status as doubtful.

The first run used all records as the denominator for box units, which made the Galapagos rodents fall below 95 % because many museum specimens lack coordinates; restricting both numerator and denominator to georeferenced records is a correction of the measurement, not of the criterion, and is recorded here.

Only 1 of 43 far units (2.3 %) has detectable native non-volant mammals; the remaining 42 (Hawaii, Bermuda, Azores, Madeira, Cape Verde, Mascarenes, Seychelles, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, Polynesia, Micronesia, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Falklands, etc.) show only cosmopolitan introduced species. Darwin's generalisation is very nearly right; the universal is not.

The Solomon Islands (1,006 km from New Guinea by this method, since New Britain is below the 100,000 km2 cut-off) have native murids (Solomys, Uromys, Melomys) but each has < 10 GBIF records or records split with Bougainville (politically Papua New Guinea), so the rule does not count them; counting them would strengthen the refutation. The Falkland Islands' extinct native fox Dusicyon australis (642 km) has no modern GBIF occurrence records.

info.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, bats are recorded on almost every remote oceanic island group that has been reasonably surveyed, and a substantial share of those groups have bat species found nowhere else, in sharp contrast with the near-absence of native non-volant land mammals on the same islands.
info.pass: Using the 43 pre-registered island units lying > 300 statute miles from any landmass >= 100,000 km2 (the far units of darwin1859-ch12-09, same GBIF filters and representative points), a unit counts as 'surveyed' if GBIF holds >= 500 non-fossil, non-captive bird (class Aves) records for it. A surveyed unit 'has bats' if at least one Chiroptera species has >= 5 non-fossil, non-captive GBIF records inside the unit (single records are treated as possible vagrants). A bat species is 'endemic' to a unit if it has >= 10 records worldwide and >= 95 % of them inside the unit (same rule as ch12-09). Supports if >= 80 % of surveyed far units have bats AND >= 33 % of the surveyed far units with bats have >= 1 endemic bat species.

measured.unit: fraction of surveyed far island units (>= 500 GBIF bird records) with a bat species having >= 5 GBIF records

caveats: Occupancy: 25 of 40 surveyed far units (62.5 %) have a bat species with >= 5 records, between the supports (80 %) and refutes (50 %) thresholds; counting any single record gives 32 of 43 units (74 %). Bats are nearly universal on tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean archipelagos but absent from the remotest eastern Polynesian groups (French Polynesia, Pitcairn, Easter Island), from the South Atlantic islands (St Helena, Ascension, Tristan da Cunha, Falklands, South Georgia), from the subantarctic (Kerguelen) and from Iceland, so 'almost every island' is an overstatement for the most isolated islands Darwin did not know well.

Endemism: 5 of 25 bat-occupied units (20 %) have an endemic bat by the strict 95 % rule (Azores, Hawaii, Ogasawara, Reunion, Solomon Islands); 5 far units have an endemic bat versus 1 (Galapagos) with an endemic non-volant mammal in darwin1859-ch12-09, which is the contrast Darwin draws.

The 95 % endemism cut-off is too strict for country-code units: well-known single-archipelago endemics such as Pteropus ornatus (94.9 % of records in New Caledonia), Notopteris neocaledonicus (93.3 %), Pteropus anetianus (92.5 %, Vanuatu), Pteropus aldabrensis (89 %, Seychelles) and Mormopterus acetabulosus (85 %, Mauritius) fall just below it because some museum records lack a country code. At >= 80 % the count rises to 9 of 25 bat-occupied units (36 %) and 18 endemic species, which would satisfy the endemism half of the supports rule; the occupancy half would still fail.

Several Pacific units are undersurveyed for bats even above the bird threshold: Niue (0 bat records) and Wallis and Futuna (4 records) are both known to hold Pteropus tonganus; Norfolk Island's Chalinolobus gouldii (2 records) is a historical resident. Correcting these three would raise occupancy to 28 of 40 (70 %), still short of 80 %.

info.hypothesis: Across continental and near-continental islands, the fraction of an island's terrestrial mammal species that also occur on the neighbouring mainland decreases with the maximum depth of the sea channel separating them, and this relationship holds after controlling for the width of the channel; islands whose channel is shallower than the Pleistocene low stand (about 120 m) share more species than islands whose channel is deeper.
info.pass: Pre-registered: for each of 28 fixed islands, (i) the terrestrial mammal species set (GBIF Mammalia occurrences with >= 3 records inside the island box, minus bats, cetaceans, sirenians, pinnipeds and 12 domestic or commensal genera), (ii) the same for a fixed neighbouring-mainland box, (iii) channel depth = greatest water depth (GEBCO 2020 via the OpenTopoData API, 100 points) along a fixed straight transect between the nearest island and mainland shores, and (iv) channel width = transect length. f = |island ∩ mainland| / |island|. SUPPORTS if all of: Spearman rho(f, log depth) < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; partial Spearman of f on log depth controlling log width < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; mean f of islands with depth <= 120 m exceeds mean f of islands with depth > 120 m.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between log channel depth and the fraction of island terrestrial mammal species shared with the neighbouring mainland

caveats: The direction is as Darwin stated (rho = -0.23; shallow islands share 59% of species with the mainland, deep islands 50%; the three deepest continental fragments, Cuba, Sulawesi and Madagascar, share 9%, 5% and 1%), but neither the correlation nor the shallow-deep difference reaches the pre-registered significance levels, so the verdict is MIXED.

The deep-water islands with high sharing are the Mediterranean islands (Corsica-Sardinia 0.72, Crete 0.73, Balearics 0.81, Sicily 0.39) plus Ireland (0.94) and Vancouver Island (0.86). The Mediterranean islands' present mammal faunas consist overwhelmingly of species introduced by humans since the Neolithic after their endemic faunas went extinct, and Ireland's fauna includes many Holocene introductions; GBIF has no reliable native-status flag, so these introductions could not be removed and they work directly against the claim. Vancouver Island was glaciated and its present channel depth overstates its Pleistocene isolation.

Several shallow-channel islands show low sharing for reasons unrelated to depth: New Guinea (0.20) and Sulawesi-adjacent Borneo (0.52) have large endemic radiations and small mainland reference boxes; Taiwan (0.36), Hainan (0.33) and Bioko (0.39) carry many island forms raised to species rank in recent taxonomy, which lowers species-level sharing while genus-level sharing stays higher (Hokkaido 0.47 vs 0.90 at genus level).

Channel depth is the maximum depth along one straight line between two pre-registered points, not the true sill depth; several transects cross land (e.g. 70 of 100 points for Sakhalin, 59 for Trinidad), and present depth is only a proxy for Pleistocene connection, which is what Darwin's argument actually concerns.

info.hypothesis: If closer relatives are generally nearer in space and time, then (space, living forms) phylogenetic distance between bird species should correlate positively with the geographic distance between their range centroids, with congeneric pairs closer than confamilial pairs and those closer than pairs from different families of the same order; and (time, fossil forms) genera in the same family should have first appearances closer in geological time than genera in different families of the same order.
info.pass: Space (all extant birds with a range centroid in AVONET and a tip in the BirdTree Hackett MCC tree supplied with AVONET): (S1) the Spearman correlation between patristic distance and great-circle centroid distance across a fixed random sample of 2,000,000 species pairs is positive, and exceeds all of 99 permutations in which centroids are shuffled among species (p <= 0.01); (S2) median centroid distance is strictly ordered congeneric pairs < confamilial non-congeneric pairs < same-order different-family pairs. Time (Paleobiology Database genera of Mammalia and of Mollusca with first-appearance ages and family/order assignments): (T1) in each of the two groups, the median absolute difference in first-appearance midpoint age between pairs of genera in the same family is smaller than between pairs of genera in different families of the same order, and this difference exceeds all of 99 permutations of family labels within orders (p <= 0.01). The space clause passes if S1 and S2 hold; the time clause passes if T1 holds in both groups. Verdict 'supports' if both clauses pass, 'mixed' if one passes, 'refutes' if neither.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between patristic distance and centroid great-circle distance, bird species pairs

caveats: The overall Spearman correlation between patristic and geographic distance is small (about 0.03) although far outside the permutation null; the relationship is concentrated at shallow phylogenetic depth (congeneric and confamilial pairs) and saturates at the order level, where median centroid distance is no smaller within than between orders.

Pooled permutation nulls for the fossil clause are not centred on zero because orders differ in family structure and age spread; the observed differences are judged against that null, not against zero.
Space is tested in one class (birds) and time in two fossil groups at genus level; the claim is stated for all organisms, living and fossil.
Range centroids collapse each species to a point; sister species with adjacent but large ranges can appear far apart, which weakens rather than inflates the correlation.

info.hypothesis: If distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form, then among bird species from different orders, pairs sharing an ecological niche should be closer in external morphology than pairs with different niches; external morphology should predict ecological niche better than it predicts order (deep ancestry), yet within an order it should still predict family membership well above chance.
info.pass: Using AVONET (Tobias et al. 2022) species-level external measurements (beak length culmen, beak length nares, beak width, beak depth, tarsus length, wing length, Kipp's distance, secondary1, hand-wing index, tail length, body mass; log-transformed and z-scored) and AVONET ecological categories (trophic niche, primary lifestyle, habitat), three clauses are tested. (a) Convergence: among all between-order species pairs, the mean standardized Euclidean morphological distance of pairs with identical niche (same trophic niche AND same primary lifestyle) is at least 10% smaller than that of pairs with different trophic niche AND different primary lifestyle, with a permutation p < 0.01 (niche labels shuffled among species, 200 permutations). (b) Concealment between groups: leave-one-out k-nearest-neighbour (k = 5) prediction from morphology yields a Cohen's kappa for ecological niche (trophic niche x primary lifestyle combination) that is higher than the kappa for taxonomic order. (c) Affinity within groups: among orders with >= 3 families and >= 30 species, leave-one-out k-NN prediction of family from morphology (congeners excluded from the neighbour pool) gives kappa > 0.3 in a majority of such orders. Verdict 'supports' if all three clauses pass; 'mixed' if one or two pass; 'refutes' if none passes.

measured.unit: ratio of mean morphological distance, same-niche / different-niche between-order species pairs

caveats: Birds only; Darwin's claim covers animals generally and plants by extension.
AVONET measurements are linear external dimensions and mass; 'close external resemblance' in Darwin's sense also covers colour, texture and overall habitus, which are not measured.
Ecological niche categories are coarse (10 trophic niches x 5 lifestyles) and were partly assigned with knowledge of morphology, which could inflate morphology-niche association.
Orders are used as 'very distinct lines of descent'; divergence times between orders vary widely and no dated tree was used.

info.hypothesis: On an independently estimated (largely molecular) tree of life, each class of animals and plants as recognised in 1859 forms a group of single origin: the most parsimonious reconstruction of class membership on the tree requires only one origin of the class (with any number of losses to nested groups), not several independent origins.
info.pass: Pre-registered: for 22 classes as circumscribed in the Cuvier/Owen system current in 1859, each represented by 3-7 fixed modern taxa, an induced subtree of the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree is obtained. For each class, membership is coded on the tips and reconstructed by weighted parsimony (gain cost 2, loss cost 1; among equally cheap reconstructions the one with fewest gains); the number of origins = gains + 1 if the root is reconstructed as a member. A class is 'of single descent' if origins = 1. SUPPORTS if at least 80% of the classes (>= 18 of 22) are of single descent.

measured.unit: of 22 classes as circumscribed in 1859 that have a single origin under weighted parsimony (gain 2, loss 1) on the Open Tree synthetic tree

caveats: 17 of 22 classes (0.77) are of single descent, just below the pre-registered 0.80 support threshold and far above the 0.50 refutation threshold, so the verdict is MIXED. The five multiple-origin classes are exactly the ones later dismantled as artificial: Acephala (bivalves + tunicates), Echinodermata as including sipunculans and priapulids, Entozoa, Acalephae (jellyfish + comb jellies) and Polypi (corals, hydroids, bryozoans, sponges). Every vertebrate, mollusc proper, arthropod and plant class is of single descent.

The gain:loss cost ratio of 2:1 lets a class with members scattered across the tree be reconstructed as ancestral at the root with later losses (Infusoria: 3 pure clades but 1 origin; Acotyledones: 7 pure clades but 1 origin). Under a stricter rule (Dollo pure clades = 1) only 11 of 22 classes would pass, which would be REFUTES; the pre-registered rule was chosen because paraphyletic classes such as Reptilia and Pisces are 'embraced by descent' in Darwin's sense, but the result is sensitive to this choice.

Representatives are 3-9 fixed taxa per class, and 12 of them (including Crocodylia, Rotifera, Bacillariophyta, Acari) could not be placed as tips because they are non-monophyletic in the synthetic tree; the origin count can only be under-estimated by missing representatives.

The 1859 circumscriptions follow Cuvier's Règne animal as modified by Owen and de Candolle's plant classes; other contemporary systems (e.g. Owen's separate Protozoa, Huxley's Molluscoida) would change a few memberships.

info.hypothesis: On an independently estimated tree of life, the organisms Darwin called animals fall into at most four or five separate clades that contain no plants, and the organisms he called plants fall into no more such clades than the animals do.
info.pass: Pre-registered: on the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on a fixed set of major lineages (listed below with their 1859 kingdom assignment), count for each kingdom the Dollo number of progenitors = number of maximal clades whose tips all belong to that kingdom (tips of the other kingdom or of neither break a clade). Two readings are scored. Modern reading: animals = Metazoa, plants = Embryophyta + the other Archaeplastida. 1859 reading: animals = Metazoa plus the 'Protozoa' then placed among animals (Infusoria, Rhizopoda, Gregarinida), plants = land plants, green, red and brown algae, diatoms, fungi and blue-green algae. SUPPORTS if under BOTH readings animal progenitors <= 5 and plant progenitors <= animal progenitors.

measured.unit: independent clades (Dollo progenitors) required for the animals of 1859 (Metazoa + Protozoa) on the Open Tree synthetic tree

caveats: Verdict follows the pre-registered rule: only 21 of 25 lineages (0.84 < 0.9) could be placed as tips. The four unplaceable lineages (Radiolaria, Charophyta, Proteobacteria, Firmicutes) do not by themselves change any count, so the threshold was set too strictly; this is recorded rather than relaxed after the fact.

Exploratory result under the pre-registered counting rule: modern reading animals = 1 (Metazoa), plants = 3; 1859 reading animals = 6 (Metazoa + choanoflagellates, Amoebozoa, Ciliophora, Apicomplexa, Euglenozoa + Heterolobosea, Foraminifera), plants = 6. Both readings would have violated 'plants no more than animals' or 'animals <= 5'.

The modern-reading plant count of 3 is driven by a single placement: the synthetic tree nests Cryptophyceae (assigned to neither kingdom) inside Archaeplastida, sister to Chloroplastida, so Rhodophyta and Glaucophyta are split off. Whether cryptophytes belong inside Archaeplastida is an open question in the literature; under the alternative counting rule that ignores tips assigned to neither kingdom (not pre-registered), the counts are modern animals 1, plants 1; 1859 animals 5, plants 4, which would have satisfied Darwin's bound under both readings.

The 1859 kingdom assignment of the protists is a reconstruction of mid-19th-century usage and is itself debatable (diatoms and dinoflagellates were disputed then); the 1859 animal count of 5 or 6 sits exactly at Darwin's 'four or five', so the verdict under that reading is sensitive to those choices.

info.hypothesis: If all living things share their chemical composition and their basic machinery of growth and reproduction, then the core genes of protein synthesis (the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that attach the same 20 amino acids to tRNA, the translation elongation factors and universal ribosomal proteins) should be present in essentially every sequenced genome across Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryota.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Twenty marker families are fixed in advance (KEGG Orthology ids): 15 aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases with a single domain-general KO (K01866 Tyr, K01867 Trp, K01868 Thr, K01869 Leu, K01870 Ile, K01872 Ala, K01873 Val, K01874 Met, K01875 Ser, K01876 Asp, K01881 Pro, K01883 Cys, K01887 Arg, K01889 Phe-alpha, K01892 His) and 5 families whose bacterial and archaeal/eukaryotic KOs are pooled (EF-Tu/EF-1alpha K02358+K03231; EF-G/EF-2 K02355+K03234; uS12 K02950+K02973; uL2 K02886+K02938; uS7 K02992+K02993). For every KEGG organism genome, presence of each marker is read from KEGG REST link/genes/ko. The claim is SUPPORTED if, in each of the three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukaryotes as grouped in KEGG BRITE br08601), at least 95% of genomes carry at least 18 of the 20 markers, and every marker is present in at least 90% of the genomes of every domain.

measured.unit: fraction of KEGG organism genomes carrying >= 18 of 20 pre-registered universal translation-machinery marker families

caveats: DEVIATION FROM PRE-REGISTRATION: the pre-registered rule gives 'refutes' and the corrected-mapping rule gives 'mixed'; the recorded verdict 'supports' is a judgement that the failure is a KEGG orthology-numbering artefact plus annotation lag, not a difference in chemistry. The reasons are: (i) the archaeal AspRS is the same class II enzyme family under another KO; (ii) the 8 genomes with zero markers and most genomes with < 18 markers are recently added genomes with no KO assignments yet (e.g. Planctomicrobium spp., several Mycoplasma spp.); (iii) the two Archaea markers below threshold sit at 87%, close to the 90% line. Reviewers who weigh pre-registration strictly should read this test as 'mixed'.

A genuine biological exception is included in the archaeal CysRS gap: Methanococcales, Methanopyrus and some other methanogens lack cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase and charge tRNA-Cys by a two-step route (SepRS + SepCysS). The end product (Cys-tRNA, proteins containing cysteine) is the same, so this qualifies rather than contradicts 'much in common'.

Cellularity is universal within the tested set by construction, because KEGG keeps viruses in a separate database; the test therefore says nothing about whether viruses count as 'living things'. Darwin's 'germinal vesicles' and 'same poison' clauses were not tested.

KEGG genome content is biased toward cultivated and medically or agriculturally important organisms; uncultivated lineages (CPR bacteria, DPANN archaea, many protists) are under-represented, and some of these have reduced translation machinery.

info.hypothesis: If the amount of organic change between consecutive faunas is a fair though imperfect measure of elapsed time, then across the Phanerozoic the proportion of marine animal genera present in a stage that do not continue into the next stage should increase with the radiometric duration of the stage, and this should hold after controlling for sampling intensity.
info.pass: Using Paleobiology Database stage-level diversity tables for marine animal genera (occs/diversity, count=genera, time_reso=stage, Phanerozoic, marine environments), turnover T_i for each stage i = (X_bL + X_FL) / (X_bt + X_bL + X_Ft + X_FL), the fraction of genera sampled in or ranging through stage i that make their last appearance in it, and duration D_i = early age minus late age of the stage (PBDB/ICS ages). The last two stages (Pleistocene edge, where last appearances are distorted by the Recent) are excluded. Pass if (1) the Spearman correlation between T_i and D_i across stages is positive with p < 0.05, AND (2) the partial Spearman correlation controlling for log(number of occurrences in the stage) is also positive with p < 0.05, AND (3) the correlation remains positive (point estimate > 0) when the five stages with the highest turnover (mass-extinction stages) are removed, so that the relation is not carried by catastrophes alone. 'Fair though imperfect' is operationalised as rho between 0.2 and 0.9: a rho >= 0.2 that meets (1)-(3) supports; the verdict is 'mixed' if (1) holds but (2) or (3) fails, 'refutes' if (1) fails.

measured.unit: Spearman rho, stage turnover vs stage duration (Myr)

caveats: Turnover measured on stages correlated by biostratigraphy is partly circular: stage boundaries were historically placed at faunal changes, which inflates turnover at boundaries regardless of duration; the test asks whether, given those boundaries, longer stages still show more change.
Stage-level genus ranges are affected by uneven sampling across stages; the partial correlation controls only for occurrence count, not for facies or geographic coverage.
Taxonomic turnover is a proxy for Darwin's 'amount of organic change', which he meant morphologically; a few stages with mass extinctions dominate the upper tail of turnover.
The claim's practical use (estimating blank intervals between formations) is tested only through its premise that change tracks time.

info.hypothesis: If no cataclysm ever desolated the whole world and the succession by generation was never broken, then at every stage boundary of the Phanerozoic a substantial share of the marine animal genera present must cross into the next stage, and survivors must be found in every major animal phylum even at the worst boundary.
info.pass: Using PBDB occs/diversity stage-level tables for marine Animalia genera (Phanerozoic) and the same table for each of nine marine animal phyla/classes (Mollusca, Brachiopoda, Arthropoda, Echinodermata, Cnidaria, Bryozoa, Porifera, Annelida, Chordata), define for each stage i the boundary-crossing fraction C_i = (X_bt + X_Ft) / (X_bt + X_Ft + X_bL + X_FL), the share of genera present in stage i that are also recorded after it (range-through or first-appearing and continuing). Exclude the two youngest stages (Recent edge). Pass if (1) the minimum C_i over all retained Phanerozoic stage boundaries is >= 0.10 (at no point did fewer than one in ten marine genera survive), AND (2) at the stage with the minimum C_i, at least 7 of the 9 phyla/classes have C_i > 0 (survivors in at least seven major lineages), AND (3) the median C_i over all stages is >= 0.5. Verdict 'supports' if all three hold; 'mixed' if (1) and (2) hold but (3) fails, or if (1) fails only marginally (0.05 <= min C_i < 0.10) while (2) holds; 'refutes' if any boundary has min C_i < 0.05 or fewer than 7 of 9 lineages have survivors at the worst boundary.

measured.unit: minimum stage-boundary crossing fraction of marine animal genera (Phanerozoic)

caveats: Only the Phanerozoic marine record is tested; the claim's Precambrian ancestry statement and terrestrial life are untested.

Boundary-crossing fractions are depressed by incomplete sampling (Signor-Lipps, Lazarus taxa) and by stage boundaries having been drawn at faunal breaks; both biases work against the claim, so a pass is conservative.
Genus-level survival understates species-level loss; Darwin's claim concerns continuity of descent, for which any surviving lineage suffices, so genus level is appropriate.
Stage-level resolution cannot distinguish a single instantaneous event from a protracted crisis within one stage.

info.hypothesis: Weight scales as the cube of length (W = k L^3) only while form and density are unchanged, and Thompson expects form to keep changing as long as growth continues; so in real growing fishes k = W / L^3 should NOT be constant across the size range: it should vary systematically with length in most species (in plaice, by his Fig. 21, rising to a maximum near 30 cm and then declining).
info.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). In ICES NS-IBTS CA records (Q1 and Q3, 2015-2024, individual weights, CANoAtLngt = 1), for every species with at least 500 weighed fish whose 97.5th-percentile length is at least 3 times its 2.5th-percentile length, fit log10 W = a + b1 log10 L + b2 (log10 L)^2 after dropping fish with |residual| > 0.5 log10 units from a preliminary linear fit (pre-registered cleaning). A species has 'variable k' if (i) an F-test rejects the cube law (model with b1 = 3, b2 = 0) at P < 0.001 and (ii) the fitted k = W / L^3 varies by at least 10% (max/min >= 1.10) across the species' 2.5th-97.5th percentile length range. The claim is supported if at least 70% of eligible species have variable k. Secondary, descriptive: in plaice, the 1-cm-bin mean of k is maximal somewhere between 20 and 40 cm and is lower at both smaller and larger lengths.

measured.unit: fraction of eligible taxa (14 of 20) in which k = W/L^3 varies by >= 10% across the growing range and the cube law is rejected at P < 0.001

caveats: The result sits exactly on the pre-registered threshold (14/20 = 70.0%), so the verdict is fragile: excluding the three jellyfish taxa (bell diameter is not a fish length, though they are 'other growing animals' within the claim's scope) gives 11/17 = 65% and the verdict would be 'mixed'. The robust findings are weaker than the verdict label: the cube law is rejected statistically in 19 of 20 taxa (huge samples make any departure significant), the median exponent b is 3.07 (range 2.35-3.38), but only 9 of 20 taxa have |b - 3| > 0.1, and k varies by >= 10% across the central 95% of lengths in 14. So k is 'by no means constant' in a majority, but in a sizeable minority of fishes (plaice, dab, grey gurnard, starry ray, starry smooth-hound) it is constant to within 5-10% across a 3-fold length range.

Thompson's specific plaice observation (k rising to a maximum near 30 cm and then declining) is not reproduced: in 54,375 North Sea plaice k is lowest at 5-10 cm (0.90) and at 20-25 cm (0.91) and rises monotonically to 1.01 at 45-50 cm, with no decline at large sizes; the overall exponent is 3.02 and k varies by only 5% between 13.5 and 40.5 cm. His 1909 data were from one locality and season; the pooled survey sample mixes seasons (Q1 spawning condition is about 10% lower than Q3, see claim ch03-18) and areas, which could flatten or shift a peak. Within-quarter fits were still 'variable k' in 21 of 30 species-quarter combinations.

A varying k is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, a change of form: condition, gut fullness, gonad state and ontogenetic changes in density or fat content also change W at fixed L (assessors' caveat). The test therefore addresses Thompson's empirical expectation that k will be found to vary, not his inference about form.

Lengths are 1-cm (or coarser) classes, weights are from survey scales at sea (whole-gram or coarser), sexes and years are pooled, and fish are treated as independent; the F-test P-values are therefore nominal. The 10% k-range threshold, not the P-value, is what separates taxa here.

info.hypothesis: The population median stature-velocity curve from birth to 20 years shows, in order: a very high velocity in infancy, a lower and nearly steady velocity through childhood, a distinct rise (adolescent spurt) in the early-to-mid teens, and a fall toward zero by the end of the teens.
info.pass: Pre-registered, evaluated on boys (the subject of Thompson's sentence) with girls reported alongside. Velocities come from pooled NHANES 2007-2018 measured stature (recumbent length < 24 months, standing height >= 24 months) using exam age in months. Model-free yearly velocity v(a) = median(height | age in [a+1,a+2) yr) - median(height | age in [a,a+1) yr), a = 0..18; smoothed velocity = derivative of a weighted smoothing spline through monthly medians. All four must hold for boys: (a) infancy: v(0) >= 2 x mean of v(4..9); (b) childhood steadiness: coefficient of variation of the smoothed velocity over ages 4-10 < 0.15 and max-min of v(4..9) <= 2.0 cm/yr; (c) adolescent quickening: max smoothed velocity in ages 10-17 >= 1.2 x the minimum smoothed velocity in ages 6-10, and the largest v(a) for a in 10..16 exceeds mean v(4..9) by >= 1.0 cm/yr with a 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples of individuals) excluding 0; (d) arrest: v(18) (18.5 -> 19.5 yr) < 1.5 cm/yr and < one third of mean v(4..9).

measured.unit: cm/yr (boys' adolescent peak yearly velocity minus mean childhood velocity, ages 4-10)

caveats: Deviation from pre-registration: the pre-registered 'weighted smoothing spline' derivative on monthly medians was numerically unstable (adjacent-year smoothed velocities swung between 2.7 and 13.8 cm/yr), so the smoothed velocity uses a fixed-bandwidth (SD 0.5 yr) local-linear Gaussian-kernel smoother on the same monthly medians; thresholds were not changed. Results at bandwidths 0.75 and 1.0 yr are reported and give the same sub-criterion outcomes for boys.

Criterion (b) is met at the threshold: the range of boys' yearly velocities between ages 4 and 10 is exactly 2.0 cm/yr (allowed <= 2.0), driven by a pre-pubertal dip to 4.7 cm/yr at 8.5-9.5 yr. Childhood velocity in boys declines slowly (7.6 -> 4.8 cm/yr smoothed, ages 3-9) rather than being flat; 'nearly steady' holds only relative to infancy and adolescence.

Cross-sectional data: population medians attenuate and spread the adolescent spurt; in girls the spurt (peak 10.9 yr) is so attenuated that its excess over childhood velocity (0.9 cm/yr) has a bootstrap CI including 0, so criterion (c) fails for girls even though the pattern is visible. Thompson's sentence is about boys, which is why the verdict is scored on boys.
Birth length is absent from NHANES, so 'infancy' velocity is measured between the 0-11 and 12-23 month medians (about 14 cm/yr), which understates the true first-year velocity.

info.hypothesis: Across human growth, body weight scales approximately as the cube of stature (log-log slope near 3), and cubing the stature-versus-age curve removes most of the difference in shape between the stature curve and the weight curve.
info.pass: Pre-registered, on pooled NHANES 2007-2018 individuals aged 0-19.99 yr with measured weight and stature (recumbent length < 24 months, standing height >= 24 months), sexes pooled with sex-specific values reported. (1) Cube tendency: the OLS slope b of log10(weight) on log10(stature) over all individuals satisfies 2.5 <= b <= 3.5 (95% CI reported; reduced-major-axis slope reported as sensitivity), and the same slope fitted to the age-median curve (monthly median weight vs monthly median stature, 0-19 yr) also lies in [2.5, 3.5]. (2) 'Mainly explains the curve difference': with monthly medians H(t), W(t) normalised to their 19-yr values, define D(p) = mean over months of |W(t)/W(19) - (H(t)/H(19))^p|. Supports if D(3)/D(1) <= 0.5, i.e. cubing the stature curve removes at least half of the discrepancy between the stature and weight curves. Both (1) and (2) must hold for 'supports'.

measured.unit: log-log OLS exponent of weight on stature, individuals aged 0-19

caveats: The two halves of the claim come apart. The allometric exponent across growth is 2.41 (CI 2.40-2.42; curve-level 2.46; RMA 2.50), below the pre-registered [2.5, 3.5] window, so weight does not vary as the cube of stature in the strict sense: proportions and composition change with age (window exponents 2.10 at 0-2 yr, 2.36 at 2-10 yr, 3.10 at 10-20 yr).

The second clause passes clearly: cubing the normalised stature curve removes 80% of its discrepancy from the normalised weight curve (D(3)/D(1) = 0.196; best exponent for curve shape 3.35), so the cubic relation does 'mainly, though not wholly' explain why the weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve, as Thompson said.

The exponent that best matches curve shapes (3.35) differs from the log-log slope (2.41) because the normalised-curve comparison weights late ages (where W/W19 is near 1) differently from a log-log fit dominated by infancy and childhood; both numbers are reported.

Cross-sectional data from a modern US population with high adolescent adiposity, which raises the 10-20 yr exponent; a leaner historical population would likely give a lower overall exponent, not a higher one.

info.hypothesis: Sex-specific population growth-velocity curves (stature, and weight as in Thompson's Fig. 5) have the same sequence of phases and nearly the same shape once shifted in time and scaled in amplitude, with the girls' adolescent acceleration beginning, peaking and ending earlier than the boys'.
info.pass: Pre-registered. From pooled NHANES 2007-2018 measured stature and weight (exam age in months), compute for each sex monthly medians, a weighted smoothing spline, and its derivative (velocity). Primary outcome = stature velocity; secondary = weight velocity. Define for each sex: takeoff age = age of the minimum smoothed velocity between 6 yr and the peak; peak age = age of the maximum smoothed velocity in 8-17 yr; end age = first age after the peak at which stature velocity falls below 1.0 cm/yr (weight: below 50% of the peak). Supports if, for stature, (i) girls' peak age is earlier than boys' by >= 1.0 yr with a 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples of individuals) excluding 0, (ii) girls' takeoff and end ages are both earlier than boys', and (iii) shape similarity: after shifting the girls' velocity curve by the peak-age difference and regressing the boys' curve on it over boys' ages 6-17 (monthly grid), Pearson r >= 0.8; and for weight, girls' peak age is earlier by >= 1.0 yr.

measured.unit: years by which the girls' stature-velocity peak precedes the boys' (boys 12.92 yr, girls 10.92 yr)

caveats: Deviation from pre-registration: as in thompson1917-ch03-05, the pre-registered smoothing-spline derivative was numerically unstable on monthly medians, so a fixed-bandwidth (SD 0.5 yr) local-linear kernel smoother on the same monthly medians is used; thresholds unchanged.

Cross-sectional velocities: population medians spread each sex's spurt, so absolute peak velocities (8.6 cm/yr boys, 7.4 cm/yr girls) are far below longitudinal peak-height velocities, but the between-sex timing difference (2.0 yr) is consistent with longitudinal literature.

The weight-velocity peak lead (2.1 yr) meets the secondary criterion as a point estimate, but its bootstrap CI [-0.92, 3.50] includes 0 because median weight by month is noisy; weight takeoff is not earlier in girls (-0.6 yr). The verdict rests on the pre-registered primary (stature) outcome.
Shape similarity (r = 0.93 after a 2.0-yr shift, boys' amplitude 1.16x girls' at the peak) was assessed over ages 6-17 only; infancy and early childhood were not part of the comparison.

info.hypothesis: If fishes approach a maximal size only asymptotically, then mean length at age in well-sampled wild fish populations keeps increasing, by ever smaller but still positive increments, through the oldest well-sampled ages, and an asymptotic growth model fits the length-at-age means better than a model in which length reaches a fixed maximum at a finite age and then stays there.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: ICES DATRAS North Sea IBTS (NS-IBTS) age records (CA record type), quarters 1 and 3, survey years 2000-2024, all species; length class converted to cm; records with a plus-group flag or missing age excluded. A species qualifies if it has at least 7 consecutive age classes starting at age 1, each with at least 50 aged fish (sum of CANoAtLngt); the included age range ends at the oldest class with at least 50 fish. For each species, mean length at age is computed (weighted by CANoAtLngt) and two 3-parameter models are fitted by weighted least squares (weights = number of fish): (i) asymptotic von Bertalanffy L = Linf (1 - exp(-K (a - t0))) with K > 0, and (ii) determinate quadratic-plateau L = Lmax - c (tc - a)^2 for a < tc, L = Lmax for a >= tc, with tc constrained to at most (oldest included age - 1) so that the model asserts a maximum actually reached inside the data. dAIC = AIC_det - AIC_VB (positive favours the asymptotic model). Late-age increments are the three increments of mean length between the last four included age classes. SUPPORTS if the asymptotic model is favoured (dAIC > 2) in at least two thirds of qualifying species AND at least 75% of all late-age increments pooled across species are positive. Requires at least 5 qualifying species; otherwise inconclusive (underpowered).

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying species in which the asymptotic model is favoured by dAIC > 2 (pre-registered threshold 2/3); fraction of late-age increments positive = 0.758 (threshold 0.75)
measured.n: 11 species, 33 late-age increments, 1111408 aged fish from 986385 CA rows

caveats: The pre-registered supports condition was narrowly missed: 7/11 = 0.636 species favour the asymptotic model against the required 2/3, while the late-increment condition (0.758 >= 0.75) was met. The result is therefore 'mixed' by rule, although most of the evidence points toward protracted growth.

In the two species where the reached-maximum model wins (whiting, lemon sole) mean length at age actually declines over the oldest ages, which neither model predicts for individual growth; the most likely cause is size-selective (fishing) mortality removing the faster growers (Lee's phenomenon) and ageing error, not cessation of growth. This biases the test against the claim.

Cross-sectional survey means pool cohorts and years (2000-2024, Q1 and Q3) and so mix cohort effects with age effects; the oldest age classes are sparsely sampled (>= 50 fish required) and trawl gear under-samples the largest fish.

The determinate alternative had to be given a specific functional form (quadratic rise to a plateau); a different plateau model could change individual dAIC values. Model selection used AIC on 7-18 age-class means, not individual-level likelihoods.

info.hypothesis: If the human curve of growth in body length has its point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life, then the velocity of body-length growth (d length / d gestational age) must still be increasing through the end of the first trimester and must already be decreasing through the third trimester, so that the velocity maximum lies between the end of the first trimester and the start of the third (about 14 to 24 completed weeks of gestation, i.e. months 4-6, centred on month 5).
info.pass: Pre-registered. Using the 50th-centile curves of international (INTERGROWTH-21st) standards for fetal crown-rump length (9+0 to 14+0 weeks) and for newborn crown-heel length by gestational age at birth (24 to 42 weeks), compute growth velocity in mm/week by finite differences of the median curve. The claim is supported if (a) median CRL velocity averaged over weeks 13-14 exceeds that averaged over weeks 9-10 (length growth still accelerating at 14 weeks), and (b) median crown-heel-length velocity averaged over weeks 24-28 exceeds that averaged over weeks 36-40 and the 24-40 velocity series has a negative linear trend (growth already decelerating from 24 weeks). (a) and (b) together bracket the velocity maximum within 14-24 weeks, which contains 'about the fifth month'. As a secondary check, the gestational age of peak velocity of INTERGROWTH-21st fetal femur length (14-40 weeks) is reported; a femur peak within 14-24 weeks or at the 14-week boundary is consistent with the claim.

measured.unit: lower bound (weeks of gestation) of the bracket containing the body-length velocity maximum; upper bound 24 weeks by criterion (b)

caveats: Both pre-registered pass conditions hold, but condition (b) is met only because velocity drops after 33 weeks: median birth length grows at an almost constant 12.5-13.5 mm/week from 24 to 33 weeks. The data therefore locate the velocity maximum somewhere between 14 and about 33 weeks (months 4-8), not sharply at month 5; Thompson's 'velocity tends to fall away' after month five is at best a gentle plateau until month 8.

The two body-length measures differ (crown-rump length before 14 weeks; crown-heel length at birth after 24 weeks) and there is a 10-week gap with no direct body-length standard, so no single smooth curve could be fitted.

Birth length by gestational age for 24-32 weeks comes from preterm births (a reference, not a prescriptive standard); preterm neonates may be smaller than fetuses of the same age still in utero, which would flatten the apparent early-third-trimester velocity.

Femur length, the only skeletal length standard spanning 14-40 weeks, has monotonically decreasing velocity from 14 weeks (peak at or before 14 weeks), i.e. a skeletal-segment inflection earlier than month 5; only whole-body length is tested as Thompson stated it.

info.hypothesis: The coefficient of variation (CV = SD / mean) of human stature and of weight at a given age tracks the mean rate of growth at that age: it falls through childhood as growth decelerates, rises again during the adolescent growth spurt, and falls after it. Hence, across ages, CV should be positively associated with growth velocity, within childhood as well as over the whole span, and the CV peak should coincide with the velocity peak.
info.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using the CDC 2000 growth-chart LMS reference tables for stature-for-age and weight-for-age (2-20 years, half-month grid, each sex), compute at each age the CV of the fitted Box-Cox distribution (mean and SD obtained by numerical integration over z in [-4, 4]; the LMS S parameter is reported as a check) and the growth velocity dM/dt (central differences of the median M, per year). For each of the four series (stature boys, stature girls, weight boys, weight girls), over ages 2.5-19.5 years: (T1) Spearman rho between CV and velocity is positive with P < 0.01; (T2) the age of maximum CV between 8 and 19 years lies within 1.5 years of the age of peak velocity (the adolescent spurt), and CV at that peak exceeds the pre-pubertal minimum CV (ages 4-11) by at least 5% of its value; (T3) within childhood, from 2.5 years to the age of minimum velocity before the spurt, Spearman rho between CV and velocity is positive (CV falls as growth decelerates). The claim is supported if T1, T2 and T3 all hold in at least 3 of the 4 series.

measured.unit: primary series (of 4) in which CV rises into the adolescent spurt (T1 and T2 pass); 0 of 4 pass the childhood test T3

caveats: The adolescent half of the claim is confirmed cleanly: in all four CDC series and in WHO boys the CV peaks within 0.5-1.2 years of peak velocity and 17-54% above its pre-pubertal minimum, and CV is positively correlated with velocity over the whole 2.5-19.5 y span (rho 0.32-0.90). The childhood half is contradicted: between 2.5 y and the pre-spurt velocity minimum (10.4 y boys, 9.3 y girls), stature CV rises monotonically (0.041 to 0.048) while velocity falls from 8.4 to 4.9 cm/yr (rho -0.996 boys, -0.79 girls; WHO: -1.0 both sexes), the opposite of Thompson's 'descends when the rate of growth diminishes'. For weight no childhood deceleration exists in the 2-20 y reference (velocity rises steadily from 1.6 kg/yr at 2.5 y to the spurt), so T3 is undefined and the childhood claim cannot be tested for weight there; in the CDC infant tables (0-36 months) weight CV does fall with falling velocity (0.15 to 0.11, rho 0.68 boys, 0.05 girls), while length CV falls (0.053 to 0.041) but not monotonically with velocity (rho -0.29, -0.37).

Deviation from the pre-registration: the CV is taken as the LMS S parameter rather than the quadrature CV of the Box-Cox distribution, because that distribution has infinite variance for L <= -0.5, which holds for weight at essentially all ages. For stature both definitions agree to 4 decimals and give identical outcomes. The verdict rule itself was applied as pre-registered; under it the weight series could never pass T3, so 'supports' was unreachable once stature failed T3, and the pre-registered 'refutes' condition (3 of 4 series with significantly negative childhood rho) could not be met either because only 2 series have a defined T3. The honest summary is: adolescent part supported, childhood part refuted for stature and untestable for weight in this range.

Thompson's own table (Bowditch) shows stature CV falling from 4.76 at age 5 to 4.40 at age 9; the modern US and WHO references show the opposite trend over the same ages (CDC boys 0.0425 at 5 to 0.0462 at 9). Bowditch's values are cross-sectional school data of the 1870s with small per-age samples; the LMS references are smoothed and much larger, and pool secular trend and mixed ancestry, which may inflate childhood variance.

Reference LMS curves are smoothed fits, not raw sample statistics, and the S curve is itself smoothed over age; Spearman P-values on a half-month grid treat each grid point as an observation and overstate the evidence, so they are reported for the sign and ordering, not as exact probabilities. The adolescent CV rise is widely attributed to variation in the timing of the spurt rather than to the rate of growth per se (the assessors' confound); this test cannot separate the two.

info.hypothesis: In North Sea plaice sampled in late winter, the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 averaged by length class rises with length to a maximum near 30 cm, close to the length at which sexual maturity begins, and then declines slowly at larger sizes.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: ICES DATRAS exchange-format CA (age/biology) records for the North Sea IBTS, quarter 1 (January-February, the closest survey season to Thompson's March 1907 sample), years 2015-2019, species Pleuronectes platessa (Aphia 127143), individual weight > 0, lengths converted to cm. Compute k = 1000 W/L^3 (W in g, L in cm) per fish, average by 1-cm length class over 15-50 cm keeping classes with >= 30 fish, smooth with a 3-class running mean, and let L* be the length of the maximum smoothed k. Maturity: from the same Q1 CA records with a maturity code, classify immature (scale code ending in 1) vs mature (codes ending 2-5), fit a logistic of maturity on length (sexes pooled; by sex reported) and take L50. Supports if all hold: (1) hump: L* is at least 3 cm above the smallest and 3 cm below the largest analysed class, and smoothed k(L*) exceeds smoothed k at both ends of the analysed range by >= 3%; (2) 25 <= L* <= 35 cm; (3) |L* - L50| <= 5 cm. Secondary (reported): the same by sex, and for quarter 3 (2017-2019).

measured.unit: cm, length class of maximum smoothed k in Q1 (upper end of analysed range 16-43 cm); k x 10^4 falls from 97.9 at 16 cm to a minimum of 93.1 at 26-27 cm and rises to 100.2 at 43 cm

caveats: The modern pattern is the inverse of Thompson's: k is highest in the smallest fish, falls to a minimum at 24-28 cm and rises again toward 40+ cm (a U, not a hump), in Q1 pooled, in each year 2015-2019, in each sex, and in Q3 (minimum 25-27 cm). No class near 30 cm is a maximum.

Scope difference: Thompson's 1907 fish came from 'a particular locality' in March with k from class mean weights; here fish are pooled across the whole North Sea survey and weighed individually. Spatial pooling can blur a local hump but cannot manufacture a minimum, and the by-year and by-sex replicates agree.

Maturity has shifted: North Sea plaice now reach 50% maturity at ~18 cm pooled (females 22.5 cm, males 15.2 cm) in Q1, far below the ~30 cm Thompson cited, so criterion (3) could not have been met at 30 cm even if a hump existed there. The k minimum (~26 cm) lies near the female L50, the opposite sign of the association Thompson proposed.
Notation: the pre-registration wrote k = 1000 W/L^3; the analysis reports k x 10^4 as Thompson did (plaice k ~ 100). The scaling does not affect any criterion.

info.hypothesis: At fixed length, plaice (Pleuronectes platessa) lose weight from about November to March/April (spawning) and regain it from May/June to November, and this cycle is caused wholly by spawning and the rebuilding of tissues and gonads. In the ICES North Sea IBTS, whose Q1 cruises run mid-January to early March (during and just after the North Sea plaice spawning season) and whose Q3 cruises run July to September (recovery), this predicts for MATURE plaice: (P1) the condition factor K = 100 W / L^3 declines with date within Q1; (P2) K rises with date within Q3; (P3) in Q1, spent fish have lower K than maturing or spawning fish of the same length. If spawning is the WHOLE cause, IMMATURE plaice should show (M) no comparable within-Q1 decline.
info.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using NS-IBTS CA records (individual weights, CANoAtLngt = 1, maturity staged, length 15-55 cm) joined to HH records for haul dates, with log10 K regressed on day-of-year with fixed effects for 1-cm length class and sex: (P1) the Q1 slope for mature fish is negative with 95% CI excluding 0 and implies a decline of at least 2% of K per 30 days; (P2) the Q3 slope for mature fish is positive with 95% CI excluding 0; (P3) in Q1, spent fish have mean log10 K at least log10(1.05) below maturing fish at the same length and sex (95% CI excluding 0); and (M) the within-Q1 decline per 30 days in immature fish is less than 50% of that in mature fish (point estimate), or is not distinguishable from 0 at the 95% level.

measured.unit: ratio of the within-Q1 (Jan-Feb) decline of log10 K per 30 days in immature plaice to that in mature plaice (pre-registered threshold for 'wholly spawning': < 0.5)

caveats: The descriptive half of the claim is strongly confirmed: at fixed length, mature plaice lose about 4.4% of their weight per 30 days through January-February (P1), regain about 4.7% per 30 days through July-September (P2), and in Q1 spent fish are 7.7% lighter than maturing fish of the same length and sex (P3); the adjusted Q3-Q1 difference is +10.9% for mature fish and is positive in every year 2015-2023 (5-14%). What is refuted is the word 'wholly': immature plaice, which do not spawn, show the same cycle (Q1 decline -5.7% per 30 days, 1.29 times the mature decline; Q3 rise +3.3%; Q3-Q1 +9.2%, positive in every year), so most of the seasonal weight cycle at fixed length is somatic (winter fasting and summer feeding), not gonadal. Within mature fish the stage pattern agrees: fish still 'spawning' lose 5.6% per 30 days while 'spent' fish are flat (+0.6%), i.e. the gonadal loss happens at spawning and then stops, whereas the somatic loss continues in all non-spent groups.

Thompson's own inference, that the spawning season can be read from length-weight data alone, is therefore not safe in general: an immature stock would show a comparable winter trough without spawning. The maturity-stage contrast (P3) does identify spawning, but it requires dissection, which is what Thompson claimed could be avoided.

Within-quarter trends mix calendar date with survey geography (different nations survey different parts of the North Sea at different dates), and fish are treated as independent (haul clustering ignored), so the standard errors are too small; the conclusion does not rest on them but on the comparison of immature with mature fish, which share the same geography and dates, and on the Q3-Q1 contrast, which replicates in every year.

Maturity is taken from the DATRAS codes at face value with the pre-registered mapping; 1480 fish with sub-staged old IBTS codes (Ba, Bb, Ca, Cb, Da, Db) and 29084 weighed plaice without a maturity stage were excluded as pre-registered. Some 'immature' fish of 25-35 cm could be mis-staged late maturers, but at that size the immature group is large (hundreds per week) and the pattern holds across weeks.

info.hypothesis: Annual ring-width chronologies of Arizona ponderosa pine over roughly 1390-1910 contain a regular oscillation with a period of about 150 years, visible as a significant spectral peak near 150 yr and as century-smoothed maxima recurring every ~150 yr.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Primary series: ITRDB chronology az572 (Flagstaff, Arizona, Pinus ponderosa, 'Modern + Archaeological', AD 570-1987), the standard index over the window 1390-1910 (521 yr). Replicate: ITRDB az547 (Walnut Canyon, Pinus ponderosa, 1420-1987) over 1420-1910. Test 1 (spectral): periodogram of the mean-removed annual index; null = AR(1) with the series' lag-1 autocorrelation and variance, 5000 surrogates; pass if the largest periodogram ordinate at periods 120-200 yr exceeds the pointwise 95th percentile of the surrogate periodograms and its period lies in 130-170 yr. Test 2 (regularity of century-smoothed maxima, Douglass's own procedure): 101-yr centred running mean of the index (using data from 1340 on so the smoothed series spans 1390-1910); find local maxima of the smoothed series separated by at least 50 yr; pass if there are at least two intervals between successive maxima and every interval lies in 125-175 yr. Supports if both tests pass on az572.

measured.unit: yr, mean interval between successive maxima of the 101-yr-smoothed Flagstaff index 1390-1910 (intervals 73, 57, 70, 68, 109); strongest 120-200-yr periodogram ordinate at 174 yr has power 1.33 vs AR(1) 95th percentile 1.64

caveats: Both pre-registered tests fail at both sites: no 120-200-yr spectral ordinate exceeds the red-noise 95th percentile (Flagstaff 174 yr: 1.33 vs 1.64; Walnut Canyon 164 yr: 2.21 vs 3.39), and century-smoothed maxima recur every 57-133 yr (means 75 and 89 yr), not every 150. The smoothed series do oscillate, but irregularly and roughly twice as fast as Thompson's figure; a 51-yr smoothing gives the same conclusion.

Sample depth is thin early in the window (Flagstaff: 1-3 trees before 1400, 3-6 in the 1400s; Walnut Canyon: 2-4 trees before 1600), so the 15th-16th-century part of the index is noisy; this weakens any periodicity test but cannot create a regular 150-yr cycle where none is detected.

ITRDB standard chronologies remove the age trend by curve fitting; Douglass smoothed raw widths of a few trees. Detrending with conservative curves preserves century-scale variance in most chronologies but could damp a very long oscillation; the 521-yr window itself limits detectable periods to well under ~260 yr for two cycles.

Not pre-registered, reported as observation only: both sites show a ~70-yr spectral peak (Walnut Canyon 70 yr at 2.4x the AR(1) 95th percentile; Flagstaff 74 yr at 1.4x), in the range of known multidecadal drought variability in the Southwest, not the 150-yr cycle claimed.

info.hypothesis: Across plant and animal species, the gametic (haploid) chromosome number n lies mostly between 6 and 16: the fraction of taxa with n < 6 is small and the fraction with n > 16 is smaller still.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Plants: species-level gametic numbers from the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB) statistics service for all four major groups (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes), using each species' median parsed n. Animals: the Animal Chromosome Count Database (ACC) table (haploid N where given, else 2N/2), one median value per species. For each kingdom compute f_low = fraction of taxa with n < 6, f_mid = fraction with 6 <= n <= 16, f_high = fraction with n > 16, at two resolutions: species level, and genus level (median of species values per genus, the primary resolution, to damp sampling bias toward well-studied genera). Supports if at genus level, in both kingdoms, f_low <= 0.10 and f_high <= 0.10 and f_high <= f_low.

measured.unit: fraction of animal genera with haploid n > 16 (plant genera: 0.320); fraction with n < 6: animals 0.080, plants 0.011

caveats: The lower bound holds (only 1.1% of plant genera and 8.0% of animal genera have n < 6) and the modal haploid number (9-13) sits inside Thompson's 6-16 window, so the claim is half right; what fails is the upper bound: 32% of plant genera and 41% of animal genera have n > 16, so the upper tail is roughly 30 and 5 times larger than the lower tail, the reverse of 'fewer still'.

Both databases over-represent studied taxa (crops, insects, vertebrates) and plants are counted as gametophytic numbers including polyploids (hexaploid wheat is n = 21). Even taking the most favourable subsets (gymnosperms 5.8% > 16; bryophytes 11%), ferns (96% > 16), vertebrates (74%) and molluscs (60%) leave the general claim refuted.
ACC records with non-numeric or range entries for 2N and N were dropped; odd 2N values (XO systems) give half-integer n, which does not affect the 6-16 binning.
Thompson wrote in 1917 from a handful of counted species; the finding reflects a century of counting rather than an error in his reading of the data available to him.

info.hypothesis: If tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120 degrees regardless of cell size, junction angles in real tissues cluster near 120 degrees more tightly than in a random partition of the plane, T-shaped junctions are rare, four cells do not meet at one point, and angle deviation does not depend on cell size.
info.pass: Exploratory, not pre-registered: the images were segmented and inspected before the pass criterion was written. Treat the verdict as hypothesis-generating; a pre-registered replication on new images is needed before it counts as a test. A tissue conforms if its junction-angle SD and its fraction of T-like junctions (largest angle >= 160 deg) are both below the random-Voronoi control. Supports if every usable tissue conforms; mixed if some do and some do not; refutes if none do.

measured.unit: tissues (of those usable) whose junction-angle SD and T-junction fraction are both below the random-Voronoi control

caveats: Exploratory, not pre-registered: the images were segmented and inspected before the pass criterion was written. Treat the verdict as hypothesis-generating; a pre-registered replication on new images is needed before it counts as a test.
One image per tissue, all from Wikimedia Commons; tissues were chosen by availability, not sampled.
Four-way junction fractions are upper bounds: the random-Voronoi control, which has no true four-way vertices, scores 8.6% because close three-way junctions merge.
Weak negative size-deviation correlations in some tissues also appear in the random control, so they are attributed to measurement noise in small cells.

info.hypothesis: If regular hexagonal packing arises only where cells are uniform in size (and forces uniform), then within an epithelium that Thompson names as the showcase of regular hexagons, the retinal pigment epithelium, the local regularity of the cell polygons must track the local uniformity of cell size: regions whose cells are more uniform in area must have a higher fraction of six-sided cells and a lower spread of neighbour numbers than regions whose cells vary more in area.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For every corrected RPE segmentation ROI of the 10 participants in Granger et al. 2018 (in vivo adaptive-optics imaging of the human RPE mosaic), identify the cells not touching the ROI border, their pixel areas and their numbers of neighbours. For ROIs with >= 30 interior cells compute the coefficient of variation of cell area (CV_A), the fraction of six-sided cells (f6) and the standard deviation of neighbour number (SD_n). The claim is supported if, across ROIs, Spearman's rho between f6 and CV_A is <= -0.3 with p < 0.01, and the mean f6 of the quartile of ROIs with the lowest CV_A exceeds that of the highest-CV_A quartile by at least 0.10 (ten percentage points). SD_n versus CV_A (expected positive) is reported as a consistency check.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between fraction of six-sided cells and coefficient of variation of cell area, across RPE regions

caveats: Within-tissue test only: the comparative part of Thompson's statement (RPE versus intestinal epithelium and parenchyma) was not tested because no comparable public per-cell segmentations of those tissues were found; what is tested is the stated rule that hexagonal regularity tracks uniformity of cell size, inside the tissue he names as the regular case.

Only 21 ROIs (8 of 10 participants) reach the pre-registered 30-cell minimum, because the grader-corrected segmentations cover only part of each ROI and peripheral cells adjacent to unsegmented area had to be dropped. With looser thresholds (15 or 20 cells, 57-82 ROIs) the correlation keeps its sign but weakens to rho = -0.24 to -0.27 (p = 0.03-0.05), as expected when per-ROI estimates become noisier; within-participant correlations are also negative but weak (mean rho about -0.15).

Even the most uniform regions are far from 'perfectly regular': the fraction of six-sided cells ranges 0.42-0.77 (mean 0.54), so Thompson's 'regular hexagons' in the RPE holds only as a statistical tendency.

A negative relation between area dispersion and side-number dispersion is partly expected from the geometry of space-filling tessellations (Lewis's law and related size-topology relations); this test confirms that geometric regularity, which is what Thompson asserted, without identifying forces.

info.hypothesis: If the sutural line of a turreted shell such as Turritella is a geodesic of the shell's enveloping right cone, then the number of whorls the suture makes cannot exceed the number of turns a conical geodesic can make: a geodesic on a right cone of apical angle alpha develops into a straight line on a sector of angle 2*pi*sin(alpha/2), sweeps at most pi of that sector, and therefore turns at most N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) times in total (and only half of that while approaching the apex). Measured whorl counts of Turritella shells must therefore satisfy N_obs <= N_geo.
info.pass: Pre-registered. From published per-specimen measurements of Turritellidae giving both the apical angle alpha and the total whorl number N_obs (Pandita et al. 2013, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6, 50 specimens of 5 species), compute N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) and the ratio R = N_obs / N_geo for every specimen with both values. SUPPORTS if at least 90% of specimens have R <= 1 (whorl count within the geodesic bound).

measured.unit: median ratio of observed whorl number to the maximum number of turns a conical geodesic can make (R = N_obs / N_geo); R > 1 is impossible for a geodesic

caveats: The test refutes the identification of the suture with a geodesic of the enveloping right cone; it does not test Thompson's purely geometric statement that a conical geodesic coils more closely toward the apex (true) nor whether the suture is locally geodesic-like over a fraction of a whorl.

The bound assumes the shell envelope is a right circular cone, which is what Thompson states; real turritellid envelopes are slightly convex or concave, but the Clairaut relation on any such surface of revolution still forbids a geodesic from winding many times toward a narrowing apex unless the sides are almost parallel.

Specimens are Neogene fossils from West Java, not the type species Turritella terebra; fossil apices are often incomplete, so whorl counts are if anything underestimates, which makes the test conservative. Apical angles are the authors' gross measurements to 0.5 degree.
Whorl counts include early whorls where the cone approximation is roughest; subtracting two whorls from every count leaves all 34 specimens above the bound.

info.hypothesis: If the permanent spiral forms of organisms (ruminant horns, molluscan and foraminiferal shells, sunflower capitula) are logarithmic spirals, then for any such structure the linear size of the growing edge (radius vector or whorl size) must increase exponentially with angle of rotation about the spiral's pole, r = a e^(b theta), and must do so better than the alternative simple spirals (Archimedean r = a + b theta, which grows linearly; Fermat / parabolic r = a sqrt(theta + theta0), which decelerates).
info.pass: Pre-registered. Only the molluscan-shell class can be tested with public data located (see interpretation). For every gastropod specimen in Collins et al. 2021 with >= 5 digitised successive half-whorl apertures, take the square root of aperture area as the linear whorl size at angles 0, pi, 2 pi, ...; for every ammonoid species in Korn & Walton 2018 with >= 5 half-whorl diameters, take conch diameter at each half whorl. Fit the three two-parameter models by least squares in the size domain and compare root-mean-square residuals. The claim (for molluscan shells) is supported if the logarithmic model has the lowest RMSE in >= 80% of gastropod specimens and in >= 80% of ammonoid species, and the median ratio RMSE(Archimedean) / RMSE(logarithmic) exceeds 1.5 in both groups. Because horns, foraminifera and sunflower capitula remain untested, the confidence attached to a supporting verdict is capped at 0.5.

measured.unit: fraction of gastropod specimens for which the logarithmic spiral has the lowest RMSE (ammonoids: 1.000)

caveats: Only the molluscan-shell class of Thompson's universal was tested; ruminant horns, foraminiferal shells and sunflower capitula (and the cordate-leaf exception) remain untested for lack of public coordinate data, so even a clean pass could not have established the universal claim.

Within molluscs the result is itself mixed: every one of 179 ammonoid species is fitted far better by the logarithmic spiral (median RMSE ratio 15 against Archimedean), but only 68% of gastropod specimens (14 of 21 species) are, and in the Struthiolariidae genus Pelicaria (36 specimens) and a handful of other species the whorl size grows closer to linearly than exponentially with angle over the digitised whorls. Collins et al. (2021) themselves report that struthiolariid coiling departs from constant-rate (logarithmic) growth.

Gastropod series are short (median 8 half-whorl apertures spanning ~3-4 revolutions with a median expansion of 1.54 per revolution), which limits discrimination between exponential and linear growth; the median RMSE ratio of 1.39 reflects that limited leverage as well as genuine departures.

Tenagodus is a siliquariid whose coiling loosens and uncoils in adulthood, so its non-logarithmic fit is expected; removing it does not change the gastropod percentage materially (it contributes 2 of 145 specimens).

info.hypothesis: If a coiled shell grows by terminal accretion without changing its shape, then within a species the dimensionless conch proportions (whorl width / diameter, whorl height / diameter, umbilical width / diameter) and the whorl expansion rate are constant across ontogeny, i.e. each linear conch dimension scales isometrically (log-log exponent 1) with conch diameter through the measured growth stages.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For each species with measurements at >= 4 growth stages (diameters), fit ordinary least squares of log(ww), log(wh) and log(uw) on log(dm) across its stages. The claim is supported if (a) the across-species median exponent for each of the three dimensions lies in [0.90, 1.10], and (b) at least two thirds of species have all three exponents in [0.90, 1.10] (shape changes by less than ~25% over a ten-fold size range). The same test on Nautilus pompilius (Thompson's showcase) is reported separately and must also meet (a) for the species-level exponents from individual trajectories.

measured.unit: across-species median log-log exponent of umbilical width on conch diameter (isometry = 1)

caveats: Both pre-registered fail conditions fire for ammonoids: the median umbilical-width exponent (0.705) is far below 0.8, and only 8.9% of species are isometric in all three dimensions; 59% of species have uw exponents below 0.8 (whorls become relatively more involute with growth).

Whorl width and aperture height are close to isometric (medians 0.96-0.97; 69-79% of species within [0.9, 1.1]), so the departure from self-similarity is concentrated in the coiling tightness, not in the whorl section.

Nautilus pompilius, Thompson's own exemplar, passes (pooled exponents 0.946 and 1.055; all 6 specimens within [0.9, 1.1]), so the claim holds approximately for the type case even though it fails as a general statement about coiled shells.

Early whorls (ammonitella and first juvenile whorls, dm < 2 mm) are included in the primary test because Thompson states the claim for the shell as a whole; excluding them makes the umbilical allometry stronger (median 0.633), not weaker.

info.hypothesis: If every increment of a spirally grown shell is a gnomon to the whole structure before it (the enlarged whole stays similar to itself), then a molluscan shell is geometrically self-similar through growth: dimensionless shape indices of the conch measured at successive diameters along one specimen's ontogeny (conch width index CWI = ww/dm, umbilical width index UWI = uw/dm, whorl expansion rate WER) stay constant, apart from measurement noise, from the end of the embryonic shell to maturity.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Walton & Korn (2018) ontogenetic conch-parameter series for 177 Devonian-Jurassic ammonoid species (Dryad 10.5061/dryad.c17p8), measured on median cross-sections at successive diameters dm. For each species keep the post-embryonic points (dm >= 2 mm) and require at least 4 points spanning at least a fourfold range of dm. For each retained index compute the log-range D = max ln(index) - min ln(index) over the series. A species is 'gnomonic' if D <= ln(1.25) (at most 25% change) for CWI, UWI and WER alike; 'allometric' if D >= ln(1.5) (at least 50% change) for at least one index; otherwise intermediate. SUPPORTS if at least two thirds of the qualifying species are gnomonic. As a secondary descriptor, the fraction of species whose indices show a monotonic trend with ln dm (|Spearman rho| >= 0.7, p < 0.05, for at least one index) is reported; it does not enter the verdict.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying ammonoid series in which at least one conch shape index changes by >= 50% over post-embryonic growth (pre-registered refutes threshold 2/3); fraction gnomonic = 0.006 (supports threshold 2/3)

caveats: The refutation is carried almost entirely by the umbilical width index: UWI changes by >= 50% in 92% of series (median change 204%), whereas the whorl expansion rate, which encodes the spiral angle, stays within 25% in 80% of series (median change 17%). The spiral itself is therefore close to logarithmic (gnomonic in Thompson's sense), while the whorl section and the degree of involution change through growth, so the enlarged conch is not similar to its earlier self. Dropping UWI, only 34% of series (27% at dm >= 5 mm) are allometric and the pre-registered rule would give 'mixed'.

Walton & Korn chose their 177 species to study pachyconic and globular ammonoids with phased ontogenies, so the sample is probably enriched in species with strong ontogenetic shape change relative to ammonoids at large.

UWI is the noisiest index at small diameters (small umbilical widths); the 2 mm cut-off and the requirement of a monotonic trend (met by 94% of series) limit but do not remove this effect; at dm >= 5 mm the allometric fraction is still 84%.

Scope: Palaeozoic-Jurassic ammonoid conchs only; Thompson's gnomon claim also covers gastropod and bivalve shells, opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns and tusks, which were not tested. The 25% and 50% thresholds are pre-registered conventions, not derived from Thompson.
