info.hypothesis: Along a radius, successive whorl breadths (and hence conch diameters measured at successive half-whorls) of Nautilus, ammonoids and spiral gastropods form a geometric progression: log(diameter) is linear in whorl number, so the whorl expansion rate is constant through ontogeny; for Nautilus the ratio per whole whorl is about 3.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For every specimen with at least four successive half-whorl conch-diameter measurements (ammonoids: stages with diameter >= 5 mm, excluding the embryonic ammonitella; Nautilus: all measured post-embryonic stages): (1) fit log(dm) against half-whorl index by least squares; the median R^2 across specimens must be >= 0.99, and the exponential (geometric) model must have lower residual sum of squares on the dm scale than a straight-line (arithmetic) model in at least 75% of specimens; (2) strict constancy: the median across specimens of the within-specimen relative range of WER, (max - min)/median over post-embryonic stages, must be <= 0.20, and no systematic ontogenetic drift (median within-specimen Spearman correlation of WER with stage between -0.5 and 0.5); (3) the median Nautilus WER (per-revolution diameter ratio) must lie in [2.6, 3.5]. 'supports' requires (1), (2) and (3).

measured.unit: median R^2 of log(diameter) vs whorl index per specimen, ammonoids (Nautilus 0.9995; gastropods 0.987)

caveats: For Nautilus and ammonoids the geometric progression is an excellent description (median R^2 0.9995 and 0.9993; the geometric model beats the arithmetic one in 100% of specimens with residuals 1-2% of the arithmetic model's) and the Nautilus per-revolution ratio is 2.87, close to Thompson's 'about three'. Strict constancy nevertheless fails: in Nautilus the ratio rises systematically through the two measured whorls (median Spearman +0.79, though only by 7% of its value), as described by Tajika et al. 2018 and later work on nautilid ontogeny.

Gastropods are where the claim is weakest: the geometric model beats the arithmetic model in only 73% of specimens (threshold 75%), median R^2 is 0.987 (threshold 0.99), and the expansion ratio of the aperture's distance from the axis declines through ontogeny in 84% of specimens (median Spearman -0.71, median within-specimen range 17%). This agrees with Collins et al. 2021, who conclude from the same material that the logarithmic-helicospiral assumptions fail in all 25 of their species.

The gastropod series are short (4-11 apertures, i.e. 2-5 revolutions) and were digitised on a single sectioned plane; short noisy series depress R^2 and make the arithmetic/geometric comparison less decisive than for the CT-based cephalopod diameters.

The ammonoid sample is biased to Palaeozoic pachyconic and globular species; Walton & Korn document multi-phase ontogenetic trajectories in these forms, so the 6% median within-species range of r is, if anything, an overestimate of constancy for ammonoids generally only in the sense that other groups could drift more.

info.hypothesis: If whorl breadths (equivalently conch diameters one revolution apart) expand by a factor r per whorl, the constant angle is alpha = arccot(ln r / 2 pi) (Thompson's own table: r = 1.5 -> 86.3 deg, 2.0 -> 83.7 deg, 2.5 -> 81.7 deg, 3.0 -> 80.1 deg, 3.5 -> 78.7 deg). The claim then predicts: Nautilus r about 3, alpha about 80 deg; for ordinary ammonoids and typically spiral gastropods alpha is usually between 80 and 85 deg (r between 1.72 and 3.00) and very seldom below 80 deg (r > 3.00).
info.pass: Pre-registered. (a) Nautilus pompilius: per specimen, the median whorl expansion rate WER (Korn's definition, (dm1/dm2)^2 over half a whorl, which equals the per-revolution diameter ratio r) over all measured post-embryonic stages; the median across specimens, converted to alpha, must lie in [78, 82] deg (r in 2.6-3.5). (b) Ammonoids: per species, the median WER over measured stages with conch diameter >= 5 mm (excluding the embryonic ammonitella), converted to alpha; at least 50% of species must have alpha in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% alpha < 80 deg. (c) Gastropods: per specimen (then averaged per species), the fitted per-revolution whorl expansion rate W from the Collins et al. 2021 helicospiral fits, converted to alpha the same way; at least 50% of species in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% below 80 deg. All three of (a), (b), (c) must hold for 'supports'.

measured.unit: degrees, median constant angle of Nautilus pompilius (r = 2.87 per revolution)

caveats: The verdict follows the pre-registered rule, which fails because only 32% of ammonoid species (threshold 40%) and 46% of gastropod species fall inside 80-85 deg. The failure is one-sided: no ammonoid and no gastropod species, and only 5% of Nautilus, fall below 80 deg, so 'very seldom less than 80 deg' is strongly supported; the typical ammonoid and gastropod sits at 85-86 deg (r 1.5-1.7), just above Thompson's upper bound rather than inside it.

The Nautilus part of the claim ('in the neighbourhood of 80 deg', 'about three times') is confirmed closely: median 80.5 deg, r = 2.87, with very low scatter across 93 specimens and three populations.

The ammonoid sample (Walton & Korn 2018) was assembled to study pachyconic and globular conchs and is 82% Palaeozoic; globular Palaeozoic goniatites have low expansion rates, so it is probably biased towards high alpha relative to the Mesozoic ammonites Thompson likely had in mind (the 3 Jurassic and 6 of 11 Permian species are in band).

The gastropod sample is 26 species dominated by four struthiolariid/turritellid species from New Zealand and Australia; species were weighted equally, but it is not a random sample of 'typically spiral' gastropods. r for gastropods was measured on digitised apertures in a single sectioned plane (centroid distance from the axis), which is noisier than CT-based cephalopod diameters.

info.hypothesis: If shells as different as Cerithium (pointed turbinate), Solarium (obtuse turbinate / trochiform), Natica (globose) and Planorbis (discoid) differ little in spiral angle alpha and mainly in the apical semi-angle theta, then across public specimens of these four body forms the between-form spread of alpha (computed from the whorl-breadth ratio R and theta with Thompson's own relation R = exp(2 pi sin(theta) cot(alpha))) must be small, of the order of a few degrees, while the between-form spread of theta spans most of its possible range.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For every specimen with >= 3 digitised successive half-whorl apertures (Collins et al. 2021 helicospiral gastropods) estimate per revolution the linear whorl-breadth ratio R (square root of the aperture-area ratio per 360 degrees, from a log-linear fit of area on angle) and the apical semi-angle theta = atan(d(r_outer)/d(y)) from the outward and axial displacement of the whorl per revolution (theta = 90 degrees for planispiral shells). For the discoid form, which that dataset lacks, use adult whorls of the planispiral ammonoid conchs of Korn & Walton 2018 (R = dm at whorl n+1 / dm at whorl n over the last full whorl, theta = 90 degrees). Compute alpha = arccot(ln R / (2 pi sin theta)) in degrees. Assign specimens to Thompson's four forms by family: pointed turbinate = Turritellidae (Maoricolpus; Thompson lists Turritella with Cerithium), obtuse turbinate / trochiform = Trochoidea (Zethalia, Cookia; Thompson's Solarium / Trochus group), globose = Tonnoidea (Tonna, Semicassis; Thompson's Natica / Dolium group), discoid = planispiral ammonoids. The claim is supported if the range of the four form-mean alphas is <= 10 degrees while the range of form-mean thetas is >= 45 degrees, i.e. alpha range < one quarter of theta range.

measured.unit: range (degrees) of form-mean spiral angle alpha across the four body forms; range of form-mean apical semi-angle theta = 81.5 degrees

caveats: The named genera (Cerithium, Solarium, Natica, Planorbis) were replaced by public specimens of the same body forms (Turritellidae, Trochoidea, Tonnoidea, planispiral ammonoids), following Thompson's own grouping of shells by form in the same table; this is a reinterpretation of the genus-level statement.
Two of the four forms (trochiform, globose) rest on two specimens each, the pre-registered minimum; the pointed-turbinate and discoid forms are well sampled (35 and 179).

The apical semi-angle measured here for the globose shells (28-37 degrees) is the cone of the digitised spire whorls, not the envelope of the whole shell including the body whorl as in Thompson's table (Natica ~70 degrees); the theta range would be larger, not smaller, with his convention, so the conclusion is unaffected.

Spiral angle expressed in degrees is compressed towards 90 degrees for all biologically realistic whorl-expansion ratios, which is part of why alpha varies little; on the scale-free measure cot(alpha), the radial-to-tangential growth ratio, the forms still differ about half as much (CV 0.40) as they do in theta (CV 0.81), so the direction of Thompson's claim holds either way, but the 'very little indeed' is partly an artefact of his angle scale.

info.hypothesis: In hollow-horned ruminants (Bovidae) the two horns of a pair are conjugate spirals: each is a helico-spiral of the same length, curvature and pitch as its partner but of opposite handedness, so that reflecting one horn in the skull's sagittal plane reproduces the other.
info.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). For at least 8 bovid crania from public 3D scans spanning at least 4 genera, extract the midline curve of each horn core from the mesh, fit a helico-spiral (constant curvature and torsion in the Frenet sense, i.e. a conical helix) to each, and compare the pair: in at least 80% of specimens the signs of the torsion of the left and right horn are opposite, and the magnitudes of length, mean curvature and mean torsion agree within 15% (|L - R| / mean of the pair).

measured.unit: bovid crania with both horn cores actually obtained (0 of 13 open candidates)

caveats: The specimens needed exist and are catalogued: 44 bovid cranium or skull media on MorphoSource, 13 of them flagged 'open' visibility, spanning 6 genera (Ammotragus, Bison, Capra, Oryx, Ovis, Qurliqnoria). What failed is access: every download route returns an Anubis bot-protection page or HTTP 404 from this host, and MorphoSource downloads require an authenticated account that accepts each specimen's use agreement. Under the pre-registered rule ('fewer than 8 specimens or 4 genera obtainable without authentication') the verdict is inconclusive, not a judgement on the claim.

Measurement datasets about bovid horns do exist (Dryad: ontogenetic allometry of horn length; horn investment in female bovids), but they record one horn length per individual or species means, so they cannot address left-versus-right mirror symmetry at all.

With an account the test as pre-registered looks tractable: the open candidates include Bison bison (15.8 MB mesh), Bison priscus, Ovis ammon polii, Capra ibex, Ammotragus lervia and Oryx gazella CT series, which would give 4-6 genera, short of the pre-registered 8 specimens unless the restricted-download items are added.

Horn cores, not sheaths, are what these scans show; Thompson's figures are of sheaths. Handedness is the same in core and sheath, but the quantitative comparison (length, curvature, torsion) would differ between the two, which the pre-registered thresholds do not account for.

info.hypothesis: Within one species of sunflower, larger capitula carry higher parastichy pairs: head diameter increases in order across the successive Fibonacci pairs (e.g. 21/34 < 34/55 < 55/89 < 89/144), so parastichy numbers rise with the size of the whole structure.
info.pass: Pre-registered. In the Turing's Sunflowers data (Helianthus annuus), restrict to heads with a recorded head (seedhead) diameter and with both parastichy counts forming an adjacent pair of a Fibonacci-type sequence (Fibonacci, Lucas, double Fibonacci or F4, as defined by Swinton et al. 2016). The Spearman rank correlation between head diameter and the larger parastichy number must be positive with rho >= 0.30 and P < 0.01, and the median head diameter must increase monotonically across successive pair classes of the main Fibonacci sequence that each have n >= 10 heads.

caveats: Head diameter was measured and reported by the growers themselves (citizen science), with unknown precision and probably mixed conventions (disc versus whole head); such noise biases the correlation towards zero, not away from it.
The sample is cultivated Helianthus annuus of many cultivars; the claim's remark about other composites is not tested.
Thompson lists 34/55, 55/89 and 89/144 as occurring in one species; here the 89/144 class has only 11 heads, though their median diameter (24 cm) is well above the 55/89 class (14 cm).
Size and developmental stage are confounded in a cross-sectional sample; the claim is about size, and that is what was measured.

info.hypothesis: Within one species, heads (or cones) carrying a given parastichy pair are split about equally between the two chiralities: the larger parastichy family runs clockwise in roughly half of specimens and anticlockwise in the other half, as in Thompson's 224 right-handed versus 243 left-handed among 467 five-eight spruce cones.
info.pass: Pre-registered. In the Turing's Sunflowers data (Helianthus annuus), restrict to heads with both a clockwise and an anticlockwise parastichy count that together form an adjacent pair of one Fibonacci-type sequence (Fibonacci, Lucas, double Fibonacci or F4, as defined by Swinton et al. 2016). Define a head as right-handed when its larger family is clockwise. Pooled over all such heads, the proportion p of right-handed heads must satisfy |p - 0.5| <= 0.10 and a two-sided exact binomial test against 0.5 must give P >= 0.05. In addition, in each pair class with n >= 20 heads, |p - 0.5| <= 0.15 or the binomial P >= 0.05. Primary counts are the photoreviewed counts (author's annotation file); the submitter counts are a secondary replication.

measured.unit: proportion of heads whose larger parastichy family runs clockwise (photoreviewed counts)

caveats: The test is on sunflower capitula, not on the Norway spruce cones Thompson cites; his spruce tally is not available as a per-cone dataset and was not re-analysed.

The sample is a citizen-science collection of mostly one cultivated species grown in many gardens; counts are subjective, but handedness (which family is larger and which way it runs) is robust to small count errors.

Heads whose two counts did not form an adjacent Fibonacci-type pair (about 40% of photoreviewed heads with two counts) were excluded by the pre-registered rule; chirality in disordered heads is not tested.

The 21/34 class (n = 29) leans right-handed (20:9, P = 0.06); it passes the pre-registered class rule only through its P value, and the two large classes lean in opposite directions, consistent with chance.

info.hypothesis: In species-level egg measurements of birds, turtles/tortoises and crocodilians, the polar axis (egg length) is never shorter than the maximum equatorial diameter (egg breadth): no hard-shelled egg is oblate or discoidal.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For each species with a mean egg length L (pole-to-pole) and breadth B (maximum equatorial diameter) in the Deeming & Ruta 2014 amniote egg compilation (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.s9227) and the 955-species bird egg-shape compilation (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.sj3tx9648), compute the elongation L/B. Groups: birds, Testudines, Crocodylia (hard-shelled, in scope); Squamata reported separately as out of scope (mostly parchment-shelled). Supports if, in every in-scope group, zero species have L/B < 1.00, and the fraction of species within 5% of a sphere (L/B < 1.05) is reported together with the minimum L/B per group.

measured.unit: minimum species-mean egg length/breadth among in-scope species (Macrochelys temminckii, 38.8 x 37.5 mm); zero of 192 species have L/B < 1

caveats: Deviation from pre-registration: the two Dryad compilations named in planned_datasets (doi:10.5061/dryad.s9227, doi:10.5061/dryad.sj3tx9648) could not be downloaded because Dryad's file downloads are gated by an interactive anti-bot (proof-of-work) challenge; the Amniote Life-History Database, which carries the same two variables (egg length, egg width) and also covers turtles and crocodilians, was substituted. Criteria and thresholds were not changed.

Coverage is modest: only 167 bird, 16 turtle and 9 crocodilian species have both egg length and width in this database, far fewer than the ~1,400 bird species of Stoddard et al. 2017. A rare oblate species could be missed; a universal negative can only be supported, not proven, by a sample.

Measurement convention limits discriminating power: because egg length is recorded along the longer (polar) axis, an oblate egg could only appear as L/B at or just below 1. The data show no species near that boundary except the alligator snapping turtle (L/B = 1.03, effectively spherical), so the data are consistent with the claim but cannot exclude an oblate egg disguised as a sphere.
One crocodilian row (L/B = 16.9) is an evident unit error in the source (width probably in cm); it does not affect the oblate count and is left as recorded.

info.hypothesis: If lateral-spined (S. mansoni) and terminal-spined (S. haematobium) eggs are mechanical variants produced by one species, then worms assigned to S. mansoni and to S. haematobium belong to one interbreeding lineage: their mitochondrial cox1 sequences should be no more divergent from each other than sequences within either nominal species, and should not form two reciprocally separated clusters.
info.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using GenBank cox1 sequences (up to 40 per nominal species, chosen by a fixed random seed from all records >= 400 bp, hybrids excluded by title), pairwise uncorrected p-distances computed on pairwise alignments over >= 300 overlapping sites: the mean S. mansoni vs S. haematobium distance is <= 0.03, or the distributions overlap (minimum between-group distance smaller than the maximum within-group distance of either species, i.e. no barcode gap).

measured.unit: mean uncorrected cox1 p-distance, S. mansoni vs S. haematobium

caveats: Only the taxonomic conclusion of the claim is tested. Whether the lateral spine is moulded in a funnel-shaped part of the ootype/uterus (the mechanism Thompson takes from Looss) is not addressed by sequence data; but since the two egg types belong to lineages about 17% divergent in cox1, more than the divergence between other accepted Schistosoma species, the egg forms cannot be variants of one species whatever their mechanical origin.

Mitochondrial distance is one line of evidence; the same conclusion is standard from nuclear genomes, chromosome structure, intermediate-host specificity (Biomphalaria vs Bulinus) and the absence of fertile S. mansoni x S. haematobium hybrids. Those were not re-analysed here.

GenBank species labels are taken at face value. A few unusually divergent 'within-species' pairs (max 7.1% within S. mansoni, 6.4% within S. haematobium, one S. japonicum sequence 25% from the rest) probably reflect mislabelled or atypical records; they make the within-species range wider, i.e. work against the verdict, which is nonetheless reached with a wide margin.
The sequenced cox1 regions vary between studies; distances were computed only on overlapping aligned columns (>= 300), and 10% of pairs with no sufficient overlap were dropped.

info.hypothesis: If buoyancy has removed the tall arched neural spines over the withers and haunches, then secondarily aquatic mammals (pinnipeds, cetaceans) should show no anterior-thoracic ('withers') peak of relative neural-spine height along the thoracolumbar column, and their anterior-thoracic spines should be relatively shorter than those of terrestrial quadrupeds; the haunch (posterior lumbar) spines should likewise not be elevated.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Per vertebra, relative spine height h = (neural spine apex to centrum reference distance) / cranial centrum height. Per species: W = mean h over T1-T4 ('withers'); P = mean h over the posterior thoracics T10-T13 (terrestrial trough region); WI = W/P ('withers index'); HI = mean h over the last three lumbars / P ('haunch index'). Test A (Carnivora landmark data, Figueirido et al. 2021): SUPPORTS-component if every pinniped species has W below the 25th percentile of terrestrial carnivoran W and one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests give p < 0.05 for pinnipeds < terrestrial on both W and WI. Test B (cetacean linear data, Gillet et al. 2019, h = Lnp/Hc; W over the first three thoracics, P over the last three thoracics, WI = W/P): SUPPORTS-component if the median cetacean WI <= 1 and at least 80% of cetacean species have WI below the minimum WI of the terrestrial carnivorans from Test A. Overall verdict 'supports' only if both components support.

measured.unit: withers index WI (mean of the two pinniped species); terrestrial carnivoran WI min 1.238, median 1.910
measured.n: 45 carnivoran species (951 vertebrae) incl. 2 pinnipeds; 74 cetacean species (204 specimens, 8722 vertebrae)

caveats: Only two pinniped species (one phocid, one otariid) are in the carnivoran dataset; sirenians are absent from both datasets, and the bird-pelvis half of the claim was not tested at all. The verdict therefore covers pinnipeds and cetaceans only, not Thompson's 'all aquatic mammals'.

The 'haunch' part is not discriminating in Carnivora: terrestrial carnivorans themselves show no posterior-lumbar spine peak (median HI 0.80 < 1), and pinniped HI falls inside the terrestrial range (p = 0.77). Thompson's haunch spines refer mainly to ungulates, for which no comparable public data were used.

Pinniped anterior-thoracic spines are reduced (W 2.3-2.7 vs terrestrial 2.6-5.3) and the withers peak is absent (WI about 1.0), but the spines have not literally 'entirely disappeared'; Otaria byronia's W lies above the lowest terrestrial species (Martes foina).

Relative spine height from landmarks includes the neural arch and depends on where the authors placed the spinous-process landmarks; the cetacean values come from a different measurement protocol, so only the within-column ratio WI is compared across datasets.

info.hypothesis: The cannon-bones (fused metacarpal III+IV, and likewise metatarsal) of ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only by a one-axis stretch: scaled to equal greatest length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's, and the residual shape difference after that single transverse scaling is small.
info.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using public osteometric measurements of adult metacarpals (greatest length GL and distal breadth Bd, or the same pair of dimensions however the source names them), with at least 10 specimens for ox (Bos taurus) and sheep (Ovis aries) and at least 3 for giraffe (Giraffa): the species median of Bd/GL, expressed relative to the ox, is 0.67 +/- 0.10 for sheep and 0.33 +/- 0.10 for giraffe. If 3D surface meshes rather than tables are used, GL is the maximum caliper length and Bd the maximum extent perpendicular to the long axis within the distal 15% of the bone, both computed from the mesh.

measured.unit: metacarpal distal breadth / greatest length, relative to ox

caveats: No public source was found that gives cannon-bone greatest length and breadth, or a measurable 3D mesh, for all three of ox, sheep and giraffe. Ox metacarpal meshes exist on MorphoSource (5 laser scans) but sheep metacarpals return nothing there and the only giraffe media is a cranium; the single Dryad giraffe limb-bone dataset is 8.5 GB of CT imagery of metatarsals with no comparative material.

The two large zooarchaeological osteometric archives that would supply ox and sheep (the Animal Bone Metrical Archive Project at the Archaeology Data Service, and Open Context) are behind bot challenges (Cloudflare 403 and Anubis) that a headless browser did not clear in this run; even if cleared, neither contains giraffe, so the giraffe third of the claim would still be missing.

The claim is not untestable in principle: measurements of a handful of museum metapodials of the three species, or scans of them, would settle it quickly. The gap is that such measurements are not published as open data. The assessors scored 'data-existence' 0.68-0.86 largely on the expectation that MorphoSource covers ungulate metapodials; for sheep and giraffe it does not.

Hit counts in the probe log are as of 2026-10-31 and will change as catalogues grow; the Zenodo 'giraffe metacarpal' query reports 119 hits only because the terms are OR-combined across full text, and its top results are unrelated.

info.hypothesis: If the claim holds, Perissodactyla and Leporidae form a clade in the current synthetic mammal phylogeny that excludes the other ungulates (Artiodactyla; also Proboscidea and Hyracoidea in the 1917 sense of Ungulata) and excludes the rodents.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Take the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree (induced_subtree API, current synth version) over these tips: Perissodactyla = Equus caballus, Ceratotherium simum, Tapirus terrestris; other ungulates = Bos taurus, Sus scrofa, Camelus dromedarius (Artiodactyla), Loxodonta africana (Proboscidea), Procavia capensis (Hyracoidea); Leporidae = Oryctolagus cuniculus, Lepus europaeus, Sylvilagus floridanus; other lagomorph = Ochotona princeps; Rodentia = Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus, Sciurus carolinensis, Cavia porcellus, Castor canadensis; outgroups = Canis lupus, Homo sapiens, Monodelphis domestica. Let C be the smallest clade containing all perissodactyl and all leporid tips. Sub-claim 1 (perissodactyls closer to leporids than to other ungulates) holds iff C contains no artiodactyl tip; sub-claim 2 (leporids closer to perissodactyls than to other rodents) holds iff C contains no rodent tip. Supports if both hold. Independent check: NCBI Taxonomy lineages (efetch) must place Perissodactyla and Leporidae in a shared named clade below Boreoeutheria that excludes Artiodactyla and Rodentia.

measured.unit: tips (of 20) in the smallest Open Tree clade containing all perissodactyl and leporid tips; it is Boreoeutheria and includes all artiodactyl, rodent, carnivore and primate tips

caveats: The Open Tree synthetic tree carries no support values; however the groupings that refute the claim (Perissodactyla with Artiodactyla and Carnivora in Laurasiatheria; Leporidae with Ochotonidae and Rodentia in Glires) are recovered by every large molecular phylogenomic study of placental mammals and are encoded in NCBI Taxonomy, which is a curated classification rather than an independent analysis.

Thompson's claim was framed as an inference from a Cartesian transformation of skull outlines; the test addresses only its phylogenetic conclusion, not whether the skull transformation itself is geometrically simple.

Proboscidea and Hyracoidea (ungulates in the 1917 sense) fall in Afrotheria, outside the clade shared by perissodactyls and leporids, so for those 'other ungulates' sub-claim 1 would hold trivially; the sub-claim fails for the Artiodactyla, the ungulates Thompson's comparison (horses, rhinoceroses vs other hoofed mammals) most directly concerns.

The induced-subtree Newick is saved under data/ and its SHA-256 recorded; re-running against a later synth version may change the version string but not the result unless mammalian phylogeny is overturned.

info.hypothesis: If the differences between the human skull and the chimpanzee (and baboon) skull form one continuous deformation whose grid areas 'increase in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order' from above downwards and from behind forwards, then the local area scale factor of the human-to-ape transformation of the lateral (sagittal) skull profile must be a smooth monotone function of antero-inferior position, with its logarithm roughly linear in that position, rather than a patchwork of region-specific changes.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Primary plan (landmark coordinates available for Homo sapiens and Pan troglodytes): generalised Procrustes superimposition of all specimens; species mean configurations; projection of the means onto the midsagittal plane (midline landmarks as they are, bilateral landmarks averaged across sides) giving a lateral profile with x = antero-posterior and y = supero-inferior axes defined by the Frankfurt-like orientation of the human mean; fit a 2-D thin-plate spline mapping the human mean to the chimpanzee mean and evaluate its Jacobian determinant J (local area ratio chimpanzee/human) at every landmark of the human mean. Define the down-forward coordinate u = (x_forward + y_downward)/sqrt(2) of each landmark. The claim is supported if (a) Spearman rho(u, log J) >= 0.6 with positive sign, (b) the sign of the correlation of log J with x_forward alone and with y_downward alone is positive in both, and (c) an ordinary linear regression of log J on u explains >= 50% of the variance in log J (the 'logarithmic order' of areas, i.e. geometric progression of area ratio with grid position). Secondary plan (only inter-landmark distances available): log of the ratio of chimpanzee to human mean distance, each distance first divided by the geometric mean of all distances in its specimen; assign each distance by the anatomical names of its endpoints to one of three ordered regions (1 neurocranium/vault/occiput, 2 orbit/upper face/nasal, 3 maxilla/palate/mandible/alveolar); supported if Spearman rho(region rank, log ratio) >= 0.6 and region medians increase monotonically 1 < 2 < 3. If the data also contain Gorilla, the same statistics are reported for Gorilla as a replication but do not enter the verdict. Because baboon (Papio) data could not be located, confidence attached to any verdict is capped at 0.6.

measured.unit: Spearman rho (region score vs size-corrected log distance ratio Pan troglodytes/Homo)

caveats: Secondary (weaker) plan: the deposit gives inter-landmark distances, not landmark coordinates, so no thin-plate-spline area ratios could be computed; distance ratios are linear rather than areal scale factors and position is an ordinal three-level region score assigned by the analyst from landmark names, not a measured coordinate.

No baboon (Papio) data were available; Thompson's statement that the baboon shows 'the same order' of deformation with greater intensity is untested. Gorilla, which Thompson also mentions, shows the same gradient with a steeper slope (0.28 vs 0.22 log units per region step), consistent with his 'increased intensity' remark.

The relation is monotone and roughly linear in log ratio across region ranks (R^2 0.48 for Pan, 0.51 for Gorilla), which is what 'approximately logarithmic order' predicts, but with only three ordinal positions a linear trend cannot be distinguished from other monotone shapes.

Within the neurocranium, cranial-base distances (APET-BA, KR-SP, BA-EAM) have positive log ratios while vault distances (BR-LD, LD-AS, OPI-LD) are strongly negative, in line with Thompson's claim that the gradient runs downwards as well as forwards; this was not a pre-registered test.

info.hypothesis: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110, whose rule is stated in one sentence, is computationally universal (Cook 2004). The published proof is a chain of exact emulations: 2-symbol Turing machines -> 2-tag systems (Cocke/Cook, Cook 2004 section 2.1), 2-tag systems -> cyclic tag systems (Cook 2004 section 2.2), cyclic tag systems -> rule-110 glider systems (Cook 2004 sections 3-4). The first two links are fully specified constructions that can be executed and checked exactly; the third relies on the glider inventory of rule 110 (Cook 2004 figure 5), whose velocities must be present in rule-110 evolutions.
info.pass: Pre-registered. (A) One-sentence rule: the sentence 'A cell becomes black if it or its right-hand neighbour is black, unless it and both of its neighbours are black' has at most 30 words and, evaluated as a Boolean predicate on the 8 neighbourhoods, reproduces all 8 entries of Wolfram's rule 110 (binary 01101110). (B) TM -> tag: for 30 random 2-symbol Turing machines with 2-4 states (every transition writes a bit, moves left or right, and changes to any state; no halting), each started from a random tape of 8 bits on each side of the head and run for 40 steps, Cook's 10m-symbol 2-deletion tag system (rules as printed on pp. 5-6 of Cook 2004) started from the encoded configuration reaches the encoded configuration of each successive Turing-machine step within 100000 tag steps; 100% of the 1200 step checks succeed. (C) Tag -> cyclic tag: for the same 30 tag systems plus 30 random 2-tag systems with 2-6 symbols and appendants of length 0-4, each run for 200 tag steps from a random tape (or until the tape empties), Cook's 2k-appendant cyclic tag system (symbol i -> N^(i-1) Y N^(k-i); appendants = encoded appendants then k empty ones) reproduces the encoded tag tape after every 2k cyclic-tag steps; 100% of checks. (D) Glider inventory: the velocities of all naturally occurring rule-110 gliders in Cook 2004 figure 5 (A 2/3, B -1/2, C 0, D 1/5, E and Ebar -4/15, F -1/9, G -1/3; H and the glider gun are stated by Cook not to arise naturally) are all present among the exactly periodic localized structures measured in claim-tests/wolfram-nks/wolfram2002-ch02-09/derived/measured.json (random initial conditions, 20 runs). 'Supports' requires A-D.

measured.unit: fraction of exact emulation checks passed (TM->tag and tag->cyclic tag)

caveats: The third link of Cook's proof (cyclic tag system -> rule 110 via glider collisions, section 4) was not executed; only the existence of the required glider species with the velocities of figure 5 was checked. Universality of rule 110 therefore rests on the published proof plus the two links verified here, which is why confidence is 0.8 rather than higher.

Deviation from the pre-registration: Cook's tag system represents the two halves of the tape in unary, so the tag tape grows like 2^(TM steps) for machines that keep moving one way. Machines were stopped once the tape would exceed 65536 symbols (16 of 30 stopped early, after 9-23 steps), giving 749 checks instead of the planned 1200. All checks performed passed; the cap was applied before seeing any outcome and is a runtime cap, not a selection on results.

The interpretation of the alignment in Cook's text (which symbol of each pair is read) was fixed by transcribing the construction and finding that the encoded configuration for a head reading 0 appears with the leading H_k1 already consumed; the check is still exact equality of the whole tape with the encoding of the independently simulated Turing machine.

'One sentence' is judged on one 21-word English sentence for rule 110; other phrasings exist. Whether 'universal' should require finite initial data with a uniform background (Cook's construction uses a periodic background and periodic right-hand data; Neary and Woods 2006 showed the emulation is polynomially efficient) is a definitional point not tested here.

info.hypothesis: Rule 90 evolved from a single black cell produces a pattern in which the triangle of the first 2^k steps is composed exactly of three copies of the triangle of the first 2^(k-1) steps (one on top, two below, with an all-white inverted triangle between them), for every k up to the depth simulated, and its rows coincide with Pascal's triangle modulo 2 as tabulated independently in OEIS A001317.
info.pass: Pre-registered: (1) for every k = 1..11 the 2^k-step triangle decomposes exactly (zero mismatching cells) into three copies of the 2^(k-1)-step triangle plus an all-white central inverted triangle; and (2) every simulated row t whose value is present in the OEIS A001317 b-file equals A001317(t) when the row's cells at positions of parity t are read as a binary number (zero mismatching rows).

info.hypothesis: There exists a system with a very short rule and a trivial initial condition whose behaviour is complex by standard operational measures: elementary rule 30 (an 8-bit rule) started from a single black cell produces a centre column that is not eventually periodic, is essentially incompressible, and passes standard randomness tests, and a space-time pattern that is far less compressible than those of nested or repetitive rules of the same description length.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Rule 30 from a single black cell on a lattice wide enough that boundaries never influence the measured cells. (a) Compressibility: the lzma-compressed size of the first 2^16 centre-column bits (packed 8 per byte) is at least 0.95 times the compressed size of 2^16 bits from os.urandom packed the same way. (b) Aperiodicity: no period p <= 2^15 holds from any offset t0 <= 2^15 within the first 2^16 centre-column bits (i.e. for every p there is a t >= 2^15 with x[t] != x[t+p]). (c) Randomness tests on the 2^16 centre-column bits: monobit frequency test p > 0.01, Wald-Wolfowitz runs test p > 0.01, chi-square test on the 256 frequencies of non-overlapping 8-bit blocks p > 0.01. (d) Pattern complexity relative to simple rules: the lzma ratio (compressed/raw bytes of the packed bit image) of the 1001-step single-cell pattern (rows of 2001 cells) is at least 5 times larger for rule 30 than for the nested rule 90 and at least 5 times larger than for the repetitive rule 250. 'Supports' requires (a)-(d). In addition the census of all 256 elementary rules by the same pattern ratio is reported (number of rules with ratio > 0.5 of rule 30's ratio), without bearing on the verdict.

measured.unit: lzma size of 2^16 rule-30 centre-column bits divided by lzma size of 2^16 os.urandom bits (threshold 0.95)

caveats: Pre-registered criterion (b) was mis-specified at its upper end: for a period p close to 2^15 only n - p - t0 positions can be compared (one position for p = 32767, none for p = 32768), so those two periods 'pass' the literal test vacuously and analysis.py reports preregistered_verdict = 'refutes'. Every period p <= 32766 is contradicted (the hardest, p = 32764, still has a mismatch at index 32768). The post-hoc rule requires at least 64 comparisons for a period to count; under it no period passes and the verdict is 'supports'. Both outcomes are recorded in measured.extra.

The complexity tests are a specific battery (lzma, periodicity, three NIST-style tests); rule 30's centre column is known to fail no standard test at this length, but a sequence can be complex under these and simple under others. Compression ratio 1.0 relative to os.urandom means lzma found no exploitable regularity, not that none exists.

The claim is a general principle; one witness confirms the existence reading. The census shows that 9 of the 256 elementary rules (30, 45, 73, 75, 86, 89, 101, 135, 149; mostly rule 30's and rule 45's symmetry equivalents) have pattern compressibility within a factor 2 of rule 30, the median rule compressing to 0.08% of raw size.

The os.urandom baseline is non-deterministic; the rule-30 compressed size (8252 bytes for 8192 raw bytes) can be compared directly with the raw size: lzma expands it slightly, as it does for random data.

info.hypothesis: The first 1,000,000 values of the centre column of elementary rule 30 started from a single black cell are not eventually periodic within that range, and the bit sequence passes the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test battery at the standard significance level.
info.pass: Pre-registered. (1) Non-repetition: for every period p in 1..500000, the final matching suffix of x[t] = x[t - p] has length less than p (no tail of the million-step sequence consists of at least two full periods of any period p <= N/2). (2) Randomness: run the following tests, implemented in numpy following NIST SP 800-22 rev. 1a, on the 1,000,000-bit sequence: frequency (monobit), block frequency (M = 128), runs, longest run of ones (M = 10000), binary matrix rank (32 x 32), discrete Fourier transform, non-overlapping template matching (m = 9, template 000000001, N = 8 blocks), overlapping template matching (m = 9, M = 1032), Maurer's universal (L = 7, Q = 1280), linear complexity (M = 500), serial (m = 16; two p-values), approximate entropy (m = 10), cumulative sums (forward and backward), random excursions (8 states) and random excursions variant (18 states), i.e. about 41 p-values. 'supports' if (1) holds, no p-value is below 1e-4, and at most 2 p-values are below 0.01 (the NIST alpha; with 41 p-values the chance of 3 or more below 0.01 under randomness is about 0.8 %). Cross-check (not part of the verdict): the first 100,000 computed bits must agree with the OEIS A051023 b-file; a disagreement means the generator is wrong and the verdict becomes 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.

measured.unit: count of periods p <= 500000 with at least two full periods (>= 64 bits) at the end of the sequence; NIST p-values

caveats: Deviation from the literal pre-registration, decided on synthetic random bits before the rule 30 sequence was examined: the periodicity criterion 'suffix length >= p' flags chance matches at tiny p (a random sequence ending in 0101 has two full periods of p = 2), so a minimum matching-suffix length of 64 bits was added. For rule 30 the longest periodic suffix over all p is 17 bits (at p = 166992), so the verdict is the same under either version of the criterion.

The battery is a faithful numpy re-implementation of 15 NIST SP 800-22 statistics, not the NIST reference C code; it was checked on pseudo-random input, on an LFSR of known linear complexity and on constructed periodic sequences. info.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the primes below 10^8, generated by the sieve of Eratosthenes (the 'simple rule'), look random in most of a pre-declared list of statistical respects when compared with Cramer's random model (independent events with probability 1/ln n), while possibly showing structure in a minority of respects.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Generate all primes below N = 10^8 by sieve; validate against the OEIS A000040 b-file (first 10000 primes must match exactly) and the published value pi(10^8) = 5761455 (OEIS A006880). Simulate the Cramer model on the same range with numpy seed 20261031 and run every statistic on both. Seven respects, each with a threshold for 'random-like': R1 coarse gap distribution: for primes in [N/2, N], maximum over j of |F_emp(30 j) - (1 - exp(-30 j / mean gap))| < 0.03, where F_emp is the empirical CDF of gaps; R2 Pearson correlation of consecutive gaps in [N/2, N]: |rho| < 0.05; R3 equidistribution over the four residue classes coprime to 12: maximum deviation of a class share from 1/4 below 0.005 (the Cramer model is evaluated on its own coprime-to-12 events); R4 counts of primes in consecutive disjoint intervals of length H = round(ln N) in [N/2, N]: total variation distance between the empirical count distribution and Poisson with the same mean < 0.02; R5 discrete Fourier transform of the indicator of primes among the 2^22 odd numbers just below N: ratio of the largest non-zero-frequency power to the mean power < 30 (a Gumbel-scale maximum for random indicators is about ln(2^21) ~ 15); R6 sequential compressibility: lzma size of the sequence of half-gaps (clipped at 255) in [N/2, N] divided by the lzma size of a seeded random permutation of the same sequence >= 0.98; R7 maximum over x <= N of |pi(x) - Li(x)| / sqrt(x / ln x) < 3. A respect is calibrated only if the Cramer simulation satisfies its threshold; miscalibrated respects are dropped and reported. PASS (supports) if the primes are random-like in at least (K - 2) of the K calibrated respects (so 5 of 7 if all are calibrated).

measured.unit: respects (of 7 calibrated) in which the primes below 10^8 are random-like at the pre-registered thresholds

caveats: The verdict follows the pre-registered rule (random-like in at most 3 of 7 calibrated respects). It refutes the claim as operationalised here; it does not show that primes are 'plainly regular' (the pre-registered regularity triggers did not fire: raw lzma ratio 0.55, largest Fourier peak carries 4.2% of the power).

Three of the four failures are small in magnitude and are the known arithmetic corrections to Cramer's model: the coarse gap CDF deviates from exponential by 0.036 (threshold 0.03; Hardy-Littlewood clustering of small gaps), counts in intervals of length 18 have Fano factor 0.76 instead of 1 (total variation from Poisson 0.078; Montgomery-Soundararajan variance deficit), and lzma compresses the gap sequence 3.8% better than its shuffle (threshold 2%; consecutive gaps are correlated, rho = -0.035, the Lemke Oliver-Soundararajan type bias). With thresholds of 0.05 for R1 and 0.95 for R6 the count would be 5 of 7 and the verdict 'supports'; the result is therefore threshold-sensitive and the pre-registered thresholds were strict.

The fourth failure is large: the prime indicator has a Fourier peak at period 3 (and smaller ones at other small primes) 87600 times the mean power, versus 15.5 for the Cramer model. This is the periodic sieve structure the book itself acknowledges as a regularity.

Respects in which the primes are random-like: residue classes coprime to 12 are equidistributed to 6e-5 (Chebyshev bias invisible at this scale), consecutive-gap correlation is below 0.05 in magnitude, and pi(x) - Li(x) stays within 1.3 Cramer-model standard scales (in fact the primes fluctuate less than the random model: -754 at 10^8 versus a model scale of about 2300).

info.hypothesis: When each of the 256 elementary cellular automata (Wolfram numbering, all 256 counted separately) is run from a single black cell on a white background, the pattern of cells that differ from the (possibly alternating) uniform background stays of bounded width for about two-thirds of the rules (~171) and grows without bound for about one-third (~85); and about 14% of all 256 rules (~36) produce growing patterns that are not space-time periodic, i.e. more complicated than repetition.
info.pass: Pre-registered: run all 256 rules for T = 4096 steps on a ring of 2T + 64 cells (so the light cone never wraps). Width w(t) = extent of cells differing from the background value at time t, where the background follows b_{t+1} = f(b_t, b_t, b_t). A rule is 'fixed size' if max_{t in [T/2, T]} w(t) equals max_{t in [T/4, T/2]} w(t), otherwise 'growing'. A growing rule is 'repetitive' if some temporal period P <= 16 and spatial shift |s| <= 16 satisfy grid[t + P, x + s] == grid[t, x] for every t in [T/2, T - P] and every x in [-t + 16, t - 16]; otherwise it is 'more complicated than repetition'. The claim passes if the fixed-size fraction lies in [0.60, 0.73], the growing fraction in [0.27, 0.40] and the more-complicated fraction in [0.10, 0.18], and if the three-way classification of every rule is identical for T = 2048 and T = 4096 (no rule changes class with the cutoff).

measured.unit: fraction of the 256 rules whose pattern stays of fixed size (170/256)

caveats: All pre-registered bands are met: 170/256 = 66.4% fixed size (band 60-73%), 86/256 = 33.6% growing (27-40%), and 37/256 = 14.5% (extent mask) or 39/256 = 15.2% (pre-registered light-cone mask) more complicated than repetition (10-18%); no rule changes class between the T = 2048 and T = 4096 cutoffs under either mask.

Deviation from pre-registration: the light-cone interior mask was found to be inappropriate for patterns growing slower than one cell per step (rules 57 and 99 grow at speed 1/2 and have period-3 interiors), so an extent-based mask was added and is treated as the primary classification; both masks give verdict 'supports' and are reported.

The 37 more-complicated rules comprise the 12 rules in the equivalence classes of rules 30, 45 and 110 plus 25 others; Wolfram states that 24 rules give nested patterns, so the census agrees with his 24 + 12 = 36 up to one rule (rule 73, whose single-cell pattern is non-periodic for every period below 600 but is not usually listed as nested).

Fixed-size versus growing and periodic versus non-periodic are decided at a finite cutoff (4096 steps, periods <= 16, shifts <= 16); the stability of every rule's class between 2048 and 4096 steps supports but does not prove the asymptotic classification. Rule 225's width (50, 97, 98 cells at 1024, 2048, 4096 steps) grows irregularly, consistent with Wolfram's square-root remark, and is correctly scored as growing.

info.hypothesis: When the 256 elementary cellular automata are run from a single black cell and classified by a fixed, calibrated compressibility criterion, about 10 produce random-looking patterns and these fall into three classes under left-right reflection and black-white complementation, while about 24 produce growing, non-periodic but highly compressible (nested) patterns.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Each rule is run for T = 4096 steps from a single black cell on a white background (zero boundary, width 2T+1). Statistics: (i) rho = 8 * lzma_bytes / cells of the central strip (columns -64..63 relative to the seed, rows 1024..4095, one byte per cell, preset 9); (ii) periodic: the strip rows are time-periodic with some period p <= 64 over rows 2048..4095; (iii) growing: the black-cell extent of row 4095 is at least 1.2 times that of row 2047, or the extent of row 4095 exceeds 64 cells while the strip is not periodic. Calibration (performed before the rules are run): random references are i.i.d. fair bits (numpy seed 20260303) in a 128 x 3072 strip; nested references are the same-size central strips of the Sierpinski gasket (Pascal's triangle mod 2), Pascal's triangle mod 3 thresholded to nonzero, and the outer products t_i XOR t_j of the Thue-Morse and of the period-doubling sequences; periodic references are random patterns of period 1..64 in time and 1..16 in space. tau_random = geometric mean of the smallest random-reference rho and the largest nested-reference rho. Classification: 'random-looking' iff rho >= tau_random; 'nested' iff not random-looking, not periodic, and growing; 'regular' otherwise. Symmetry classes: orbits under reflection (swap left and right inputs) and complementation (conjugation by colour swap). Secondary, reported but not decisive: for nested rules, the black-cell count exponent D = log2(N(4096)/N(2048)) with N(t) = black cells in rows 0..t-1, and the width exponent log2(width(4095)/width(2047)); the number of clusters when D is binned to 0.1 and the width exponent to {about 1, about 0.5} is compared with Wolfram's 'three fundamentally different forms'. 'supports' if the random-looking count is in [8, 12] and forms exactly 3 symmetry classes, and the nested count is in [20, 28].

measured.unit: rule counts (of 256)

caveats: Both pre-registered count windows were met: 9 random-looking rules (Wolfram: 10) in exactly 3 symmetry classes, represented by rules 30, 45 and 73 (the classes {30, 86, 135, 149}, {45, 75, 89, 101} and {73, 109}), and 24 nested rules (Wolfram: 24). The one missing random-looking rule is 109, the complement-reflection partner of 73: under this criterion its central strip is time-periodic (period 3), i.e. the randomness of rule 109's single-seed pattern lies outside the central 128 columns or is of a kind the strip statistic does not capture. The random/non-random gap is huge: the nine rules have rho 0.57-1.11, the next rule 0.085.

The nested count of 24 agrees with Wolfram's number but not entirely with his membership: this census includes the rule 110 class (110, 124, 137, 193), which is compressible, growing and non-periodic but which Wolfram would not call nested, and excludes rules such as 60/195 (growth is one-sided, so the seed-centred strip sits on the pattern's periodic edge), 151/183 and 225 (background-flipping rules whose central strip is periodic at this scale). The agreement in count is therefore partly coincidental and the membership differences are reported for transparency.

A bug was fixed between the first and the final run: with array width 2T+1, zero-boundary defects of rules with f(000) = 1 (background flips every step) reached the last 64 rows of the central strip and made 54 regular rules look non-periodic (first-run nested count 78 -> 'refutes'). The array was widened by 128 cells on each side so the strip is causally isolated from the boundary; nothing else in the pre-registered procedure was changed.

The secondary 'three forms' check for nested rules was not reproduced: the black-cell exponent D separates the rule 90/22 form (D = 1.585, 13 rules), the rule 150 form (1.694) and the rule 110/182 group (about 2.0), but is meaningless for background-flipping rules (D 0.73-0.99), so 7 bins were found. Wolfram's forms are visual and his third form (rule 225, width ~ sqrt(t)) is not in this nested list at all.

info.hypothesis: Every one of the 65,536 basic two-colour mobile automata (rule maps the colours of the active cell and its two neighbours to a new colour for the active cell and a move left or right), started from all-white cells, produces a step sequence that is eventually periodic or otherwise highly compressible (nested); no basic rule produces a step sequence whose compressibility is in the range of random or complex sequences. In the extended family in which the rule also rewrites both neighbours (2^32 rules), such poorly compressible behaviour exists but is rare.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Encoding: the behaviour of a mobile automaton is summarised by its step sequence s_t in {0,1,2,3} = 2 * (new colour of the active cell) + (1 if the active cell moves right else 0); for the extended family s_t additionally records the two neighbour colours written (16 symbols), and the sequence of active-cell positions is determined by it. Calibration (performed before the mobile automata are run, on reference sequences only): rho(L) = 8 * lzma_size(sequence of L symbols, one byte each, preset 9) / (L * log2(alphabet size)). References over a 4-symbol alphabet: periodic sequences with periods 1..500 (numpy seed 20260306), nested sequences (Thue-Morse, period-doubling, Fibonacci word, paper-folding, ruler sequence mod 4), and random sequences (numpy random symbols; rule 30 centre bits paired). The complexity threshold tau is the geometric mean of the largest rho(8000) over the periodic and nested references and the smallest rho(8000) over the random references. Stage 1: all 65,536 basic rules, 2000 steps (vectorised); a rule is 'periodic' if its last 1000 symbols have a period p <= 500. Stage 2: every non-periodic rule is run for 16000 steps and rho is computed on symbols 8000..16000 (tail); a rule is 'complex' if rho > tau. Stage 3: any rule flagged complex is re-run for 64000 steps and rho on symbols 32000..64000 is required to still exceed tau (guards against long transients). Extended family: 100,000 rules sampled uniformly (numpy seed 20260306), same three stages with the 16-symbol alphabet and a 16-symbol calibration run analogously. 'supports' if no basic rule is complex after stage 3 and the fraction of complex extended rules is <= 1 %. Secondary check reported but not decisive: the number of basic rules with non-periodic step sequences, which Wolfram gives as 218 (p. 72).

measured.unit: rule counts; fraction of 100,000 sampled extended rules with tail rho above tau

caveats: The universal clause was tested exhaustively: 65,318 basic rules are eventually periodic within 2000 steps (period <= 500) and the remaining 218 (exactly the number Wolfram reports on p. 72 for rules whose active cell sweeps back and forth) have tail step sequences at least as compressible as the Thue-Morse reference (max rho 0.122 vs tau 0.454), i.e. nested, not complex. No basic rule approached the complexity threshold.

The extended-family clause was only partly tested: in 100,000 sampled neighbour-updating rules, 882 (0.9 %) were not periodic within 2000 steps, consistent with Wolfram's 'more than 99 % repetitive', and all of them compressed like nested sequences (max rho 0.079); no complex rule was found, which supports 'rare' (upper bound about 3 in 100,000 at 95 %) but means the existence of complex extended rules, which Wolfram illustrates on pp. 74-75, was not independently confirmed here.

Compressibility of the step sequence is a proxy: a rule with an extremely long transient (> 2000 steps before periodicity, or > 8000 before a nested regime) would be handled by the later stages only if it was non-periodic at 2000 steps; a rule periodic within 2000 steps but complex later would be missed. The 64000-step confirmation stage was never needed.

The threshold tau was fixed by calibration on classical sequences before any mobile automaton was run; random references give rho > 1 because of lzma's fixed overhead at 8000 symbols, which only widens the margin.

info.hypothesis: Every parallel substitution system in which each element is replaced according to its own colour alone (a context-free morphism iterated from a single element) produces a nested pattern: operationally, the sequence it generates has sub-exponential subword complexity (at most quadratic, as Pansiot's theorem gives for pure morphic words), never the near-maximal complexity of a random or 'complex' sequence; whereas substitution systems whose replacement depends on a neighbouring element can produce sequences of near-maximal subword complexity.

For every run that reaches 2^15 symbols ('growing'), compute the subword complexity p(n) (number of distinct length-n factors) of the first min(len, 2^17) symbols for n = 1..20. The claim passes if every growing neighbour-independent run has p(20) <= 10^4 and p(20)/p(10) <= 8 (a quadratic law gives 4, an exponential law about 2^10), and if the Thue-Morse system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 10} reproduces OEIS A010060 and the Fibonacci system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 0} reproduces OEIS A003849 term for term over the available b-file terms. Discriminating power: the neighbour-dependent control family (2 colours, replacement of each element determined by the pair (element, right neighbour), replacement strings of length 1 or 2, 1296 systems, right-most element paired with colour 0) must contain at least one system whose growing run has p(20) > 2 x 10^4 and p(20)/p(10) > 8; otherwise the test cannot separate the two families and the verdict is at most 'inconclusive'.

measured.unit: maximum subword complexity p(20) over all 5109 growing neighbour-independent runs (random reference 32319)

caveats: Every claim-side criterion passed exactly as pre-registered: 0 of 5109 growing neighbour-independent runs exceed p(20) <= 10^4 or p(20)/p(10) <= 8 (maxima 231 and 3.56, against 32319 and 31.6 for a random string; the ratio never exceeds the quadratic value 4, as Pansiot's theorem predicts for morphic words), and the Thue-Morse and Fibonacci outputs match OEIS A010060 (16384 terms) and A003849 (10946 terms) without error.

info.hypothesis: Among two-block cyclic tag systems started from a single black element, at least one produces a sequence whose length grows at a steady linear rate while the fluctuations about that growth behave like a random walk (unbounded, diffusive scaling) and the leading-element sequence that drives them is incompressible to a substantial degree.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 225 cyclic tag systems with two blocks, each block a binary string of length 0-3 (15 choices per block), initial sequence {1}, Wolfram's update (remove first element; if it was 1 append the current block; blocks alternate every step). Stage 1: run each system 100,000 steps; a system is 'growing' if the sequence never empties and its final length is >= 1000. Stage 2: run each growing system 1,000,000 steps and compute (i) linear fit of length L(t) vs t: R^2 >= 0.999 and local growth rates over 10 equal windows all within 25% of the global slope ('steady growth'); (ii) Hurst exponent H of the detrended residual r(t) = L(t) - (a + b t), estimated as half the log-log slope of Var[r(t+tau) - r(t)] over tau = 2^0..2^13, in [0.35, 0.65] ('random-walk-like fluctuations'); (iii) lzma (preset 9 | EXTREME) compressed size of the packed leading-element bit sequence >= 0.25 bits per symbol ('incompressible driver'). The claim PASSES if at least one system satisfies (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously. Secondary, reported but not decisive: whether the book's own examples (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} and (e) {{1,1,1},{0}} pass.

measured.unit: systems passing all three pre-registered criteria

caveats: By the letter of the pre-registration the composite test fails: 0 of 225 systems pass all three criteria, because no growing system compresses to more than 0.115 bits per symbol (criterion iii). The verdict is recorded as 'mixed' rather than 'refutes' because the two criteria that address what Wolfram actually plotted (steady growth, random-walk-like fluctuations) are met by 12 systems including the book's example (e) (H = 0.469, residual range ~ +-400 after 10^6 steps, matching the book's plot), while criterion (iii) measures something the claim does not assert.

Criterion (iii) was miscalibrated: a cyclic tag tape is a self-copying object (each appended block is a fixed image of an earlier tape symbol), so an LZ-type compressor exploits long repeated segments even when the growth fluctuations are diffusive; a Markov sequence with the same local statistics compresses to 0.73 bits/symbol, the real tapes to 0.06-0.12. That the drivers are this compressible is nevertheless a genuine respect in which these sequences are not random, which Wolfram's 'in many respects' leaves room for.

The book's example (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} has H = 0.23 (sub-diffusive, residual range ~ +-50 after 10^6 steps, consistent with the book's own plot) and so fails the random-walk criterion; of the two named examples only (e) has random-walk-like fluctuations by this measure.
The Hurst estimate for all-ones tapes (zero fluctuation) is set to 0; the two such rules were excluded from the Hurst count.

info.hypothesis: Within the family of the simplest arithmetic iterations, repeated multiplication by a fixed small integer m viewed as a base-b digit array (Wolfram's opening example, pp. 116-120), some members produce digit arrays whose interior is incompressible with digit frequencies indistinguishable from uniform, while the trivial members (m a power of b) are detected as highly compressible.

For each pair build the digit array of rows m^t written in base b; take the interior window of each row consisting of digit positions between 25% and 75% of that row's length (least significant digit = position 0), concatenate all interior digits in row order into one byte string (one digit per byte). Measure (i) bits per digit = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size / number of digits; (ii) maximum absolute deviation of any digit-value frequency from 1/b. A pair is 'complex' if (i) >= 0.8 * log2(b) and (ii) <= 0.02; a pair is 'simple' if (i) < 0.1 * log2(b). The claim PASSES if at least one pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' AND every pair with m a power of b (m = b^j, j >= 1, e.g. (2,2), (4,2), (8,2), (9,3), (3,3), ...) is 'simple' (validity check that the measure separates trivially regular digit arrays). Reported, not decisive: how many of the 64 pairs are complex, and whether the pairs with m and b sharing all prime factors (e.g. (6,2), (4,8), (2,4)) behave differently.

measured.unit: pairs (m,b) with m not a power of b whose interior digit array is 'complex' by the pre-registered criteria

caveats: The 10 non-complex non-trivial pairs split into two explicable groups: (2,4), (2,8), (4,8), (8,4), (3,9) where m and b are powers of a common integer (the pre-registered 'm is a power of b' control missed this symmetric case; they compress to < 0.001 of the bound, i.e. are trivially regular), and the five m = 6 pairs in bases 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 where the trailing zeros of 6^t = 2^t 3^t occupy 1/log_b(6) of each row and intrude into the fixed 25%-75% window, lowering compression ratios to 0.30-0.83 and biasing digit frequencies.

Incompressibility by lzma over about 3.6 million interior digits (for 3^t in base 2: 1.086 bits/digit, digit frequencies within 0.0004 of 1/2) is evidence against periodic or nested structure at these scales, not a proof of normality; the digits of 3^t in base 2 are not proven to be normal.
The test covers the book's opening family (powers in positional notation) only; the claim's other illustrations in Chapter 4 (e.g. the 3n/2 system, iterated maps) were not tested.

info.hypothesis: In any integer base, every rational p/q has an eventually periodic digit expansion with period at most q - 1 (and preperiod + period at most q), every eventually periodic digit sequence is the expansion of a rational number, and the published digit expansions of irrational constants show no eventual periodicity.

measured.unit: rational expansions violating period <= q-1 or preperiod + period <= q (out of 194,550)

caveats: Both directions are classical theorems; the computation confirms the forward direction exhaustively for all denominators up to 20,000 in three bases (the bound period = q - 1 is attained, e.g. for full-reptend primes), agrees with OEIS A007732 on all 10,000 tabulated decimal periods, and confirms the converse constructively on 20,000 random eventually periodic patterns.

A finite digit string cannot establish that a number is not eventually periodic; part (3) only checks that 10,000 published digits of sqrt(2), e and pi show no two agreeing repeats for any period up to N/3 (the maximal agreement found was 1.33 periods, consistent with chance), which is a consistency check, not a proof of the 'only rationals' clause.

Terminating expansions are counted as eventually periodic with repeating 0 (period 1), following OEIS A007732; under the alternative convention (repeating b-1) they are still eventually periodic, so the verdict does not depend on this choice.

For each a: (1) take the first N = 20000 positive zeros of f(x) = sin x + sin(a x), each verified numerically (|f(x)| <= 1e-8), labelled A if it is a zero of sin((1+a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(1+a)) and B if it is a zero of cos((1-a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(a-1)); (2) build the substitution word s_1 = A^{c_1} B, s_n = s_{n-1}^{c_n} s_{n-2} (equivalently the composition tau_{c_1} ... tau_{c_n}(A)) to length >= 200000 from the continued fraction theta = [0; c_1, c_2, ...]. measured.unit: a-values (of 31) whose crossing word and substitution word have identical factor sets for all n <= 24

caveats: The identification of 'the generalized substitution system' with the standard Sturmian construction (rule tau_c: A -> A^c B, B -> A at the step whose partial quotient is c) is the tester's; the book does not print the rule. The directive sequence is exactly the partial quotients of (a-1)/(a+1), as the book states, because the word's own slope theta/(1+theta) has continued fraction [0; c_1+1, c_2, c_3, ...].

Equality of factor languages (and complexity n+1) is the appropriate finite test because the substitution system fixes the slope but not the intercept of the mechanical word; the crossing word's intercept is fixed by the offset pi/(a-1) of the B family.
The result is for a > 1; by rescaling x the a < 1 case is the same with the roles of the families exchanged. Rational a (periodic curves) are outside the irrational scope tested and were not sampled.

caveats: Parts (1)-(3) passed exactly as pre-registered: 0 of 4,020,999 itinerary bits differ from the seed digits; all 999 odd denominators q <= 2000 give purely periodic itineraries whose period equals the multiplicative order of 2 mod q (max 1996 = q - 3 for q = 1999); every seed class has identical lzma ratio for seed and itinerary (the itinerary is literally the digit string); periodic seeds compress to 0.011-0.019 and Thue-Morse to 0.017 against a random reference of 0.168-0.171, while a random-bit seed gives 0.170.

The A004539 b-file has only 1000 terms, so the sqrt(2) identity check used 999 instead of the planned 10000 digits; the compressibility comparison for sqrt(2) used 10000 digits computed with math.isqrt, which agree with all 999 published digits.

info.hypothesis: Directed networks in which every node is of one type and has exactly two outgoing connections can realize, through the connection pattern alone, structures equivalent to d-dimensional arrays for every d, as well as trees and nested (fractal) structures. 'Equivalent to a d-dimensional array' is taken in Wolfram's two senses: (i) grouping nodes into identical blocks yields exactly the d-dimensional grid (each block connected to its 2d neighbouring blocks), and (ii) the number of nodes reachable within r connection steps grows like r^d (the network dimension criterion of NKS chapter 9).
info.pass: Pre-registered. (1) Arrays: for d = 1..6 construct the network by one uniform rule: each lattice point x of Z^d is a block of d nodes (x, i), i = 0..d-1, and node (x, i) has exactly two outgoing connections, to (x + e_i, (i+1) mod d) and (x - e_i, (i+1) mod d). Verify (a) every node has out-degree exactly 2 and the rule is identical for every node; (b) exact structural equivalence: on the torus (Z_L)^d with L = 5, contracting each block to a point gives a multigraph whose edge set equals the d-dimensional grid's edge set {x <-> x +- e_i} with every block connected to exactly 2d distinct neighbouring blocks (exact set comparison); (c) dimension criterion: breadth-first search along connections from one node of the infinite network, counting N(r) = nodes within r steps; the growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 20 d must lie within 0.5 of d for d = 1, 2, 3, 4 (so that it rounds to d), and is reported (not scored) for d = 5, 6. (2) Trees: the infinite binary tree (node k connects to 2k+1 and 2k+2) has N(r) = 2^(r+1) - 1 for r <= 15 (exact). (3) Nested: the level-7 Sierpinski gasket graph (3 corner nodes of degree 2, all others of degree 4) is given an Eulerian orientation along an Euler circuit plus a directed 3-cycle through the corners, which must give every node out-degree exactly 2; its undirected growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 64 from a corner must lie within 0.3 of log2(3) = 1.585, the gasket's dimension. 'Supports' if (1a), (1b), (1c), (2) and (3) all hold.

measured.unit: growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) of the out-degree-2 block network for d = 1..6 (pre-registered window: within 0.5 of d for d <= 4)

caveats: Deviation from the pre-registration: for d = 5 and 6 (reported, not scored) the BFS radius was reduced from 20d to 8d because the 20d search for d = 6 visited 13 million nodes (68 s and several GB in a first run; it gave exponent 5.756 and the d = 5 run at radius 50 gave 4.815). At radius 8d the exponents are 4.74 and 5.65, still rounding to d and above the plain lattice ball's finite-radius exponents (4.26 and 4.96), so the conclusion is unchanged.

The claim is existential and is settled by the exact quotient check for d <= 6 together with the uniform rule, which is defined for every d (the same code runs for any d; only the search radius limits the computation). The growth-exponent check is Wolfram's operational notion of dimension and confirms the effective geometry without using the block structure; its finite-radius bias is quantified by the lattice reference.

One construction per structure type is tested (block arrays; binary tree; Eulerian-oriented Sierpinski gasket). The gasket orientation plus corner 3-cycle is one way to get out-degree exactly 2 for every node; the undirected growth exponent 1.612 and directed 1.594 are both within 0.03 of log2(3), the gasket's Hausdorff dimension.

Whether the resulting networks are 'equivalent' to arrays in any stronger sense (e.g. as substrates for network cellular automata, NKS p. 1031) was not tested; the block-quotient isomorphism and dimension are the two senses stated in the pre-registration.

info.hypothesis: For every one-dimensional local constraint system (a set of allowed length-w colour words over k colours) that admits any bi-infinite satisfying arrangement, there is a purely periodic satisfying arrangement, and its period can be taken at most V = k^(w-1).
info.pass: Pre-registered: across all enumerated or sampled constraint systems, every system that admits a valid word of length 4V + w (the operational test of satisfiability, independent of any cycle argument) also admits a periodic arrangement u^infinity with |u| <= V whose every cyclic window of length w is allowed; and every system with no such long valid word has no periodic arrangement either. Zero violations in both directions.

measured.unit: fraction of satisfiable constraint systems that have a periodic solution with period <= k^(w-1)

caveats: The claim is a theorem (a non-empty one-dimensional shift of finite type contains a periodic point, from a cycle in its de Bruijn graph); the computation confirms it exhaustively for all two-colour constraints with windows up to 4 and all four-colour constraints with window 2, and by sampling for windows 5 (two colours) and 3 (three colours). The maximal minimal period found (8 for k = 2, w = 4; exactly the two de Bruijn-cycle constraint sets) matches the bound V = k^(w-1).

Satisfiability was operationalised by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement, but the equivalence itself relies on finiteness of the vertex set, so the two indicators are not logically independent even though they are computed by different algorithms.
Wolfram's 'simple' is read as 'periodic'; the observed minimal periods are small (at most V), but 'simple' is not otherwise quantified.

info.hypothesis: The set of 56 allowed 3x3 templates shown on NKS p. 221 is satisfied by a shifted rule-30 space-time pattern (with the boundary structures shown in the figure), uses all 56 templates, encodes rule 30 in its interior templates, and admits no spatially periodic pattern containing the first template, consistent with the pattern being forced.
info.pass: Pre-registered. (T) Templates: the 56 templates are read automatically from the figure image fig-c.png of p. 221 (14 x 4 grid, 3 x 3 cells each, dark fraction of a 9 x 9 pixel patch at each cell centre > 0.5 = black); the extraction must yield 56 distinct templates listed in strictly decreasing order of their 9-bit binary value (Wolfram's usual ordering), which is the check that the transcription is sound. (A) Realisability and exhaustiveness: the candidate pattern is defined as follows, with rows indexed downward and columns rightward. Rows 0 and 1 are black for all columns <= C+1 and white for columns > C+1; columns C and C+1 are black in every row >= 0; every other cell with row < 2 or column > C+1 is white, and all cells above row 0 are white; interior cells (row t >= 2, column x <= C-1) are a(t, x) = rule30(a(t-1, x), a(t-1, x+1), a(t-1, x+2)), i.e. rule 30 shifted one cell to the left per step, using the black columns C, C+1 as fixed neighbours. On a window of 300 rows and 300 columns to the left of and below the corner (plus a white margin of 3 cells above and to the right), every 3 x 3 block must be one of the 56 templates, and every one of the 56 templates must occur. (R) Rule identification: a template is 'interior' if neither of its 3-cell rows is a boundary row (rows 0-1 or the two black columns); the test reports how many templates satisfy the relation middle-left = rule30(top row) and bottom-left = rule30(middle row), and lists the remaining templates. (U) No periodic alternative: for every horizontal period w = 1..9, build the transfer graph whose nodes are pairs of consecutive rows (r0, r1) on a cylinder of circumference w and whose edges (r0, r1) -> (r1, r2) exist when all w cyclic 3 x 3 blocks of (r0, r1, r2) are allowed; a valid pattern periodic horizontally with period w exists iff this graph has a cycle, and such a pattern contains template 1 iff some edge inside a non-trivial strongly connected component (or a self-loop) has template 1 among its w blocks. The claim PASSES if (T) holds, (A) holds in both directions, and (U) finds no cycle edge containing template 1 for any w <= 9. (R) is reported, not decisive.

measured.unit: number of cycle edges (doubly periodic valid patterns, periods 1-9) containing template 1; 0 = no periodic competitor

caveats: Pre-registered decision: all three decisive parts hold. (T) The automatic transcription yields 56 distinct templates in strictly decreasing binary order with no ambiguous cells. (A) The candidate pattern (two-row black band, two-column black wall below its right end, interior a(t,x) = rule30(a(t-1,x), a(t-1,x+1), a(t-1,x+2)) growing leftwards from the wall) contains exactly the 56 templates on a 300 x 300 window: no disallowed block and no unused template, so the published set is precisely the block set of this shifted rule-30 pattern. (U) No horizontally periodic valid pattern of period 1-9 (and, supplementary, 10-11) contains template 1.

(R) 46 of the 56 templates satisfy the shifted rule-30 relation in both row pairs; the 10 others (templates 1, 2, 3, 10, 45, 46, 47, 51, 52, 53) are the band, wall and corner templates, consistent with the construction being 'derived from rule 30' plus boundary structures.

Uniqueness on the infinite plane is not finitely verifiable; what was shown is that no spatially periodic alternative with period <= 11 exists. Periodic patterns without template 1 do exist for every period tested (e.g. the all-white plane; 47 distinct templates appear on cycles), which is why the caption requires template 1 to appear at least once. The pattern is unique only up to translation, and its interior is 'largely random' in the sense that rule 30 from this boundary is (not separately tested here).

The candidate pattern was inferred from the templates by constraint propagation over rows 2-4 before pre-registration (disclosed); the exact figure layout (band thickness, wall) was read from the inset of fig-a and confirmed by (A). Template extraction depends on fixed pixel coordinates for this image version (sha256 recorded).

info.hypothesis: For every finite deterministic discrete system we enumerate, every orbit (from every possible state) becomes eventually periodic, and its eventual period is at most N, the total number of possible states of the system (and the transient plus period is also at most N).
info.pass: Pre-registered: across all enumerated systems and all initial states, 100% of orbits satisfy period <= N and transient + period <= N (zero violations), where N is the exact number of distinct global states of the system.

measured.unit: fraction of orbits with eventual period <= N and transient + period <= N

caveats: The claim is a theorem (pigeonhole principle on a finite state set), so a finite enumeration can only fail to refute it; the enumeration here covers three concrete families exhaustively up to the stated sizes and finds the bound tight (period = N in degenerate 1-cell systems, period = N - 1 for x -> 3x mod 199).
Wolfram's bound is on the eventual period; the test also checks the slightly stronger transient + period <= N, which is what the pigeonhole argument actually gives, and it held in every orbit.
Systems whose next state depends on more than the current state (external input, randomness, unbounded memory) are outside the claim's scope and were not tested.
