info.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the centre column of rule 30 started from a single black cell (an initial condition with no randomness) passes a standard battery of statistical randomness tests as well as the centre column of rule 30 started from a random initial condition and as well as a pseudo-random reference stream, whereas a nested deterministic sequence (Thue-Morse) fails the same battery.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Sequences of N = 2^20 bits: (S1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (S2) rule 30 centre column from a random initial row (numpy seed 20261031, width 2N+1, so that the column is exactly the random-initial-condition case); (S3) numpy PCG64 bits, seed 20261031; (S4) the Thue-Morse sequence. Battery of 10 tests, each giving a p-value with pass meaning p >= 0.01: monobit frequency; block frequency (M = 128); runs; longest run of ones (M = 10000, K = 6); serial (m = 16, minimum of the two p-values); approximate entropy (m = 10); cumulative sums (minimum of forward and backward); discrete Fourier transform spectral test; autocorrelation (lags 1..64, Bonferroni-corrected normal p-value of the largest |r|); and a 16-bit non-overlapping block chi-square uniformity test. Also record the lzma compression ratio of the packed bits. PASS (supports) if S1 passes at least 9 of 10 tests and has lzma ratio >= 0.99, S2 and S3 each pass at least 9 of 10, S4 fails at least 4 tests, and the first terms of S1 agree exactly with the OEIS A051023 b-file over the whole length of the b-file.

measured.unit: randomness tests passed (p >= 0.01) by the rule 30 single-cell centre column, out of 10

caveats: Passing a finite statistical battery is practical randomness, the sense the book uses; it does not establish algorithmic randomness or exclude a regularity invisible to these tests (the sequence is of course computable).

The 16-bit block chi-square test has expected count 1 per cell, so its chi-square p-value is approximate (the true null variance of the statistic is about 1.5 times the chi-square value); the same approximation is applied to all four sequences and S1 passed it with p = 0.26.

S1's smallest p-value is 0.037 (approximate entropy, m = 10); with ten tests at alpha = 0.01 a single marginal value is expected. S2 (random initial row) had its smallest p-value at 0.018 (cumulative sums). Both rule 30 columns are statistically indistinguishable from the PCG64 stream in this battery, while Thue-Morse fails 7 of 10 tests and compresses to 0.4% of its size.
Only rule 30 was tested. Rule 22, also named in the claim's context, gives a nested pattern from a single black cell, and the book's example on p. 261 is rule 30.

info.hypothesis: Rule 90 is additive (linear over GF(2)): its local rule is l XOR r, so every evolution is the XOR superposition of shifted copies of the single-cell nested (Pascal mod 2) pattern. Consequently a biased random initial condition leaves a permanent trace: at every time t = 2^k each cell is the XOR of exactly two initial cells, so the density returns to 2p(1-p) forever for initial density p, and the single-cell pattern itself is nested, not random. Rule 22 (non-additive, class 3) instead forgets the initial density: from any initial density the density converges to one common value.
info.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Additivity: the rule-90 local map phi satisfies phi(a XOR b) = phi(a) XOR phi(b) for all 64 pairs of 3-cell neighbourhoods, and the rule-22 map does not; (B) superposition: for 50 random initial conditions on a cyclic lattice of width 513 run for 256 steps, the rule-90 evolution equals the cellwise XOR of the shifted single-cell evolutions exactly (100% of 50*256 rows); (C) single-cell pattern: for rule 90 from one black cell the row at t = 2^k (k = 0..10) has exactly 2 black cells and the row at t = 2^k - 1 has 2^k black cells (nested, Pascal mod 2); (D) persistence in rule 90: with initial densities p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a measured window of 100000 cells (array padded by 1024 cells on each side so boundaries never reach the window), the measured density at t = 2^k for k = 0..10 is within 0.01 of 2p(1-p) in all 33 cases, and at t = 1024 the three densities differ from the p = 0.5 density by more than 0.1; (E) loss of memory in rule 22: with p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5} on the same windows, the time-averaged densities over t = 512..1024 differ from one another by less than 0.01 (max minus min). 'Supports' requires A-E.

measured.unit: largest |density(t=2^k) - 2p(1-p)| over p in {0.05,0.1,0.2}, k = 0..10 for rule 90 (threshold 0.01)

caveats: Part C initially failed for a trivial reason unrelated to the claim: the single-cell array was two cells too narrow and the fixed-zero boundary cells coincided with the two black cells at t = 1024. The array was widened by one cell on each side (commit history shows the change); no threshold or criterion was changed.

The densities of 100000 cells in one row are correlated (in rule 90 at t = 2^k, cells 2^(k+1) apart share an initial cell), so the binomial standard error (0.0012 for p = 0.1) understates the sampling error; the pre-registered 0.01 tolerance was chosen to absorb this and the largest deviation observed was 0.0031.

Rule 22's late-time density of about 0.351 from all four initial densities agrees with the known asymptotic density of rule 22 from random initial conditions; convergence is complete by t ~ 128 even for p = 0.05.

'Cannot generate randomness intrinsically' is interpreted structurally (every pattern is a superposition of the nested single-cell pattern); whether XOR-superposed nested patterns count as 'random' under some statistical test is not what is being tested. Rule 90 from a p = 0.5 random row does look random and has density 0.5 at all times, consistent with 'randomness from the initial conditions'.

info.hypothesis: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, every rule that is additive (linear over GF(2)) can emulate itself with blocks of cells and yields an exactly self-similar (nested) pattern from a single black cell; after removing trivial rules and identifying rules related by reflection or by the sublattice (shear) relation between rules 60 and 90, exactly two additive classes remain, represented by rules 90 and 150; self-emulation among the remaining 248 rules is uncommon, but rule 184 has it with blocks of three cells.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Definitions: a rule f is additive iff f(x XOR y) = f(x) XOR f(y) for all pairs of 3-cell neighbourhoods x, y (which forces f(000) = 0). Rule f self-emulates with block size b >= 2 and t >= 1 steps iff there are two distinct b-cell blocks B0, B1 such that for every arrangement of 2k+1 blocks (k = ceil(t/b)) drawn from {B0, B1}, running f for t steps leaves the centre block equal to B_{f(c-1, c0, c1)}, where c-1, c0, c1 are the bits represented by the three central blocks; this is the block-emulation notion of NKS pp. 269-271 and note p. 1118, which allows t != b. The search covers b in {2, 3, 4}, t in {1, 2, 3, 4} and all block pairs. Trivial rules: 0, 204 (identity), 170 and 240 (shifts). Equivalences for 'fundamentally different': reflection (rule 60 <-> 102) and the sublattice relation p90[t, 2j - t] = p60[t, j], verified computationally on the first 256 steps from a single black cell. Nested: the single-cell pattern p satisfies p[2t, 2i] = p[t, i] for all 0 <= t < 256 and |i| <= t. Clause A passes if every additive rule self-emulates with b = t = 2 and every non-trivial additive rule is nested in this sense. Clause B passes if the non-trivial additive rules fall into exactly two equivalence classes, one containing 90 and one containing 150. Clause C passes if rule 184 self-emulates with b = 3 for some t <= 4 and the fraction of the 248 non-additive rules with at least one self-emulation in the searched range is <= 0.25. 'supports' if A, B and C all pass.

measured.unit: rule numbers; fraction of the 248 non-additive rules with at least one block self-emulation (b <= 4, t <= 4)

caveats: All three pre-registered clauses passed: exactly 8 additive rules exist, each self-emulates with 2-cell blocks and 2 steps (the Frobenius identity f^2 = f at stride 2 over GF(2)) and the four non-trivial ones are exactly self-similar at scale 2; after identifying 60/102 with 90 through the verified sublattice relation the additive rules fall into the two classes {60, 90, 102} and {150}; rule 184 self-emulates with the 3-cell blocks 010/101 and 3 steps, as Wolfram says, and only 15 of the 248 non-additive rules (6 %) have any block self-emulation in the searched range.

'Fundamentally different' required an interpretive choice: rule 60 (and its mirror 102) is additive and nested but is not related to 90 by reflection or colour complement; it is the rule 90 pattern restricted to the sublattice i + t even. Without that identification the claim's 'precisely rules 90 and 150' would be 'rules 60, 90 and 150'. The test records this explicitly.

The 15 non-additive self-emulating rules are the affine rules 15, 51, 85, 153, 165, 195 (complements/XOR with 1), the AND/OR-type class-1 rules 128, 136, 192, 238, 252, 254, 255, the shift-like rule 226 and rule 184. Larger blocks or more steps (b > 4, t > 4) might reveal further self-emulating rules; 'rather rare' is confirmed only within the searched range.

The claim's sub-clause that additivity implies self-emulation in general (for any number of colours and neighbours) was tested only for the elementary rules; the argument via the Frobenius endomorphism is standard but was not checked beyond them.

info.hypothesis: Widely deployed linear congruential generators x_{n+1} = (a x_n + c) mod m that were chosen to have maximal period nevertheless produce consecutive d-tuples lying on a small number of parallel hyperplanes (Marsaglia 1968: at most (d! m)^(1/d)), a gross deviation from uniform randomness that is visible at sample sizes far below the period and that standard empirical tests detect.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Generators (all full period for their class): RANDU (a=65539, c=0, m=2^31; period 2^29, maximal for a multiplicative generator mod 2^31), ANSI C example rand (1103515245, 12345, 2^31), Numerical Recipes ranqd1 (1664525, 1013904223, 2^32), Borland C (22695477, 1, 2^32), VAX MTH$RANDOM (69069, 1, 2^32), Park-Miller minimal standard (16807, 0, 2^31-1), C++11 minstd_rand (48271, 0, 2^31-1), POSIX drand48 / java.util.Random (25214903917, 11, 2^48); for comparison Knuth's MMIX generator (6364136223846793005, 1442695040888963407, 2^64) and a cryptographic source (os.urandom). (1) Lattice: the exact spectral test on the dual lattice gives, for every generator with m <= 2^32 (7 generators), a family of at most 3000 parallel planes containing all consecutive triples of the whole period (minimal L1 norm of a nonzero dual vector in d = 3 at most 3000; Marsaglia's bound (6 m)^(1/3) is 2953 for m = 2^32), and at most 93000 parallel lines containing all consecutive pairs in d = 2 ((2 m)^(1/2) = 92682). (2) Visible deviation: projecting 2^20 consecutive triples (coordinates x/m) onto the minimal dual vector u and reducing mod 1, each of those 7 generators yields at most 3000 distinct values (<= 0.3% of 2^20) while os.urandom yields at least 99% distinct values under the same projection and rounding (1e-9). (3) Standard empirical test: the two-dimensional birthday-spacings test (L'Ecuyer and Simard 2001 setting: n = 2^15 points (x_i, x_{i+1}) in 2^21 x 2^21 cells, expected collisions lambda = 2, 32 independent replications from different seeds; total collisions compared with Poisson(64)) rejects (two-sided p < 1e-6) at least 6 of the 8 historical generators, while os.urandom and MMIX are not rejected (p > 1e-3). 'Supports' requires (1), (2) and (3).

measured.unit: largest number of parallel planes containing all consecutive triples, over the 7 historical generators with m <= 2^32 (threshold 3000; each has 2^29 to 2^32 triples)

caveats: Borland's generator is listed with modulus 2^31 by Wikipedia and 2^32 by other sources; 2^32 was used as pre-registered (both are full period and share the low 31 bits).

The claim says generators 'one after another' deviated substantially; the set tested is the eight most widely deployed historical generators, not a random sample. The one that passed the birthday-spacings test at this sample size (drand48, period 2^48) still shows its lattice: its 2^20 triples project onto only 83834 distinct values (8%) of a possible 2^20, versus 99.996% for os.urandom; L'Ecuyer and Simard's rule predicts birthday-spacings failure for it at n of order 16 * 2^16 points, not tested here.

Knuth's 64-bit MMIX generator (post-dating most of the historical generators) passes both empirical tests at these sample sizes, as pre-registered for the contrast; it still has a lattice (about 2.9 million planes in 3 dimensions). The claim as stated concerns deployed generators up to 2002.
Spectral values agree with published ones where known (RANDU: 15 planes, S_3 = 0.008; Park-Miller: S_2 = 0.34 as in Knuth TAOCP 3.3.4), which checks the lattice code.

Statistics: Spearman rank correlation rho for each (rule measure, behaviour measure) pair within each family (8 pairs). measured.unit: Spearman rho between rule complexity and lzma size of the space-time diagram; fraction of 1024 Hamming-1 ECA pairs whose random-IC lzma sizes differ by more than half the family range

caveats: The pre-registered decision rule is degenerate and the verdict is therefore recorded as inconclusive rather than as the 'refutes' it literally produces: the rule required a rule 'at the minimum value of each rule measure' to reach the top behavioural quartile, but the minimum of every measure is attained only by constant rules (rule 0; the three constant totalistic codes; for the gate count, the eight 0-gate projections/negations), which cannot produce complex behaviour under any definition. The condition therefore tests nothing about the claim. This is an error in the pre-registration, discovered only after the run.

Post hoc (not pre-registered): at the lowest non-constant complexity levels there are rules in the top behavioural quartile, as the claim asserts: with 2 ANF monomials rules 60, 90 and 102 (nested), with 1 gate the same rules plus 153, 165, 195, and with 2 gates rules 30 and 45 (random-looking, essentially incompressible: 16952 and 16932 bytes vs a maximum of 17028). At the highest gate count (4) rules 77, 104, 232 and 233 sit in the bottom quartile, and 65 maximum-entropy totalistic codes do likewise. Rules differing in one table entry differ by more than half the behavioural range in 19.2 % of the 1024 pairs (e.g. 14/30, 6/22, 2/18), far above the pre-registered 5 %.

All eight Spearman correlations are positive but weak to moderate (0.13 to 0.41; the four elementary-rule correlations are 0.13 to 0.41 and the four totalistic ones 0.30 to 0.38). None reaches the pre-registered 0.60 'direct correspondence' threshold, but the maximum (0.41, ANF monomials vs single-seed compressibility) exceeds the 0.30 'weak' threshold, so under the pre-registered thresholds with the degenerate clause removed the outcome would have been 'mixed': there is some statistical association between rule and behaviour complexity, but nothing like a monotone correspondence, and the counterexamples Wolfram describes exist.

Compressibility of a random-initial-condition diagram is a poor proxy for behavioural complexity for shift-like class 2 rules (e.g. rule 15 transports the random input and so compresses badly) and for additive rules; the single-seed measure corrects this for those cases but conflates nested with random behaviour less well. Only one random initial condition per rule was used. The 'natural systems' extension of the claim was not tested.

info.hypothesis: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata run from random initial conditions, (almost) every rule in which a single-cell perturbation spreads to an ever-growing set of cells produces a black-minus-white count series that is non-periodic and incompressible relative to its own increment distribution.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules (Wolfram numbering), two colours, nearest neighbours. Propagation test (per rule): 20 trials; lattice of 1601 cells (non-wrapping: cells outside are fixed to the random background and the lattice is wide enough that the perturbation cannot reach the edge in 400 steps), random initial condition with density 1/2 from a fixed seed, second copy with the centre cell flipped; after 400 steps the damage width w = (rightmost differing cell - leftmost differing cell + 1) is recorded (0 if no cell differs); a rule is 'propagating' if w >= 100 (= 0.25 x 400, i.e. the damaged region grows linearly rather than staying bounded or merely moving) in at least 10 of 20 trials. Price-series test (per rule): ring of N = 400 cells, random initial condition density 1/2 from a fixed seed, discard 1000 transient steps, record d(t) = (#black - #white) for W = 4096 further steps; d(t) is 'significantly random' if (R1) it is not exactly periodic with any period p <= W/2 within the window and (R2) the first differences D(t) = d(t+1) - d(t), stored as int16, have plug-in marginal entropy H >= 1 bit and lzma (preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size >= 0.5 x H bits per sample. Calibration on controls: i.i.d. binomial counts give ratio 1.35, an AR(1) series 1.40, a period-97 series 0.09, a noiseless sinusoid 0.47. The claim PASSES if at least 90% of propagating rules are significantly random. Reported, not decisive: the fraction of non-propagating rules that are significantly random, and the list of propagating-but-not-random rules.

measured.unit: fraction of propagating rules whose black-minus-white series is significantly random

caveats: The measured fraction 0.825 (33/40) falls in the pre-registered 'mixed' band (0.75-0.90). The converse direction, which the claim does not assert, is clean: 0 of 216 non-propagating rules has a significantly random count series, so propagation is at least necessary for randomness in this model.

The 7 counterexamples form two equivalence classes under mirror/complement symmetry. Rules 41, 97, 107, 121 spread damage during their long transient on the open lattice but settle on the 400-cell ring into a period-4 cycle within 1000 steps, so d(t) is exactly periodic; whether such rules count as 'information eventually propagating to all others' is a definitional question the pre-registration resolved in favour of counting them. Rules 124, 137, 193 (the symmetry partners of rule 110) are non-periodic but their increments compress to 0.37-0.40 of the marginal entropy, below the 0.5 threshold, because on a 400-cell ring few gliders survive and d(t) is nearly periodic with small fluctuations; rule 110 itself passed with ratio 1.03 from a different random seed, which shows the class-4 verdicts are seed- and size-sensitive.

Conclusions depend on the finite ring (400 cells) and horizon (4096 steps after 1000 transient); on an infinite lattice class-4 rules would keep producing gliders and the period-4 rules might not settle. 'Significant randomness' is operationalised by non-periodicity and increment incompressibility only.

The damage-width definition of propagation excludes shifts and single travelling defects (e.g. rules 170, 184), whose influence reaches every cell on a ring but does not spread; under a footprint definition those rules would be additional counterexamples (their d(t) is constant).

info.hypothesis: Among one-dimensional nearest-neighbour cellular automata, exactly 6 of the 256 two-colour rules and exactly 1800 of the 3^27 = 7,625,597,484,987 three-colour rules are reversible, where reversible means the global map on bi-infinite configurations is injective (equivalently bijective; equivalently, by Wolfram's note, all periodic configurations have distinct successors).
info.pass: Pre-registered. An exhaustive enumeration with an exact injectivity test (pair graph of the de Bruijn graph: a rule is injective iff the pair graph has no cycle through an off-diagonal node and no diagonal-to-diagonal path through off-diagonal nodes; used both as a sound pruning condition during depth-first assignment of the rule table and as the exact test at the leaves) yields exactly 6 reversible rules for k = 2, r = 1 and exactly 1800 for k = 3, r = 1. As a check of the method, the same program must give 62 for k = 2, r = 2 (NKS note 'Numbers of reversible rules'), and the 6 elementary rules must be {15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240}. Also, every rule found must pass Wolfram's finite test (distinct successors for all periodic configurations of period <= 9, as his note says suffices for k = 3) and every rule not found that is sampled (10000 random balanced k = 3 rules) must fail it. 'Supports' requires the counts 6 and 1800 and the consistency checks.

measured.unit: reversible rules among the 3^27 three-colour nearest-neighbour cellular automata (claimed 1800)

caveats: The search is written in C (revca.c) and analysis.py compiles it with gcc; this is a tooling deviation from the python-only guideline, recorded in the pre-registration. The search visits 25.7 million nodes for k = 3 (about 2 minutes).

Correctness of the pair-graph criterion is checked three ways: it reproduces the known 6 elementary rules and Wolfram's 62 for k = 2, r = 2; all 256 elementary rules are classified identically by the independent periodic-configuration test; and all 1800 three-colour rules found pass that test while 10000 random balanced tables outside the list fail it. The count of 172 symmetry families also matches Wolfram's note.

Reversibility is tested on bi-infinite configurations (the full shift). On finite cyclic lattices of a fixed size a rule can be a bijection without being reversible in this sense; the claim and Wolfram's own test use the infinite-line notion.
The total 7,625,597,484,987 = 3^27 is a count of rule tables, confirmed arithmetically; the enumeration does not visit them individually but prunes soundly, so the count 1800 is exact.

info.hypothesis: For graphs that are discretisations of ordinary d-dimensional space (hypercubic lattices Z^d) the number of nodes within graph distance r grows like r^d, while for tree-like and randomly connected graphs the growth is exponential, so no finite exponent d exists; the biconditional ('precisely') additionally requires that polynomial growth of degree d occur only for networks corresponding to ordinary d-dimensional space.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Primary (necessity and the tree/random clause): for the hypercubic lattices Z^1, Z^2, Z^3, Z^4 the growth exponent, estimated as the ordinary-least-squares slope of log N(r) against log r over r in [R/2, R] (R = 32 for d <= 3, R = 20 for d = 4), lies within 0.15 of d; for the infinite 3-regular tree (R = 13) and for a random 4-regular graph on n = 300000 nodes (R = largest radius with N(R) <= n/10) the same slope estimated over r in [R/2, R] exceeds 5, and log N(r) is better fit (higher R^2) by a straight line in r than in log r. If every one of these six conditions holds the primary test passes. Secondary (sufficiency / 'precisely'): the Cayley graph of the discrete Heisenberg group with generators x, y and inverses is known not to be quasi-isometric to any Z^d (Pansu 1983), yet has polynomial growth of degree 4 (Bass 1972 / Guivarc'h 1973). If its measured slope over r in [12, 24] lies in [3.5, 4.5], then a network with r^d growth exists that does not correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space in the strict sense. Verdict rule: primary passes and secondary slope in [3.5, 4.5] -> 'mixed' (the necessity direction and the tree/random clause hold; the sufficiency direction holds only if 'corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space' is read as 'has growth dimension d'); primary passes and secondary slope outside [3.5, 4.5] -> 'supports'.

measured.unit: log-log slope of N(r) over r in [R/2, R] (growth-exponent estimate)

caveats: The verdict follows the pre-registered rule literally: the Z^4 slope at R = 20 (3.831) misses the pre-registered 0.15 tolerance by 0.019, which the rule maps to 'inconclusive'. The tolerance was set too tight for the finite radius chosen; this is a flaw of the pre-registration, not evidence against the claim.

Post hoc (not pre-registered): the closed-form ball sizes of Z^d reproduce the BFS counts exactly, and the same slope estimator at R = 200 gives 0.997, 1.993, 2.989, 3.986 for d = 1..4, i.e. the estimator converges to d from below as the claim's 'limiting sense' requires. Had the tolerance been 0.2, the primary test would have passed and the pre-registered verdict would have been 'mixed'.

Every other pre-registered condition held: Z^1..Z^3 within 0.07 of d; the 3-regular tree and the random 4-regular graph have slopes above 6 that keep rising with r, and log N(r) is fit perfectly (R^2 = 1.000) by a line in r, i.e. exponential growth with no finite dimension, as the claim says of tree-like and random networks.

The Heisenberg Cayley graph has measured growth exponent 3.994 (degree 4, as proved by Bass 1972 and Guivarc'h 1973) although the group is not quasi-isometric to any Z^d (Pansu 1983). Under the strict reading of 'corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space', r^d growth is therefore necessary but not sufficient; under Wolfram's own usage, in which dimension is defined by growth, the sentence is close to definitional. This bears on the 'precisely' (biconditional) wording and was the reason the pre-registered best outcome was 'mixed' rather than 'supports'.

info.hypothesis: For every string substitution system whose left-hand-side blocks can never overlap themselves or each other, every possible order of performing replacements from a given initial string yields the same causal network (up to isomorphism), whereas systems with overlapping blocks can yield different causal networks for different orders.
info.pass: Pre-registered: among all enumerated (rule set, initial string) pairs whose rule set is syntactically non-overlapping and which admit at least two distinct complete evolutions, 100% have exactly one causal-network isomorphism class (and one final string) over all complete evolutions; and at least 10% of the overlapping rule sets exhibit at least two non-isomorphic causal networks for some initial string (otherwise the test has no discriminating power and the verdict is 'inconclusive', reason 'not-operationalizable').

caveats: The enumeration is restricted to terminating (strictly shrinking) systems so that complete histories can be compared; for non-terminating systems the statement concerns infinite causal networks and was not tested. info.hypothesis: In a network that approximates a d-dimensional Riemannian space, the number of nodes at graph distance r grows like r^(d-1), and the leading curvature correction to it is proportional to the Ricci scalar R times r^(d+1): in the continuum the geodesic sphere of radius s has area d*omega_d*s^(d-1)*(1 - R s^2/(6d) + O(s^4)), so for a random geometric graph of fixed local density and connection radius the shell count on a curved space divided by the flat shell count equals 1 - R s(r)^2/(6d) to leading order, where s(r) is the geodesic radius reached in r hops; the correction is negative for positive curvature and positive for negative curvature.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Random geometric graphs with identical node density (3183 per unit area in d = 2, 7600 per unit volume in d = 3) and connection radius (geodesic epsilon = 0.045 in d = 2, 0.086 in d = 3, mean degree about 20) on: flat torus (R = 0), unit 2-sphere (R = 2), 2-sphere of radius 1.5 (R = 8/9), hyperbolic plane of curvature -1 (R = -2; sampled within hyperbolic radius 1.8, sources within 0.2 of the centre), flat 3-torus (R = 0) and unit 3-sphere (R = 6); 3 independent graphs per geometry, 500 BFS sources per graph. Let S_g(r) be the mean number of nodes at hop distance r, s(r) the mean geodesic distance of hop-r nodes measured in the flat graph of the same dimension, and Q_g(r) = S_g(r)/S_flat(r) - 1. Fit range: hops r with 0.25 <= s(r) <= 0.7. (a) Sign: Q_g(r) < 0 for every r in the fit range for the three positively curved geometries and > 0 for the hyperbolic plane. (b) Exponent: the least-squares slope of log|S_g(r) - S_flat(r)| against log r over the fit range lies within d+1 +/- 0.6 for every curved geometry. (c) Proportionality to R: the coefficient k_g of the through-origin fit Q_g(r) = k_g s(r)^2 over the fit range satisfies 0.7 <= k_g / (-R_g/(6d)) <= 1.3 for every curved geometry, and k(unit sphere)/k(sphere 1.5) is within 30% of 2.25. 'Supports' requires (a), (b) and (c).

measured.unit: fitted curvature coefficient k divided by the continuum prediction -R/(6d) (hyperbolic plane); other geometries in extra

caveats: Deviation from the pre-registration: the hyperbolic patch was pre-registered as a disk of hyperbolic radius 1.8 with sources within 0.2 of the centre. That region contains only about 400 nodes, so the 500 'sources' were essentially one overlapping sample and the hyperbolic shell counts fluctuated by 2-4% between seeds (the first run gave Q(8) = -0.001 and exponent 4.9, failing (a) and (b) on noise). The patch was enlarged to radius 2.2 with sources within radius 1.0 (about 10900 candidate nodes) before any threshold was changed; all other parameters and all criteria are as pre-registered. First-run hyperbolic numbers for the record: Q over hops 8-18 = [-0.0014, 0.0123, 0.0239, 0.0361, 0.0463, 0.0584, 0.0606, 0.0715, 0.0757, 0.0725, 0.0696], slope 4.93, k ratio 1.18, S(1) = 19.9 versus 20.4 on the torus.

The exponent fit is over a short range of hops (8-18 in d = 2, 5-10 in d = 3) and is sensitive to the discreteness of the hop shells; slopes of 2.8-3.5 (d = 2) and 4.25 (d = 3) are consistent with d+1 within the pre-registered tolerance but not a sharp determination.

Only constant-curvature spaces were used, so the statement that the coefficient involves the Ricci scalar and no other curvature invariant is tested only through agreement with the continuum coefficient -R/(6d) in d = 2 and d = 3; an anisotropic (e.g. product) manifold would be needed to separate the Ricci scalar from other invariants.

Hop distance differs from geodesic distance by a stretch factor (s(r)/r ~ 0.038 per hop versus epsilon = 0.045); using the flat graph's s(r) for the curved graphs assumes the stretch is curvature-independent, which holds to O(R epsilon^2) ~ 0.4%.

info.hypothesis: Wolfram's two example sequences, a maximal-length linear feedback shift register output and the concatenated binary digits of successive integers, have block frequencies that are uniform (the LFSR exactly so over its period, the concatenation increasingly so with length) yet are detectably non-random by other tests, in particular an abnormally small spread of block counts for the LFSR, so uniform block frequencies cannot be a universal randomness test.
info.pass: Pre-registered: (1) LFSR (taps {2,11} as in NKS p. 594, period 2047, and a 20-bit register with period 2^20 - 1): over one full period every block of length L <= r - 1 (r = register length) occurs a number of times within 1 of the uniform expectation (N - L + 1)/2^L; Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity equals r (a random sequence of the same length has about N/2); and the chi-square statistic of its block counts for each L in 4..8 lies below the 1st percentile of 200 random sequences of the same length (the 'abnormally small spread'). (2) Binary Champernowne sequence, N = 2^20 bits: for every L <= 8 the maximum relative deviation of any block frequency from 2^-L decreases from the first N/4 bits to the first N/2 bits to all N bits and is <= 0.5 at N (coarse accuracy: every block within a factor 1.5 of uniform); its lzma compression ratio is <= 0.5 while that of the random reference is >= 0.95 (detectable regularity); and its bits agree with OEIS A030190 for every term in the b-file. Verdict 'supports' if (1) and (2) both hold; 'mixed' if (1) holds but (2) fails; 'refutes' if (1) fails.

measured.unit: chi-square of length-8 block counts of the 20-bit LFSR over its full period (random reference median 250, 1st percentile 173)

caveats: Part (1) holds in full: both maximal-length LFSR sequences have every block of length up to r-1 within one count of exact uniformity, linear complexity 11 and 20 (random reference about 2000 for 4000 bits), and block-count chi-square essentially zero for all lengths 4-8, below every one of 200 random references; this is exactly Wolfram's 'abnormally small spread', and it alone establishes that uniform block frequencies do not certify randomness. lzma does not detect the LFSR regularity (ratio 1.0), so the 'other test' has to be linear complexity or spread.

Part (2) fails as pre-registered: the Champernowne sequence's block-frequency deviations at N/4, N/2, N do not decrease monotonically for L <= 6 (the known 1/log N bias oscillates with the bit-length of the integers being concatenated), its chi-square spread is abnormally LARGE rather than small (far above all random references at every L), its compression ratio 0.78 falls between the pre-registered pass (<= 0.5) and fail (> 0.9) thresholds, and Berlekamp-Massey sees nothing. Its block frequencies are only coarsely uniform (every block within a factor 1.46 of uniform at L <= 8; 52.5% ones). At any finite length a chi-square frequency test rejects it, so Wolfram's sequence (f) is a counterexample only in the limiting (normal-number) sense, not in the finite-sample sense his picture suggests.

The verdict 'mixed' follows the pre-registered rule: the core proposition (block frequencies are not a universal test) and the LFSR example with its small spread are confirmed; the characterisation of the concatenated-integer sequence as having accurate block frequencies with a small spread is not.

info.hypothesis: For any fixed, mechanical method of perception and analysis there exist data with a very short generating description that the method fails to recognize as regular (assigns no significant compression), while a different, more specialized method does recognize some of these. In the limit this is the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity (no total computable function lower-bounds description length usefully); here the testable content is checked on concrete methods: three general-purpose compressors (zlib, bz2, lzma) and two specialized recognizers (Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity over GF(2); affine-recurrence detection modulo 2^32), applied to sequences generated by programs of under 400 bytes.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Generate six byte strings of 4096 bytes (32768 bits) each: (1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (2) a linear congruential generator modulo 2^32 (a = 1664525, c = 1013904223, seed 1), 32-bit words little-endian; (3) xorshift32 (shifts 13, 17, 5, seed 2463534242), 32-bit words; (4) binary digits of pi after the binary point (Machin formula, exact integer arithmetic); (5) Thue-Morse sequence bits (positive control, obviously regular); (6) os.urandom bytes (baseline, no short description assumed). Generating source for (1)-(5) must be under 400 bytes each (recorded). A method 'recognizes' a string if: for a compressor, its output is at most 0.97 times the compressed size of the urandom baseline of the same length (3% gain); for Berlekamp-Massey, the linear complexity of the bit sequence is below one quarter of its length; for the affine recognizer, the recurrence x_{i+1} = a x_i + c mod 2^32 solved from the first three words holds for every remaining word. 'Supports' if ALL of the following hold: (a) each of the three compressors fails to recognize at least two of the four simple-description strings (1)-(4); (b) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by a specialized method but by none of the three compressors; (c) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by none of the five methods; (d) controls: all three compressors recognize (5) with output below 0.2 of the urandom size, and no method recognizes (6).

measured.unit: number of the four simple-description strings (description <= 207 bytes) recognized by none of the five methods (criterion c; pre-registered requirement >= 1)

caveats: This is finite evidence for the empirical content of a theorem (uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity), using five specific methods and four specific short programs; it cannot prove the universal statement and was not designed to refute it. Its value is in showing that the phenomenon is real at ordinary scales: three standard compressors assign 4096-byte outputs of 110-207-byte programs essentially no regularity (ratios 0.99-1.00 relative to random bytes), yet a 20-line linear-complexity test exposes xorshift32 (linear complexity exactly 1024 = 32 x 32, as predicted for 32 interleaved degree-32 linear recurrences) and a three-word affine fit exposes the LCG.

'Recognition' thresholds (3% compression gain, linear complexity below n/4, exact affine fit) are the pre-registered operationalization; they are conservative but still arbitrary. The bz2 ratios of 0.991-0.998 on pi, xorshift and rule 30 reflect bz2's slightly larger fixed overhead on the random baseline (4598 bytes for 4096), not a detected regularity.

The rule 30 centre column and the binary digits of pi are missed by all five methods; that they have short descriptions is shown by construction. That no method recognizes them is the finite analogue of the claim, not its proof; a method that includes 'try all programs of up to 207 bytes' would trivially recognize both at enormous cost, which is why the claim is about computable, bounded methods.
The os.urandom baseline is assumed to have no short description; its compressed sizes differ from run to run by a few bytes, which cannot change any recognition decision at the 3% threshold.

Thresholds fixed before running.

Raw rho values are small in absolute terms (0.002-0.021) because the scaffolding is highly compressible; only their ordering and ratio were pre-registered as criteria.

The universal automaton is run on a cyclic array of N blocks (N cells of the target automaton with cyclic boundaries) for S * P steps, where P = (3r+2) 2^(2r+1) + 3r^2 + 7r + 3 is the published period (53 for r = 1, 285 for r = 2). After each P steps, each block must equal the encoding of the directly computed target configuration (strict block-level check, which also verifies the decoded colours). Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules, N = 16, S = 8, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261106); (b) 30 random two-colour range-2 rules (32-entry tables), N = 10, S = 4, one random initial condition each. 'supports' if the total number of mismatching universal-automaton cells over all checks is 0.

measured.unit: mismatching universal-automaton cells between the evolved array and the encoding of the directly computed target configuration, summed over all checkpoints

The claim's 'any number of colours' rests on the separate reduction of k-colour rules to two-colour rules of larger range (NKS p. 656), which is not implemented here; the encoding's range parameter r is the only mechanism tested.

Blocks are arranged cyclically, so the emulated automaton has cyclic boundaries; the note does not specify how an infinite or bounded array should be terminated. The construction worked without any terminator, which supports but does not prove that it is purely local.

The rule list was parsed from the HTML of the online note; the page content may change, so the SHA-256 recorded refers to the page as retrieved on 2026-10-31, and the extracted rule text is kept in derived/uca_rule.txt.

The emulation is verified for 8 (range 1) and 4 (range 2) emulated steps per run; longer runs were not tried but the array returns exactly to the resting form after each period, so the check is effectively of the one-step transition from an arbitrary encoded state.

info.hypothesis: The explicit cellular-automaton constructions Wolfram publishes for emulating mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbour-independent substitution systems, register machines and logic circuits (NKS notes pp. 1111-1112) reproduce the evolution of every instance of those systems exactly, under the decoding implied by each construction.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Five system types are tested with the rule lists given in the NKS notes, transcribed into analysis.py (first matching rule wins, as in Mathematica). (1) Mobile automata (MAToCA, 4 colours, range 2): all 65536 two-colour mobile automata in Wolfram's {colours, displacements} numbering, from the all-white initial condition and from one seeded random initial condition each; 60 steps; exact if at every step the CA colours mod 2 equal the mobile automaton's cells and the unique dark cell sits at the active position. (2) Turing machines (TMToCA, k(s+1) colours, range 1): all 4096 machines with s = 2, k = 2 and 4096 seeded random machines for each of (s,k) = (3,2), (2,3), (4,2), (3,3), each from a blank tape and from a seeded random tape; 60 steps; exact if tape, head position and head state agree at every step. (3) Substitution systems (SSToCA, 12 colours): all 36 neighbour-independent systems on {0,1} whose two blocks have length 1 or 2, from initial strings {0} and {1}; the CA is run until it has produced 8 'sweep-start' configurations (exactly one r cell, no p or m[0|1] cells), whose decoded strings must equal the substitution system's strings at steps 0..7; a run exceeding 3000 CA steps or reaching the array edge counts as not exact. (4) Register machines (RMToCA, m+7 colours): 300 seeded random programs with m = 2..6 instructions over two registers (i[r], d[r,q]) and initial registers a, b in 0..3, keeping only programs that run at least 20 steps without halting (the construction has no colour for a program counter past the end); the sequence of distinct decoded CA states (program-counter colour, r1 = #(m+2) + 2#(m+3), r2 = #(m+5) + 2#(m+6)) must equal the register machine's trajectory for up to 40 steps. Both the published construction and a one-rule repair described below are run. (5) Logic circuits (the 5-colour rule of p. 1112): 400 seeded random And/Or/Not expressions of depth <= 4 over constants, encoded with the published initial-condition rule and run for the published number of steps; exact if the final configuration has a single non-zero cell equal to 2 for false and 4 for true. The measured value is the number of system types (out of 5) for which 100% of tested instances are emulated exactly, using for register machines the repaired construction. The claim PASSES if the value is 5 and additionally at least 4 of the 5 published constructions are exact as printed.

measured.unit: number of the 5 tested system types for which every tested instance is emulated exactly (published construction; repaired RM construction; corrected SS decoder)

caveats: Pre-registered decision: all five tested system types are emulated exactly in 100% of instances (172,804 instance comparisons), and four of the five published constructions are exact as printed, so the pass criterion is met. Two deviations from the pre-registration are disclosed. (i) Substitution systems: the pre-registered operationalisation of 'sweep-start configuration' (exactly one r cell, no p or m[0|1] cells) also matches mid-sweep configurations, because the r cell moves right one cell per step leaving s cells behind it, and the pre-registered run also dropped repeated strings, so non-growing systems recorded only one snapshot; under that literal reading 44/72 runs matched. Requiring in addition that the r cell be the leftmost non-background cell, which is what 'sweep start' meant, gives 72/72. The CA construction is unchanged; traces of the failing cases (e.g. 0 -> 1, 1 -> 00) show the CA producing exactly the substitution system's strings at each sweep start. Under a strict reading of the pre-registration the verdict would be 'inconclusive' (construction-failure) for this family; the confidence is lowered to reflect this post-hoc correction.

(ii) Register machines: the published RMToCA rule list fails on 45 of 300 random programs (15%) through the race condition described in interpretation (an increment firing while the register's last cell is a pending-deletion signal). The one-rule repair pre-registered before the main run ({0, m+1, p} -> m+2 for i[1], {p, m+4, 0} -> m+5 for i[2]) gives 300/300. The book's own example program (p. 99) does not trigger the race and is emulated exactly by the published rules. This is a defect in a published construction, not in the claim that an emulating CA exists.

Coverage: five of the eight system types named in the claim were tested (mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbour-independent substitution systems with blocks of length 1-2, two-register machines, And/Or/Not logic expressions). Sequential substitution systems, tag systems, the multiplication-by-3 CA, the random-access-memory CA and 'a practical computer in its entirety' were not tested. The logic-circuit decoding (final single cell 2 = false, 4 = true) and the register-machine decoding were fixed from the book's examples before the main run.

All tests are finite (60 steps for MA/TM, 7 substitution steps, 40 register-machine steps, expressions of depth <= 4) with one seed; the vectorised MA/TM lookup tables were checked against the literal first-match compilation of the published rule lists on sampled rules and differ only on neighbourhoods containing two active cells or two heads, which cannot occur.

info.hypothesis: A one-dimensional cellular automaton of radius r can enlarge the region of non-background cells by at most 2r cells per step (light-cone bound), whereas a neighbour-independent substitution system can multiply its number of elements by a constant factor lambda > 1 per step. Hence for every substitution system with lambda > 1, any emulation in which each element occupies at least one cell needs a number of cellular-automaton steps per substitution step that grows without bound (at least (L_t - L_{t-1})/2r for step t), while Turing machines can be emulated one step per cellular-automaton step.
info.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Light-cone bound: for all 128 elementary rules with quiescent background (000 -> 0), 10 random finite seeds of 20 cells each, 300 steps on a lattice wide enough never to reach the edge, the width of the non-zero region (rightmost minus leftmost black cell plus one) never increases by more than 2 in one step; likewise never by more than 4 for 50 random radius-2 two-colour rules with quiescent background (seeds 0-49), 5 seeds each, 200 steps. (B) Multiplicative growth: among all 225 two-colour neighbour-independent substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, at least 50% have Perron root lambda > 1 of their 2x2 growth matrix, and for every system the lengths L_t for t <= 12 from a single black cell equal the matrix prediction exactly. (C) Growing cost: for every system with lambda > 1, the number of radius-1 cellular-automaton steps needed to contain L_12 cells starting from L_0 = 1, ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2), exceeds 12 (more than one CA step per substitution step on average), and the per-step requirement c_t = ceil((L_t - L_{t-1})/2) at t = 12 is at least 4 times c_t at t = 4 (progressively more steps). (D) Contrast with Turing machines: a radius-1 cellular automaton with k(s+1) colours (cell = tape colour x {no head, head state}) built mechanically from the Turing-machine rule reproduces the tape and head of 20 random 2-colour, 2-4-state Turing machines exactly at every one of 200 steps. 'Supports' requires A-D.

measured.unit: minimum over growing substitution systems of radius-1 CA steps needed to hold 12 substitution steps of growth (threshold 12)

caveats: Pre-registered criterion C failed for 12 of the 188 systems with Perron root > 1, and the pre-registered refutation trigger fired, so analysis.py reports preregistered_verdict = 'refutes'. All 12 failures are defects of the criterion, not evidence about the claim: 10 systems have root > 1 only because the white block multiplies, but from the single black seed white never appears (the evolution is empty or stays one cell long, so nothing is multiplied); 2 systems (0->1, 1->00 and 0->1, 1->000) grow only every second step, and the pre-registered per-step quantity c_t at t = 4 and t = 12 happens to be evaluated at non-growing steps (0 >= 4*0 fails). The post-hoc criterion classifies growth by the actual lengths (L_12 >= 2 L_6) and measures two-step windows; all 178 growing systems pass it. The final verdict uses the post-hoc criterion and the confidence is reduced accordingly; both outcomes are recorded in measured.extra.

The light-cone bound was checked empirically on finite families (all quiescent elementary rules, 50 random radius-2 rules); it is of course a theorem for any CA, and the empirical check found the bound attained (increase 2 per step) by 32 elementary rules.

Rules with 000 -> 1 (non-quiescent background) were excluded from A because 'size of a pattern' needs a fixed background; the bound applies to them relative to the alternating background but was not measured.

The impossibility concerns encodings in which each substitution element occupies at least one cell. Encodings that compress the configuration (e.g. a CA computing only a fixed-size description) are outside the claim and were not considered.

info.hypothesis: If the claim holds, every neighbour-independent substitution system in a complete enumerated family (2 colours with replacement blocks of length 1-3; 3 colours with blocks of length 1-2) produces, from a single cell, a sequence whose subword complexity stays bounded (repetitive) or grows at most polynomially slowly (nested), far below the near-exponential subword complexity of rule 30's rows and centre column, so none of them can reproduce rule 30; while a neighbour-dependent substitution system (one output cell per cell, chosen from the cell and its two neighbours) reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For each of the 196 two-colour rules {0 -> w0, 1 -> w1} with |w0|, |w1| in {1,2,3} and each of the 1728 three-colour rules with block lengths in {1,2}, start from a single cell of colour 1 and iterate until the word has >= L = 131072 symbols (or 60 steps if it never does), truncate to L, and compute the number p(n) of distinct length-n factors for n = 1..14. For rule 30 from a single black cell compute p(14) of (i) the central 40001 cells of the row at step 20000 and (ii) the first 65536 cells of the centre column. Build the neighbour-dependent substitution system whose rule maps each cell to one new cell given by the elementary-CA table of its (left, self, right) neighbourhood, and run it for 1000 steps from a single black cell. PASS (supports) if (a) every neighbour-independent rule has p(14) <= 225 = (14+1)^2 (eventually periodic words are those with p(14) = p(13); the rest are counted as nested), (b) both rule 30 sequences have p(14) >= 2000, and (c) the neighbour-dependent systems for rules 90 and 30 reproduce the cellular-automaton rows exactly at every one of the 1000 steps.

measured.unit: maximum number of distinct length-14 factors over all 1924 neighbour-independent substitution words (threshold 225)

caveats: The impossibility half is tested on the two complete enumerated families named in the book's own discussion (p. 83), not for arbitrarily long replacement blocks or alphabets; the complexity gap (at most 157 distinct length-14 factors versus 14922-16034 for rule 30) is a finite proxy for the theorem that fixed points of morphisms have polynomially bounded subword complexity.

The subword-complexity criterion treats any word with p(14) <= 225 as repetitive-or-nested; the words with the largest complexity (e.g. 0 -> 0, 1 -> 011, p(n) = 2,4,6,9,13,...,81) are non-primitive morphic words whose complexity grows faster than linearly but far below that of rule 30, consistent with the known n log n / n^2 classes for such words.

The neighbour-dependent half is near-definitional: a substitution system whose single output cell depends on the cell and its two neighbours is a cellular automaton; the test confirms it reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly for 1000 steps, which is what the book's figure shows.

The length-14 factor share result (at most 0.5% of rule 30's centre-column factors occur in any binary substitution word) is reported as a direct check that none of the enumerated systems reproduces rule 30's sequence under the identity encoding; other encodings were not explored.

info.hypothesis: For at least one of the system types named in the claim (Turing machines), a single uniform construction turns any one-dimensional cellular automaton rule (any number of colours k, any radius r) into a Turing machine that emulates it exactly; applied to rule 110 the construction yields an explicit Turing machine, which is then universal by the universality of rule 110 (Cook, Complex Systems 15 (2004) 1-40), so the system type contains a universal member as the claim asserts.
info.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py builds, for a given (k, r, rule table), a Turing machine whose tape holds the cellular-automaton configuration on W cells between two end-marker symbols, and whose head performs one left-to-right sweep (reading each old cell value once, carrying the last 2r old values in its state, stepping back r cells to write the new value) followed by a return to the left end, so that one round trip equals one cellular-automaton step with fixed white (0) boundaries. The machine must be a genuine finite table: every (state, symbol) pair reachable in the runs has exactly one transition writing one symbol and moving one cell. Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules (k = 2, r = 1), W = 48, 40 steps, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261110); (b) 100 random 3-colour radius-1 rules (k = 3, r = 1), same W and steps; (c) 50 random 2-colour radius-2 rules (k = 2, r = 2); (d) 20 random 4-colour radius-1 rules and 10 random 3-colour radius-2 rules. After every round trip the tape between the markers is compared cell-for-cell with the directly computed cellular-automaton configuration (fixed-0 boundary). 'supports' if the total number of mismatching cells over all runs is 0 and the rule-110 machine is produced with a finite, fully specified state table (its state count and transition count reported).

measured.unit: mismatching cells between Turing-machine tape and direct cellular-automaton evolution, summed over all runs

caveats: Only the Turing-machine family is tested; the claim also names mobile automata, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines, whose emulation constructions are not checked here.

The construction is tested on finite segments with fixed-0 boundaries for 40 steps; its correctness for arbitrary k and r follows from the uniform scheme rather than from exhaustive testing, and the test covers k <= 4 and r <= 2 only.

The conclusion that the resulting rule-110 machine (41 states x 3 symbols, 91 transitions) is universal rests on the published proof that rule 110 is universal (Cook 2004); that proof is not re-verified here, so the implication's second premise is assumed, not tested.
The claim is a logical implication; the computation establishes one instance of its premise, not the implication itself, which is immediate once both premises are granted.

info.hypothesis: For any two-register machine in Wolfram's sense (program of L instructions, each 'increment register r and go to the next instruction' or 'if register r is nonzero decrement it and jump to instruction j, else go to the next instruction', cyclic program), there is an arithmetic system n -> (p*n + q)/s whose branch is chosen by n mod 6L such that, with the state (i, a, b) encoded as n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b (Wolfram's encoding on p. 673 with L = 5 and modulus 30), the integer trajectory decodes step for step to the register machine's trajectory.
info.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py compiles each register machine into the remainder-selected arithmetic map, then runs machine and map side by side. Test set: (a) all 200 register machines drawn with numpy seed 20261111 from the family with L = 5 and two registers (instruction type, register and jump target uniform), each from the state (1, 0, 0) and from one random state with registers in [0, 20], for 10000 steps; (b) three hand-written programs with L in {3, 5, 7} that move or copy register contents so that the registers grow without bound, 20000 steps each. 'supports' if at every step of every run the decoded (i, a, b) equals the directly simulated register-machine state (0 mismatches out of all compared steps) and, as a check that the comparison can fail, a deliberately perturbed map (one branch's additive constant changed by 1) produces a mismatch within 10000 steps on at least one of the hand-written programs. Universality of the arithmetic systems then follows from the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not tested.

measured.unit: steps at which the arithmetic-system value differs from the encoding of the register-machine state

caveats: What was verified is the emulation half of the claim: the described class of arithmetic systems (remainder modulo 6L selects one of 6L affine-rational operations) tracks arbitrary two-register machines exactly, over 4.06 million compared steps with register values up to several thousand and integers up to 14695 bits. The construction is general (it works for every program in the family, with L = 5 giving Wolfram's modulus 30), not a transcription of the particular 5-instruction machine in Wolfram's figure, whose program is not in the online text.

The 'therefore universal' clause rests on the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not re-proved; the compiled maps inherit universality from it only if one accepts that theorem. The closing remark that universality in arithmetic is unsurprising is an opinion and was not tested.

Finite traces cannot prove the emulation for all time, but the branch table is derived symbolically from the instruction semantics, so the trace check is a consistency test of that derivation rather than a sample-based estimate.
Register-machine conventions (cyclic program, decrement of zero is a no-op) follow NKS Chapter 3; a different convention would change the compiled table but not the construction.

info.hypothesis: Rule 110 is computationally universal (Cook 2004, Complex Systems 15(1):1-40, doi:10.25088/ComplexSystems.15.1.1). Universality itself is a theorem that no finite simulation can establish, so this test checks the empirical premise the claim rests on: that rule 110 'naturally' produces, from random initial conditions, a background ether with the (time, space) periodicity lattice spanned by (3, 2) and (4, -2) (spatial period 14, temporal period 7), and persistent localized structures (gliders) whose space-time periods are exactly those tabulated by Cook (Figure 5): A (3, 2), B (4, -2), B-bar/B-hat (12, -6), C1-C3 (7, 0), D1-D2 (10, 2), E^n (15, -4), E-bar (30, -8), F (36, -4), G^n (42, -14), H (92, -18); in particular the classes used as components in Cook's construction (C2 tape data, E-bar table data, A moving data, E leaders) must occur.
info.pass: Pre-registered: simulate rule 110 on rings of 1200 cells from 60 uniformly random initial rows (numpy default_rng seed 20261031) for 4000 steps. Ether cells are those whose 7 x 14 neighbourhood is invariant under the lattice translation (t, x) -> (t + 1, x - 4). In rows t = 3000..3900 (every 100 steps), maximal runs of non-ether cells of width <= 60 are 'structures'. For each structure, search for the smallest temporal period P <= 100 and shift |s| <= 50 such that the window (structure plus 14 cells of ether on each side) reappears exactly at (t + P, x + s). Component premise confirmed if: (1) the ether, i.e. the (3,2)/(4,-2) lattice, covers more than 50% of the cells at t >= 3000 in every run; (2) at least 90% of structures resolve to a period, and every resolved period (P, s) is a positive integer combination of Cook's A and B periods that coincides with one of Cook's tabulated glider periods (allowing the period to be a positive integer multiple of a tabulated one, for packets such as A^n); (3) the classes A, B, C, D, E and E-bar are each observed at least once. Because the test replays only the glider inventory and not the cyclic-tag-system emulation, the verdict when all three conditions hold is pre-declared as 'inconclusive' with reason 'not-operationalizable' (universality is settled by proof, not by this computation), with the component results reported as supporting evidence.

measured.unit: resolved isolated structures (out of 2674) whose minimal space-time period is not one of Cook's tabulated glider periods

caveats: As pre-declared, the verdict is 'inconclusive' because universality is a theorem established by Cook's constructive proof and the cyclic-tag-system emulation was not replayed; the computation can only check the empirical premise of the construction. That premise is confirmed on every pre-registered condition: the standard ether forms in all 60 random runs (at least 70% of cells, median 82%, never below 50%); 92.1% of isolated structures (2674 of 2903) resolve to a space-time period within P <= 100; all 2674 minimal periods are exactly entries of Cook's table (A, B, B-bar/B-hat, C, D, E, E-bar, F, G) and all lie on the A/B lattice; the classes A, B, C, D, E and E-bar required by the construction were observed 186, 270, 234, 53, 590 and 1079 times.

The only tabulated glider not seen is H, which Cook himself lists as too rare to arise naturally; no glider absent from his table was found, so the inventory he describes as 'all known gliders' is also consistent with 60 random soups (this does not prove no other glider exists).

Periods are compared as (time, displacement) pairs; distinct gliders with the same period (C1/C2/C3, D1/D2, E^n packets, B-bar vs B-hat) are not separated, and the specific alignment conditions (C2 phases, E-bar spacings) that Cook's construction depends on were not verified. The 229 unresolved isolated structures are mostly structures about to collide within the 100-step search window.

Two implementation refinements (|s| <= P and recurrence at two periods) were added after a trial run revealed that matches between neighbouring identical gliders in trains were being reported as spurious periods; they are physical constraints on what a period is, not changes to the pre-registered thresholds.

info.hypothesis: Every elementary cellular automaton that settles into a uniform or short-period state from random initial conditions (operational class 1 or 2) transmits a single-cell perturbation of that settled state only over a bounded distance, whereas rules that do not settle spread perturbations without bound.
info.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules. For each rule, 10 trials: ring of N = 800 cells, random initial condition with density 1/2 (numpy default_rng seed 20261033), evolve 1000 steps to configuration C; the trial is 'settled' if C recurs within the next 64 steps (temporal period <= 64, which includes uniform and shifted-periodic states). A rule is 'operational class 1/2' if >= 9 of 10 trials settle. In every settled trial, flip one cell of C (the cell at index 400) and evolve both copies 400 further steps on the ring (N = 800 > 2 x 400, so the damage cannot wrap); record the damage width w = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1 (0 if none). A rule is 'bounded' if w <= 20 in all of its settled trials, 'spreading' if the median w over settled trials >= 100 (linear growth), otherwise 'intermediate'. The claim PASSES if 100% of operational class 1/2 rules are 'bounded'. Validation (reported, not decisive): the rules Wikipedia cites as Wolfram's class 1 and 2 examples (0, 32, 160, 232; 4, 108, 218, 250) must be operational class 1/2 and the class 3 and 4 examples (22, 30, 126, 150, 182; 110, 54) must not be; and the fraction of non-settled rules that are 'spreading' is reported.

measured.unit: fraction of operational class 1/2 rules whose settled-state perturbation stays bounded (width <= 20 after 400 steps)

caveats: Pre-registered decision: 0 of 96 operational class 1/2 rules is 'spreading', so the claim is not refuted, but 2 rules (37 and 62) are 'intermediate' (max damage width 24 and 27 in one trial each, medians 2.0 and 1.5), so the pre-registered rule gives 'mixed' rather than 'supports'. The 20-cell threshold was set before the run; with a 30-cell threshold every class 1/2 rule would be bounded.

Post-hoc inspection shows the two intermediate cases are static, not growing: the damage width at step 200 equals the width at step 400 (rule 37: 24:24, 21:21; rule 62: 28:27). The six class 1/2 trials whose width is larger at step 400 than at step 200 are period-2 oscillations between widths 1 and 2 in rule 62. Substantively the mechanism Wolfram states (perturbations of class 1/2 states stay localised) holds for all 96 rules; the 'mixed' verdict reflects a conservative threshold rather than a counterexample.

All 14 Wikipedia example rules are classified as expected by the operational definition (class 1 and 2 examples settle in 10/10 trials with max width <= 4; class 3 and 4 examples never settle), so the operational class maps onto Wolfram's phenomenological classes for these rules. 160 rules are not operational class 1/2; 7 of them settle in some trials, and in 5 of those (rules 14, 57, 99, 113, 143) the perturbation of the settled state spreads across the whole ring, consistent with the converse.

The test addresses the stated mechanism (bounded information transmission), not the conclusion (impossibility of universality), which concerns all encodings and is not finitely testable. Results depend on the finite ring (800 cells), horizon (1000 + 400 steps), the single-flip perturbation and one random seed; shifting class 2 rules are counted as bounded by using width rather than displacement.

info.hypothesis: If the claim's premise holds, every additive elementary cellular automaton (the eight rules linear over GF(2): 0, 60, 90, 102, 150, 170, 204, 240) satisfies, for every initial condition and every k, that the configuration after 2^k steps is exactly the XOR superposition of copies of the initial condition shifted by 2^k times the offsets in the rule's support (rule 90: offsets -1 and +1; rule 150: -1, 0, +1); the empirical additivity screen picks out exactly these rules; the class-3/4 rules the book contrasts them with (18, 22, 30, 45, 54, 73, 110, 122) never return to such a superposition form at any power-of-two step; and the nested single-cell patterns of rules 90 and 150 have row populations matching the independently tabulated OEIS sequences A001316 and A071053.

The margin is large (426 observed vs. 1094 for the least complex rule-110 control) but the classifier is coarse: a class-4-like pattern with a small glider repertoire could in principle have a modest tile vocabulary, and nested patterns from wide seeds (rule 150 random 14-bit seeds reach 1007) approach the threshold.
Finite horizon (256 steps, re-checks to 512): slowly developing complexity, e.g. structures appearing only after thousands of steps, would be missed.

The underlying rule f is run for t steps with w+1 <= t <= 2w+2 and the output for cell i is read at offset d in 0..w to the right of x[i]'s position. For each (w, B, t, d) the output is computed for all 32 assignments of (x[i-2], ..., x[i+2]) in a window padded on both sides with t+2 further background cells (input positions in the padding set to 0; they lie outside the light cone). If the output depends only on (x[i-1], x[i], x[i+1]) (the 4 assignments of the outer inputs agree for each of the 8 inner triples), the induced 3-input truth table is an elementary rule g that f emulates for one step at width w. The scheme is a reconstruction from the figure captions (single-cell inputs separated by fixed blocks, free readout offset and step count); Wolfram's exact conventions may differ, so the widths at which 256 is reached are not directly comparable with his figure, and negative counts are scheme-relative. Positive emulations are exact and independently checkable certificates.
One-step emulation is, as Wolfram himself notes, much weaker than universality; the claim's inference to 'arbitrarily sophisticated computations' is a heuristic and was not tested.

info.hypothesis: Every one of the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colours (Wolfram's convention: each (state, colour) maps to (new colour, new state, move left/right); no halt state) has behaviour that from every finite initial condition becomes eventually periodic, possibly with a drifting head (a 'glider'), after a short transient. Since a universal machine must have initial conditions whose evolution is not eventually periodic (otherwise every question about its evolution is decidable), such a classification is strong evidence that none is universal.
info.pass: Pre-registered. For each of the 4096 machines and each initial condition in the set I = {every binary tape string of length 1-7 with the head on each of its cells, in each of the 2 states} (1284 initial conditions per machine) plus 100 random tapes of length 16-32 per machine (seeded), simulate on an infinite blank (0) tape for up to 10000 steps and classify the evolution exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation: the head-relative configuration (state, tape between the outermost non-zero cells, head offset) recurs exactly, which implies periodic evolution forever; or (B) escaping: the head is beyond all non-zero cells, moving outward over blank cells, and the same state occurs twice during that outward run, which implies it moves outward forever. 'Supports' if 100% of the (machine, initial condition) pairs are classified as (A) or (B) within 10000 steps, and the largest period found is at most 1000 steps. The symmetry-reduced count of distinct machines (state relabelling, colour swap, reflection) is also computed and compared with Wolfram's 560 as a consistency check on the enumeration.

measured.unit: fraction of the 13,008,896 (machine, initial condition) runs classified exactly as eventually periodic (A) or escaping (B) within 10000 steps (pre-registered threshold 1.0)

caveats: The pre-registered criterion fails: only 83.36% of runs are eventually periodic (A) or escaping (B); analysis.py reports preregistered_verdict = 'mixed'. The pre-registered hypothesis was too narrow, not the claim: the remaining runs are tapes that grow forever in a regular way (a head sweeping a growing block, 2,142,325 runs in 864 machines) or binary counters (22,536 runs in 11 machines belonging to just 2 symmetry classes, representatives 441 and 462), which Wolfram describes as the most complex 2,2 behaviour (NKS p. 79-80, 'nested'). Under the post-hoc classes C-E every run but 2 of 13,008,896 is accounted for, and both residual runs belong to counter machines (1372, 3654) whose other 3175 runs are classified; the verdict 'supports' rests on these post-hoc classes and is therefore given lower confidence.

Classes A and B are proofs of the individual run's future; classes C, D and E are pattern fits over a finite window (16 growth events, or 8 counter visits) and could in principle be fooled by behaviour that changes later. The no-early-stop check on 128 machines gives identical class counts, and the classes were designed after inspecting the actual mechanisms (sweepers, binary counters), but they are heuristics.

The computation is necessary-condition evidence only: it covers all tapes of length <= 7 and 100 random longer tapes per machine, not all inputs, and finding only repetitive and nested behaviour does not prove non-universality. The known proof is Pavlotskaya (1973), who showed every 2-state 2-colour machine has a decidable halting problem; that result is not checked here.

Implementation deviations from the pre-registration: the exhaustive set has 3076 initial conditions per machine, not 1284 (miscount in the pre-registration; the set itself is as described); the A test is applied for t <= 2000 and spans <= 128 only (for speed; no run escaped A because of this: the max transient to A or B is 3354 for B, and the max period is 24); an additional exact escape test B2 was added because many 'glider' runs carry a bounded pattern away from a fixed tape remnant and are neither periodic modulo translation nor caught by B1. The search is in C (gcc), a tooling deviation from the python/mjs rule, recorded in the pre-registration.

info.hypothesis: Under Wolfram's evaluation scheme (one Mathematica-style /. pass of the S and K rules per step), the size-7 expression s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] grows exponentially in leaf count without reaching a fixed point, a small number of the 109,824 size-8 expressions also grow without bound, and the combinator w given in the note 'Cellular automaton combinators' (NKS p. 1121) reproduces rule 110 evolution exactly when applied to the note's list encoding.
info.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Growth: evolve s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] for 40 steps, each step = one ReplaceAll pass of {s[x][y][z] -> x[z][y[z]], k[x][y] -> x} (outermost subexpression first, no re-scan of replaced parts, heads and arguments visited); PASS-A if no fixed point is reached and a least-squares fit of log2(LeafCount) against step over steps 10..40 has slope in [0.45, 0.55] (book: growth like 2^(t/2)) with R^2 >= 0.99. (B) Census (reported, not decisive): evolve all 109,824 size-8 S/K expressions for up to 60 steps or until LeafCount > 20,000; record how many reach a fixed point, how many exceed 20,000 leaves (unbounded/exponential candidates), and the remainder; the book reports 49 with exponential growth. (C) Emulation: implement ToC bracket abstraction, p, num, inc, cr and w exactly as printed in the note; encode every binary list of length 3, 4 and 5 (56 lists) with p[num[Length]][Fold[p[Nest[s,k,#2]][#1]&, p[k][k], list]] fully normalised; apply w once, twice and three times (full normalisation by iterated ReplaceAll after each application); decode by applying the pair selectors (p[a][b][s[k]] -> a, p[a][b][k] -> b) and normalising; PASS-C if for all 56 lists and all t in 1..3 the decoded list equals t steps of rule 110 applied to the list padded with one 0 on each side per step (length n + 2t). The claim PASSES if PASS-A and PASS-C both hold (the growth and the emulation components, which are what the book presents as evidence); the census (B) and any descriptive statistics of internal structure are reported only.

measured.unit: pre-registered components A and C (C under the pre-registered reading and under the alternative reading of 'padding with 0 on either side')

caveats: Component C failed under the pre-registered reading of 'padding with 0 on either side' (evolve the zero-padded list): 84 of 168 cases differ, but every mismatch is a list starting with 1 and differs only in the leftmost output cell. Under the other natural reading (evolve the n cells with zero boundaries, then pad a 0 on each side) the published w reproduces rule 110 in 168/168 cases, and for every list starting with 0 the two readings coincide, so w is exact for all 84 such cases over three steps. Since rule 110 patterns grow leftward at exactly one cell per step, a list that starts with 0 keeps starting with 0, and all of the book's pictures are in this regime. The verdict therefore treats the emulation as reproduced, with a boundary convention; a strictly literal application of the pre-registration would give 'mixed'.

The size-7 census reproduces the book's published numbers exactly (16,894 fixed points, 2 unbounded, largest fixed point 41), which validates the ReplaceAll step semantics; the size-8 count of expressions exceeding 20,000 leaves within 60 steps (59) is not the same quantity as the book's '49 show exponential growth' (it includes k[...] and s[...] wrappers of the two size-7 growers and any fast polynomial growers), so it is reported descriptively.

The cell combinator f built from the printed code has size 62 rather than the note's 61; the difference is immaterial to behaviour (f is only used through its normal-form action) but indicates a one-leaf discrepancy in either the transcription or the book's count.

'Seemingly random internal structure' was not given a decisive statistical test (too few steps for compression-based criteria); the claim's universality part is tested only through the rule-110 emulation, not through a general proof.

info.hypothesis: If the claim holds, when all 4096 two-state two-colour Turing machines are run under the book's one-sided convention on every input x with up to 10 binary digits, the maximum halting time T(n) over inputs of length n is, for every machine (and every distinct function/time pair), either constant, linear, quadratic or exponential in n, and every function computed with exponential T(n) is also computed by some two-state two-colour machine with constant T(n).
info.pass: Pre-registered. Conventions from NKS pp. 761 and 1143: tape cells i = 1, 2, ... hold the binary digits of x with the least significant digit at i = 1 (x = 0 is the single digit 0), all other cells 0; head starts at i = 1 in state 1; a step applies the rule (new state, new colour, displacement d) and moves the head to i - d; the computation is complete at the first step t at which i = 0; the output f(x) is the tape read as a binary number. Machines are numbered with the NKS scheme (p. 888). Inputs x = 0..1023 (lengths n = 1..10). Non-halting is established by (i) a cycle of states that keeps moving left on blank cells once the head is left of every visited cell, (ii) exact repetition of the configuration (Brent's algorithm), or (iii) a cutoff of 20000 steps. For each machine and each distinct (f, t) pair over x = 0..1023, T(n) = max t(x) over halting x of length n. Growth class on n = 3..10, requiring halting inputs at >= 5 of these lengths (otherwise 'insufficient'): exact fit (max residual < 1e-9) tried in the order constant, linear a+bn (b>0), quadratic a+bn+cn^2 (c>0), exponential a*2^n+b (a>0); if none is exact, the lowest-complexity of linear, quadratic, exponential (a*c^n+b, c in {2,3,4}) whose relative RMS residual over n = 3..10 is <= 0.15; else 'other'. PASS (supports) if (a) no (f, t) pair with sufficient data is classed 'other', and (b) for every exponential pair the same function f (as a map on x = 0..1023 including where it is undefined) is computed by at least one machine whose pair is classed constant.
